description: National motorcycle baseline from MSF riding practices: gear, controls, braking, lane position, and hazard avoidance. Helmet laws, lane splitting, and BAC numbers stay in state files because they are not national.

questions.q: MSF uses SEE to mean
options: Search, Evaluate, Execute
Signal, Enter, Escape
Speed, Engine, Emergency
Stop, Exit, Evaluate
questions.explanation: Search for hazards, evaluate what they will do, then execute a smooth action. It replaces the older SIPDE habit.

questions.q: A motorcycle helmet should be
options: Any cap with a brim
DOT-compliant, snug, and fastened
Worn only on highways
Loosened so it can come off in a crash
questions.explanation: A loose helmet flies off. Fasten the strap every time. Eye protection is still required even with a windshield.

questions.q: Minimum protective gear for a ride includes
options: Whatever the passenger wears
Shorts and sandals if it is hot
Jacket, pants, boots, gloves, eyewear, helmet
A helmet and gloves, with any clothes
questions.explanation: Most riders who go down slide. Gear takes the abrasion that skin cannot. A jacket, long pants, over-the-ankle boots, gloves, eye protection, and a helmet.

questions.q: T-CLOCS is a pre-ride check of
options: The passenger's helmet only
Tires, Controls, Lights, Oil, Chassis, Stands
Traffic, Cars, Lanes, Officers, Curves, Signals
Throttle only
questions.explanation: Walk through T-CLOCS before you ride. A soft tire or a loose chain is easier to fix in the driveway. Tires and wheels, Controls, Lights and electrics, Oil and fluids, Chassis, Stands.

questions.q: In a normal stop, most of the stopping power comes from
options: Dragging a foot
The rear brake alone
The front brake
The engine only
questions.explanation: The front brake does roughly 70 percent of the work. Use both brakes together, squeezed and pressed smoothly.

questions.q: If the front wheel locks you should
options: Jump off
Apply the rear brake harder and keep the front locked
Hold the lever until you stop
Release the lever at once, then reapply
questions.explanation: A locked front wheel loses steering and can throw the bike. Rolling rubber can be steered. Release the lever immediately so the wheel can roll, then reapply with less pressure.

questions.q: With motorcycle ABS you should
options: Brake firmly and let ABS work
Use only the rear brake
Pull in the clutch and coast
Pump both brakes
questions.explanation: ABS needs steady pressure. Pumping defeats it. Squeeze and press firmly and hold, letting ABS pulse.

questions.q: You should not brake hard while you swerve because
options: The horn will not work
It can stand the bike up or slide the tire
Swerving requires the rear brake to be locked
The clutch must be dumped
questions.explanation: Separate the two responses. Brake in a straight line, or swerve, then brake once you are straight. Braking and swerving at the same time can stand the bike up or slide the tire.

questions.q: The center of a traffic lane often
options: Is the only legal position
Is the cleanest part of the pavement
Collects oil drips and debris
Is reserved for motorcycles by federal law
questions.explanation: Positions 1 and 3 are the tire tracks. Use the center when you need to be seen or to avoid a hazard on both sides. The left or right tire track is usually a better place to ride.

questions.q: A motorcycle is entitled to
options: The shoulder as its only space
The stripe between lanes
Half a lane next to a car
The full width of a lane
questions.explanation: Do not ride side by side with a car in one lane. Whether lane splitting is legal is a state rule, not a national one.

questions.q: Following distance on a motorcycle should be at least
options: Two seconds, more in bad conditions
Half a car length
Whatever the car behind you accepts
One second
questions.explanation: Two seconds is the dry-pavement minimum. Add time when the surface or the light is worse. Two seconds, and more in a group, at night, or in bad weather.

questions.q: In a staggered group formation
options: Riders pair up side by side in one lane
Riders alternate sides of the lane
Everyone rides the center stripe
The group uses the shoulder
questions.explanation: Staggering gives each rider a space cushion and a way out. Pass and change lanes one at a time. The leader rides in the left track and the next rider rides in the right track, about one second back, with two seconds to the rider directly ahead.

questions.q: Most crashes between a motorcycle and a car happen
options: Only when the motorcycle is parked
On straight rural roads with no intersections
At intersections, often a car turning left
Only at night
questions.explanation: Assume the turning driver does not see you. Slow, cover the brakes, and have an escape path. At intersections, often when a car turns left across the rider.

questions.q: Target fixation means
options: Checking the mirror every five seconds
Focusing on the instrument cluster
Looking through the turn to where you want to go
Staring at a hazard so you steer into it
questions.explanation: You go where you look. Look at the escape path, not at the debris or the cliff.

questions.q: To be seen in traffic you should
options: Use your headlight, bright gear, and position
Ride in blind spots so you are close
Weave continuously
Ride with the headlight off to save the battery
questions.explanation: Conspicuity helps. It does not replace an escape path. Do not sit in another driver's blind spot. Use the headlight, bright gear, and a lane position where drivers can see you, and assume they still might not.

questions.q: A car's blind spot is a bad place to ride because
options: The car's mirrors show you clearly there
The driver may change lanes into you
It is the safest cushion
Horns do not work beside a car
questions.explanation: If you cannot see the driver's face in their mirror, move forward or drop back. The driver can change lanes into you without seeing you.

questions.q: Painted lines, manhole covers, and steel plates are
options: Required paths for motorcycles
Better traction than dry pavement
Slippery, especially when wet
A good place to brake hard
questions.explanation: Cross them upright, without braking or turning if you can. The first minutes of rain float oil up onto the surface.

questions.q: Railroad tracks cross your lane. What does the MSF manual say is usually safer?
options: Crossing them in a lean
Braking hard on the rails
Swerving to hit them at exactly 90 degrees
Riding straight within your lane
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "Usually it is safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks. Turning to take tracks at a 90° angle can be more dangerous — the direction may put you into another lane of traffic." For tracks that run parallel to your path, cross at an angle of at least 45°.

questions.q: On gravel or a dirty shoulder you should
options: Slow first, then stay smooth
Accelerate and lean hard
Drag the rear brake the whole way
Brake hard and turn
questions.explanation: Loose surfaces punish sudden brakes and sudden leans. Do the slowing while you still have pavement. Slow before you get there, then hold a steady throttle and avoid sudden inputs.

questions.q: Countersteering means
options: Turning the handlebar opposite the way you want to go at parking-lot speed only
At speed, pressing the handgrip in the direction of the turn so the bike leans that way
Weighting the outside peg to stand the bike up
Using only the rear brake to turn
questions.explanation: Press right, go right. Press left, go left. It is how a motorcycle turns once you are moving.

questions.q: In a curve you should look
options: Down at the tank
At the outside edge next to your front tire
Through the turn to the exit, where you want to go
Back at the entrance
questions.explanation: Your eyes lead the bike. Look through the turn, not at the hazard on the inside.

questions.q: Slow, look, press, and roll means
options: Slow in the middle of the turn with the front brake
Look at your knee and chop the throttle
Press the rear brake in the lean
Slow before, look, press to lean, then roll on
questions.explanation: Do the braking while the bike is straight. A steady throttle in the curve settles the suspension. Slow before the turn, look through it, press the handlebar to lean, and roll on the throttle gently.

questions.q: If an animal is small and a swerve would put you into traffic, you should
options: Swerve at any cost
Brake hard in a straight line
Lay the bike down on purpose
Accelerate into the animal
questions.explanation: Laying a bike down is not a strategy. It removes your brakes and your steering. Slow as much as you can in a straight line and stay up.

questions.q: At night you should
options: Follow a car one second back so its lights are yours
Ride at the same speed as in daylight if you know the road
Slow so you can stop within the distance your headlight shows
Use only the high beam behind other traffic
questions.explanation: If you cannot stop within what you can see, you are overdriving the headlight. Increase following distance.

questions.q: A passenger should
options: Put both feet down at stops while seated sideways
Be carried if there are no passenger pegs
Sit on the tank
Use the pegs, hold on, and lean with the bike
questions.explanation: A passenger who leans the wrong way fights the turn. Do not carry a passenger unless the bike is equipped for one. Use footpegs, hold the rider or the passenger holds, and lean with the bike rather than against the turn.

questions.q: Alcohol affects a motorcycle rider by
options: Impairing balance and judgment
Matter only over the car BAC limit
Wearing off if you ride fast
Improving balance
questions.explanation: Do not ride after drinking. The legal BAC number is a state law and is not a safe amount on two wheels. Impairing balance, vision, and judgment at levels that would be less obvious in a car.

questions.q: Tire pressure should be checked
options: Only when the tire looks low
Cold, with a gauge, before you ride
While the tire is hot from the highway
By kicking the sidewall
questions.explanation: Low pressure overheats the tire and hurts handling. Use the pressure on the bike's sticker or the manual, not a guess.

questions.q: A driver turning left across your path is best handled by
options: Laying the bike down
Speeding up and assuming they will stop
Slowing, ready to brake, with an out
Riding in their blind spot
questions.explanation: Left-turn crashes are the classic car-versus-motorcycle collision. Make eye contact when you can, and still be ready to brake. They may not see you. Slowing, getting ready to brake, and having an escape path.

questions.q: The friction zone is
options: The center of the lane
The space between two cars
The area of the front brake that locks the wheel
The clutch range where the bike starts to move
questions.explanation: Slipping the clutch in the friction zone, with a little throttle, is how you control a slow ride. The clutch range where the bike starts to move and you can creep smoothly.

questions.q: Engine braking alone in an emergency is
options: Not a substitute for both brakes
Required before you touch the front brake
Safer than ABS
The fastest way to stop
questions.explanation: Downshift to help, but the brakes do the stopping. Use both.

questions.q: The first minutes of a rain are especially slick because
options: The rain washes the road instantly
Oil and debris float on top of the water
Tires grip better when they are cool
Painted lines dry first
questions.explanation: Ease off, avoid paint and metal, and add following distance until the rain has washed the surface.

questions.q: Before you change lanes on a motorcycle you should
options: Assume cars will yield
Rely on the mirror only
Signal, mirror, and head check
Swerve first and signal after
questions.explanation: Mirrors do not cover the angle beside your shoulder. A head check does. Signal, check the mirror, and turn your head to check the blind spot.

questions.q: Eye protection is needed because
options: Goggles are only for dirt bikes
A helmet's face opening is always sealed
A windshield blocks every stone and insect
Wind and debris can blind you instantly
questions.explanation: A face shield or goggles is part of the ride, even if the bike has a windshield. Wind, bugs, and debris can take your vision in a second.

questions.q: Entering a curve too fast is best fixed by
options: Look through, lean more, roll off smoothly
Putting a foot down
Straightening up and braking hard
Grabbing the front brake while leaned over
questions.explanation: A sudden front-brake grab while leaned is how riders fall on the inside. Do the slowing before the next curve. Looking through the turn, pressing the bars to tighten the lean if you still have grip, and rolling off the throttle smoothly.

questions.q: When a group needs to pass a slow vehicle, riders should
options: Pass side by side
Pass one at a time and return to formation
Use the shoulder together
Follow the leader into the oncoming lane as a pack
questions.explanation: One at a time keeps an escape space. Reform the stagger after the pass.

questions.q: A chain that is dry, rusty, or hanging slack should be
options: Sprayed with water
Ignored until it breaks
Cleaned, lubed, and adjusted
Replaced by a piece of rope
questions.explanation: A thrown chain can lock the rear wheel. Check it during T-CLOCS. Cleaned, lubricated, and adjusted to the spec before you ride.

questions.q: Covering the controls as you approach an intersection means
options: Coasting in neutral
Taking both hands off to stretch
Riding with the brakes locked
Fingers and toe ready on the brakes
questions.explanation: Covering shortens reaction time. It is not the same as riding the brakes. Having your fingers on the front brake and your toe ready at the rear so you can stop sooner.

questions.q: Wind from a passing truck can
options: Push you sideways
Be ignored at highway speed
Only affect the passenger
Hold the motorcycle in its lane
questions.explanation: A loose, controlled grip lets the bike move under you without a tank-slapper. Do not fight every gust with a stiff arm. Grip the bars loosely enough to steer and be ready to lean.

questions.q: Riding between lanes of stopped cars is
options: A national right
Legal only where allowed
Required in work zones
Safer than a lane
questions.explanation: Lane filtering and lane splitting are state laws. The national rule is that you are entitled to a full lane, not to the space between cars. Otherwise stay in a lane. Legal only where your state allows it.

questions.q: A bag or a passenger load should be
options: Held between your knees if there is no strap
Hung from the turn signal
Tied on the handlebars
Kept low and secure so it cannot shift
questions.explanation: A load that shifts will steer the bike for you. Do not block lights or the steering. Kept low and secure so it cannot shift into the wheel or the controls.

questions.q: Fatigue on a motorcycle is dangerous because
options: A faster pace wakes you up
It only matters after midnight
You miss hazards and react late
Coffee removes it
questions.explanation: Stop before you are weaving. A motorcycle gives you no second chance at a nod. A tired rider misses hazards and reacts late, and there is no passenger seat to rest in.

questions.q: A grooved pavement or a bridge grating can
options: Require a locked front brake
Be crossed only in a deep lean
Increase grip in the rain
Make the front end feel loose
questions.explanation: The weave feels worse than it is if you look far ahead and do not chop the throttle. Hold a steady speed and look ahead, not down.

questions.q: Threshold braking is
options: Braking firmly, just short of lockup
Using only the rear brake
Downshifting without the brakes
Braking so hard the front wheel locks and stays locked
questions.explanation: On a bike without ABS, you ease off a hair if the tire starts to howl, then reapply. ABS does that modulation for you. Braking firmly, just short of a lockup, and adjusting pressure as the weight shifts forward.

questions.q: An escape path is
options: The shoulder you must always use
Open space you keep to move into
The oncoming lane as a habit
Only useful on the freeway
questions.explanation: Position the bike so you are not boxed in. A cushion is part of SEE. A space you keep beside or ahead of you so a car that misses you has somewhere to go and so do you.

questions.q: Where do the greatest number of car-versus-motorcycle crashes take place?
options: On empty freeways, almost always as a simple rear-end by the motorcycle
In marked parking stalls, mostly from forgetting the side stand
Only on mountain switchbacks when the bike is leaned over
At intersections, often when a car turns left across the rider
questions.explanation: Most car-motorcycle crashes happen at intersections, and the usual pattern is a driver turning left across the rider.

questions.q: A left-turning sedan cuts across the lane you are riding through. Which crash is that?
options: The classic intersection crash of a car turning left across a motorcycle
A freeway merge crash that rarely involves any turning movement
A low-speed drop caused only by grabbing the clutch
A wind-gust crash that starts only beside a passing truck
questions.explanation: The basic course treats a left turn across the rider at an intersection as the typical car-motorcycle collision.

questions.q: Traffic is flowing on a green and an oncoming driver begins turning left. What should you prepare for?
options: A planned lay-down as the primary way to avoid the car
A cut across your path, so slow down, cover the brakes, and keep an out
A guaranteed yield
A need to accelerate and squeeze past the turning car's front bumper
questions.explanation: A left turn across your lane is the common intersection threat. Reduce speed, cover the brakes, and keep a stop or a swerve available.

questions.q: You have the green, yet a car in the oncoming turn bay keeps creeping forward. How do you ride?
options: Swing into the opposing lane so the car can finish the turn sooner
Stare at the car's grille so the motorcycle will steer around it by itself
Treat the possible left turn as live, slow, and stay ready to brake or swerve
Hold speed because a green light means every oncoming driver must wait
questions.explanation: A green light does not erase the left-turn crash. Slow down and keep either a straight stop or a swerve ready.

questions.q: An oncoming driver waves you through and then rolls the wheels into a left turn. What is true?
options: A wave means the turn is cancelled and you should speed up through the gap
You should lay the bike down before the bumper reaches your lane
You should move onto the painted centerline and share the car's path
A wave is not proof you were seen, so cover the brakes and keep an escape
questions.explanation: Do not assume a driver who gestures or looks has actually seen you. Slow, cover the brakes, and keep an out.

questions.q: Someone in the opposing left-turn lane looks straight at your helmet and still eases out. What follows?
options: Do not trust the look
Eye contact proves the driver will wait, so hold your speed
Lock the rear brake and hold it until the car stops moving
Move into the car's blind spot so you are harder to turn into
questions.explanation: A driver can look toward a motorcycle and still not perceive it. Slow, cover the brakes, and have space to escape.

questions.q: At a busy signal, the car opposite you has a left-turn arrow that just turned yellow. What is the hazard?
options: You should stare at the yellow lens until the bike has passed the corner
The driver may still rush the left turn across you as the light changes
A yellow arrow means the motorcycle must stop in the intersection box
The only risk now is a truck gust from behind you
questions.explanation: Intersections stay dangerous while a driver tries to beat a changing left-turn light. Cover the brakes and keep an out.

questions.q: Two oncoming cars are stacked to turn left, and the second one is hidden behind the first. Why slow?
options: You should speed up to pass both cars before either one moves
Hiding behind the first car is the safest place for you to ride
The second driver may turn across you without a clear view of the motorcycle
Stacked cars always cancel each other's turn and leave the lane empty
questions.explanation: A following left-turner often never sees the motorcycle. Slow and be ready; do not assume the lead car blocks the threat.

questions.q: Crossing a suburban intersection, you notice a car nosing out of a side street on your right. What is the move?
options: Speed up so you pass the bumper before the driver can look
Ride in the driver's blind spot until you clear the corner
Lay the motorcycle down if the bumper moves even an inch
Slow and be ready
questions.explanation: Drivers pulling out from side streets often miss motorcycles. Reduce speed and be ready to brake or escape.

questions.q: A driveway on the left has a car with its nose at the sidewalk, aimed across your lane. What should you do?
options: Slow and cover the brakes
Maintain speed, since driveway traffic must always finish the look first
Swerve left into the driveway to go behind the car
Stare at the front license plate so you will not hit the car
questions.explanation: A driver leaving a driveway is a common failure to see a motorcycle. Slow down and be ready to stop or swerve. A driveway pull-out is a classic miss.

questions.q: Near a crowded parking-lot exit, a sedan rolls toward the road without a full stop. How should you respond?
options: Grab the front brake and hold it locked while you look at the driver
Ease off and cover the controls so you can brake now if the car enters
Honk once and then accelerate through the exit path
Move onto the sidewalk so the car can have the whole lane
questions.explanation: Parking-lot exits behave like driveway pull-outs. Drivers often miss riders, so slow down and be ready.

questions.q: A shopping-center drive slopes down to the street, and a van is rolling toward the gutter. What is the risk?
options: You should ride the painted edge line to share the van's exit
You should look only at the van's windshield and ignore an escape path
The driver may pull out and miss you, so slow and stay ready to stop
A downhill driveway is safe
questions.explanation: Treat a vehicle leaving a commercial drive like any other pull-out miss. Slow, cover the brakes, and keep an out.

questions.q: From a rural mailbox pull-off, a pickup starts to enter your lane late. What is the trained response?
options: Close the gap so the pickup driver is forced to wait
Swerve onto the gravel shoulder at the last moment while braking hard
Assume the driver saw your headlight
Slow and be ready to brake
questions.explanation: A vehicle entering from the roadside can easily miss a motorcycle. Reduce speed and be prepared to stop straight or escape. Late entries from the roadside are classic misses.

questions.q: While a side-street sedan inches forward, the driver turns their head toward you and then looks away. What now?
options: Still slow and cover the brakes
Take the glance as a yield and accelerate through the intersection
Stop in the driver's blind spot and wait to be noticed
Plan to slide the bike if the sedan moves another foot
questions.explanation: Looking toward a rider is not the same as seeing the rider. Slow, cover the brakes, and keep an escape. A glance does not mean the driver accepted you.

questions.q: Covering the controls as you near a cross street means which hand and foot setup?
options: The throttle pinned open so engine braking cannot slow you
Fingers on the front-brake lever and your toe ready at the rear brake
Both hands off the grips so you can wave at turning drivers
The clutch pulled in and the front brake ignored until the car moves
questions.explanation: Near an intersection, cover the controls: fingers on the front brake and a toe ready at the rear so you can brake immediately.

questions.q: Fingers already resting on the front lever at an intersection are there for what reason?
options: So you can swerve and brake as hard as possible at the same time
So the rear brake can be left completely unused
So you can take the slack out and brake now if a car turns across you
So you can lock the front wheel before you decide whether to stop
questions.explanation: Covering the front brake shortens the time to a stop. Use it with the rear, and do not lock the front wheel.

questions.q: Your toe hovers over the rear pedal while you approach a corner cross street. Why?
options: So you can stomp and hold a locked rear wheel through the intersection
So engine braking can replace both brakes if a car pulls out
So you can drag the rear brake while you lean hard on painted arrows
So the rear brake is ready together with the front if you must stop now
questions.explanation: Cover the rear brake with your toe near intersections so both brakes are available immediately.

questions.q: Why cover the brakes before a car actually enters your lane, instead of after it moves?
options: Reaction time is shorter if your fingers and toe are already on the controls
Covering the brakes makes the headlight flash so drivers must yield
Early covering locks both wheels and keeps them locked until you pass
It tells you to ride in the car's blind spot until the corner is clear
questions.explanation: The point of covering the controls is to be able to brake now, before a pull-out or left turn uses up the gap.

questions.q: What is an escape path while you ride through traffic?
options: The blind spot next to a truck trailer
Open space beside you or ahead of you that you can use to avoid a crash
The painted centerline you share with a car that is beside you
A deliberate slide on your side if a stop looks inconvenient
questions.explanation: An escape path is space beside or ahead of you. Protect that space so a stop or a swerve is still possible.

questions.q: A gap in the lane to your left is open as you near a busy crossing. How should you think about it?
options: It is useful only if you stare at the car that might turn
It matters only after you have already locked the front wheel
It can be your escape path, so do not give it up without a reason
It is wasted space you should close by riding the lane line
questions.explanation: Space beside you is an escape path. Keep it available as you approach an intersection threat.

questions.q: You are following a car by less than a second as you both near an intersection. What did you give up?
options: Nothing important, because the car ahead will block every left-turning driver
Only fuel, because a short gap improves your chance to swerve and brake together
The need to be seen
The escape space ahead of you
questions.explanation: Following too close erases the space you would use to stop or swerve. Open the gap so an escape still exists.

questions.q: If a tailgater closes on your rear fender near a commercial strip, what should you change?
options: Increase the gap ahead of you so you still have room to stop smoothly
Brake-check the tailgater so they drop back immediately
Speed away in anger and weave through the cars in front
Move into a car's blind spot and hold that spot until they pass
questions.explanation: When someone tailgates, add space in front. Do not brake-check and do not speed off in anger.

questions.q: Speeding up through a gap in anger because a car is tailgating you fails for what reason?
options: It forces the tailgater to pass on the right inside your lane
It replaces the need to cover the brakes at the next intersection
It throws away judgment and can leave you with even less escape space
It is the basic-course method for ending a tailgate
questions.explanation: Do not speed away in anger. Add space in front of you and let a safe pass happen without a fight.

questions.q: Target fixation on a motorcycle means which steering result?
options: You automatically steer away from anything you look at
The bike goes straight no matter where your eyes point
Staring at an escape path makes you hit the obstacle
You tend to steer toward whatever you keep staring at
questions.explanation: Target fixation means you steer toward the thing you stare at. Look at the escape, not at the obstacle.

questions.q: A couch cushion lies in your lane and a clear patch is to the right. Where should your eyes go?
options: To the clear escape path
Onto the cushion until the front tire has passed it
At the cushion's shadow so the bike will dodge by itself
Down at your front fender so you can watch the tire hit it
questions.explanation: Look at the escape, not at the obstacle. Staring at the cushion can make you steer into it.

questions.q: You see a deep pothole late, with open pavement just to one side. What does staring at the hole do?
options: It locks both brakes in a useful way while you swerve
It pulls your steering toward the hole instead of toward the open pavement
It guarantees the suspension will absorb the hole without a path change
It is better than looking at the clear pavement beside the hole
questions.explanation: Because you steer toward your gaze, look through the escape beside the pothole, not down into the hole.

questions.q: Debris blows out of a truck bed into your lane, and the next lane over is empty. How do you look?
options: Look back at the truck driver until the debris stops moving
Look down at the tank so you do not overreact
Look toward the empty lane you want
Stare at the largest piece so you can brake and swerve together
questions.explanation: Pick the escape with your eyes. Staring at the debris is target fixation and can steer you into it.

questions.q: A crash scene is off the shoulder, and traffic beside you is tight. Where do you aim your eyes?
options: At the wreck until you have passed it
At the bystanders
At your mirror
Ahead through your own escape
questions.explanation: Riders steer toward what they stare at. Look along your path, not at the crash scene. At the wreck you might drift toward.

questions.q: If you fixate on a car that is turning across your bow, what is the likely steering error?
options: The motorcycle drifts toward that car instead of toward an open escape
The motorcycle always snaps away from the car you watch
Eye focus replaces the need to cover the brakes
Fixation is useful
questions.explanation: Target fixation sends you toward the threat you stare at. Look to the escape and be ready to brake or swerve.

questions.q: Looking through the open space beside an obstacle helps because
options: It is a substitute for slowing before railroad tracks or gravel
Your hands tend to steer the motorcycle where your eyes are aimed
The obstacle becomes less slippery if you refuse to look at it
It allows a hard brake and a hard swerve at the same instant
questions.explanation: Look at the escape, not the obstacle. Vision leads steering, which is why target fixation is dangerous.

questions.q: Be seen in daytime traffic by combining which habits?
options: Riding in a car's blind spot so only the mirror shows a small shape
Hiding behind a tall van until the intersection is behind you
Headlight on, bright gear, and a lane position drivers can actually see
Headlight off to save the battery, plus dark gear in the center of the lane
questions.explanation: To be seen, ride with the headlight on, wear bright gear, and choose a lane position where the driver can see you.

questions.q: Your high-visibility jacket and a lit headlight still fail if you choose which place to ride?
options: The left tire track, where a left-turning driver has a better view
A position with space ahead so you can brake early
An outside line in a curve that improves your view down the road
A car's blind spot, where the driver cannot see you even in bright gear
questions.explanation: Bright gear does not help inside a blind spot. Do not ride where a driver cannot see you.

questions.q: Riding beside a car, tucked by the rear door, is a bad place to be because
options: The driver can change lanes or turn without ever detecting the motorcycle
Blind spots are the most visible place for a left-turning driver
It is the best escape path when a truck passes in the wind
It lets you share the lane legally with the car beside you
questions.explanation: A car's blind spot hides you. Ride where you can be seen, not beside the driver's rear quarter.

questions.q: You have been beside a car's rear door for several seconds. What should you change?
options: Brake hard while you swerve toward the car's lane line
Move forward or drop back so you are out of that blind spot
Stay there because the mirror has already shown the driver everything
Tap the car with your foot so the driver knows you are present
questions.explanation: Do not linger in a blind spot. Change position so the driver can see you in a mirror or with a glance.

questions.q: Hiding behind a tall van as you both approach a light hides you from whom?
options: Only from pedestrians, and only when your headlight is on
From the wind
From drivers who may turn left across the lane or pull out from the side
From nobody, because the van makes your motorcycle easier to notice
questions.explanation: Do not hide behind another vehicle at an intersection. A lane position that lets turning drivers see you is safer.

questions.q: Daytime headlight use on a motorcycle is mainly for what traffic purpose?
options: To warm the bulb so it will work only after dark
To signal that you are giving up the lane to any nearby car
To replace bright gear and a visible lane position entirely
To help drivers see you, especially at intersections where they might turn
questions.explanation: Ride with the headlight on so drivers have a better chance of seeing you before a left turn or a pull-out.

questions.q: Nighttime conspicuity still depends on more than a headlight. What else matters?
options: Bright or reflective gear and a lane position that stays out of blind spots
Dark clothing, because it hides road glare from your mirrors
Riding the lane line so cars can share your space after dark
Following one second behind a truck so its lights mark you
questions.explanation: At night, a headlight plus bright or reflective gear and a visible lane position help drivers pick you out.

questions.q: A driver who glances at your lane and then pulls away from the curb has done what?
options: Ended the hazard, so covering the brakes is no longer useful
Maybe looked without seeing you, so slow, cover the brakes, and keep an out
Confirmed a yield
Given you permission to ride in the door's blind spot
questions.explanation: Do not assume a glance means you were seen. Slow down, cover the brakes, and preserve an escape path.

questions.q: Eye contact from a driver waiting on a side street is best treated as
options: A cue to lay the motorcycle down before the bumper moves
Proof you should stare at the driver's face until you pass
Unreliable, so you still slow and stay ready to brake or escape
A contract that the driver will wait no matter what
questions.explanation: Eye contact does not prove the driver identified a motorcycle. Slow, cover the brakes, and have an out.

questions.q: When a dog darts from between parked cars and traffic is tight on your left, what should you do?
options: Always swerve, even if the swerve carries you into the next lane
Always hit the dog
Lay the bike down so you slide under the dog
Brake straight and stay up if a swerve would put you into that traffic
questions.explanation: If a small animal and a swerve would put you into traffic, brake in a straight line and stay upright.

questions.q: If a squirrel bounds into your lane with cars beside you, which plan fits the course?
options: Brake straight and stay up rather than swerving into the cars
Swerve first and squeeze the front brake hard during the swerve
Aim at the squirrel and keep the throttle steady on purpose
Drop the bike onto its side as the preferred technique
questions.explanation: Do not teach an automatic swerve into traffic for a small animal. Brake straight and keep the bike up.

questions.q: A rabbit on the centerline is small, and your escape to the right is a live lane. What is the better action?
options: A deliberate slide
Straight-line braking while you stay upright
A hard swerve toward the live lane while the front brake is locked
Staring at the rabbit so fixation steers you cleanly around it
questions.explanation: When the swerve is into traffic, brake straight for the small animal and stay up. Do not swerve by habit.

questions.q: A deer is standing in your lane ahead. What does the MSF manual say to do for larger animals?
options: Speed up to get past it
Lay the motorcycle down
Brake and prepare to stop
Kick at it as you pass
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "For larger animals (deer, elk, cattle) brake and prepare to stop — they are unpredictable."

questions.q: Do not treat every animal as the same hazard. What is the small-animal rule when lanes are full?
options: Lay the bike down whenever an animal is smaller than the wheel
Brake straight and stay upright if swerving would put you into traffic
Swerve first, then sort out the traffic you entered
Hit every animal so you never change line
questions.explanation: Small animal plus traffic beside you: brake straight and stay up. A large animal may instead call for an escape path.

questions.q: Never teach one animal response for every case. Which statement matches the course?
options: Always hit the animal so the motorcycle stays predictable
Always slide the bike on purpose before you reach the animal
Small animals with traffic beside you call for a straight stop
Always swerve for every animal, no matter what is beside you
questions.explanation: The plan depends on the animal and the space. Do not always swerve, and do not always hit it. Large animals may need an escape.

questions.q: As a truck passes you closely, the wind can do what to the motorcycle?
options: Glue you to the lane so no control change is ever needed
Require you to grab the bars and fight the gust rigidly
Mean you should brake hard while you lean the bike over
Push you sideways, so keep a loose grip and be ready to lean
questions.explanation: Wind from a passing truck can push you. Use a loose grip, be ready to lean, and do not fight the bars.

questions.q: Before you reach a gravel patch you can already see, what does 'set up' mean?
options: Choose speed and path before the tires are on the gravel
Wait until the front tire is in the gravel, then grab the brake
Swerve and brake hard together once the gravel starts to slide
Lay the bike down just as the shoulder gravel begins
questions.explanation: Gravel is a hazard you set up for before you are on it. Slow and pick a steady path early. After.

questions.q: Painted arrows you can see in your lane are a reason to do what before the tires arrive?
options: Ignore them because paint is only a hazard at night
Set up early: adjust speed and stay upright rather than braking on the paint
Brake hardest when the tire is centered on the arrow
Lean the bike over on the arrow so you finish the turn sooner
questions.explanation: Painted arrows are hazards you prepare for before you reach them. Do not wait until you are on the paint to decide.

questions.q: Tracks you can see ahead of an intersection should change your plan when?
options: After you lock the front brake on the rails
Once you have ridden along the slot to test traction
Before you are on them, so speed, line, and body are already set
Only after the front tire drops toward the slot
questions.explanation: Railroad tracks are a hazard you set up for before you arrive. Decide the crossing path and speed early.

questions.q: Setup for a dirty stretch of pavement means you have already done what?
options: Accelerated so you spend less time on the bad surface
Moved your eyes down to the front tire as you enter
Started a hard swerve at the same moment you brake
Slowed and chosen a steady path before the surface change
questions.explanation: Set up before the hazard. Gravel, paint, and tracks should be handled with a plan made ahead of the tires.

questions.q: Loose gravel at a corner entrance is visible from half a block away. When do you slow?
options: Before the gravel, then hold a steady throttle and avoid sudden inputs on it
In the middle of the gravel with a sudden front-brake grab
After the rear tire starts to slide, with a locked rear pedal
Never, because gravel only matters if it is wet
questions.explanation: Set up for gravel before you are on it. Slow first, then be smooth rather than making a sudden move on the loose surface.

questions.q: A turn arrow is painted across your path just as the lane bends. What is the early setup?
options: Ride along the arrow's long edge while you trail the rear brake hard
Reduce speed before the paint and cross it upright instead of braking on it
Lean harder once the tire is on the arrow
Stare at the arrowhead so you steer along the paint
questions.explanation: Painted arrows are a set-up hazard. Make the speed and lean decision before the tire reaches the paint.

questions.q: You can see rail grooves shining after a light rain. What belongs in the approach, not on the rails?
options: A hard lean that puts the tire in the slot
A plan to ride parallel in the groove until the street ends
The speed change and the crossing angle, chosen before the tires get there
A last-second lock of the front brake on the steel
questions.explanation: Set up for tracks before you are on them. Do not invent the plan after the tire is already on the steel.

questions.q: Search early for cars that might enter from driveways as you ride a commercial street. Why so early?
options: A pull-out is a classic miss, and you need time to slow and cover the brakes
Early searching causes target fixation on every parked car
Driveway cars are harmless if your headlight is on
You only need to search after the car's bumper is in your lane
questions.explanation: Drivers leaving driveways often miss motorcycles. Search early, slow, and be ready before the car commits.

questions.q: Keep an escape beside you while a line of cars waits to turn left from the cross street. Why?
options: You should use that space to lay the bike down if a tire twitches
One of them may turn or creep out, and you need space that is not a blind spot
Escape space is optional once you have made eye contact
The space should be closed so you can share a lane with the lead car
questions.explanation: An escape path is space beside or ahead of you. Keep it when side-street traffic may pull out.

questions.q: Your out ahead shrinks when you close up on a car before a blind intersection. What did you lose?
options: The duty to wear bright gear
Nothing, because a one-second gap is the longest gap the course allows
Time and space to brake if a driver turns left or pulls out
Only the wind effect from a truck that already passed
questions.explanation: Following too close removes your escape. Leave room ahead so a pull-out or a left turn does not trap you.

questions.q: Lane position for being seen at a left-turn threat should accomplish what?
options: Hide you in the center, stacked behind a taller vehicle
Place you on the lane line so you share space with a car
Park you beside a trailer until the signal changes
Put you where the turning driver can see you
questions.explanation: Be seen with lane position as well as with the headlight and bright gear. Do not hide where the driver cannot pick you out. Hidden in a blind spot or behind a car.

questions.q: Being seen includes refusing which comfortable habit?
options: Lingering where mirrors cannot show you
Wearing a light-colored jacket on a gray day
Riding with the headlight switched on in daylight
Leaving space ahead so you can brake early
questions.explanation: A blind spot is a bad place to ride. Being seen means headlight, bright gear, and a position the driver can actually detect. Lingering where a mirror cannot show you, then assuming the driver knows you are there.

questions.q: While you approach a hillcrest intersection, a car on the right is rolling toward the stop line. What is your action?
options: Move into the opposing lane to give the car your lane
Slow and cover the brakes in case it pulls out
Speed up to beat the car
Stare at the car's hood ornament until you have passed
questions.explanation: A vehicle pulling out from a side road is a classic miss. Slow and be ready before you reach the corner. Slow and cover the brakes in case the driver pulls out without seeing you.

questions.q: As you enter a town, repeated driveways line the right side. How should that change the ride?
options: Look only at the driveway mouths and ignore the lane ahead
Turn the headlight off so drivers are not distracted
Expect pull-outs, slow enough to brake, and keep an escape instead of hiding
Ride the paint so each driveway car can share the lane with you
questions.explanation: Driveways are classic places drivers miss motorcycles. Slow, be seen, and keep space to stop or swerve.

questions.q: When railroad tracks cross ahead of a green light, the hazard plan starts where?
options: On the rails themselves, with a hard lean and a locked front brake
After you have ridden along the slot to the next block
Only if a train is already on the crossing
On the approach, before the tires reach the rails or the slot
questions.explanation: Tracks are a hazard you set up for before you are on them. Choose speed and crossing line early.

questions.q: When painted arrows glisten in a light drizzle, waiting until you are on them is wrong because
options: You must slow and straighten before the paint
Paint is sticky in drizzle and rewards a hard lean
Arrows are only decorative and never change traction
You should lock the rear brake and hold it across the arrow
questions.explanation: Set up for painted arrows before you reach them. Do not brake hard or lean hard once you are on the wet paint. The setup, including speed and an upright bike, has to happen before the paint.

questions.q: When loose gravel trails out of a construction apron into your tire track, you should
options: Swerve sharply and brake hard in the same motion
Slow before the gravel, then stay smooth
Grab the front brake as the front tire enters the pile
Stare at the stones so fixation carries you around them
questions.explanation: Gravel is a before-you-arrive hazard. Slow first, then avoid sudden brake, lean, or throttle inputs on the loose surface. Set up by slowing before the gravel, then stay smooth once you are on it.

questions.q: Sun glare is in the face of a driver waiting to turn left across you. What should you assume?
options: You should turn the headlight off to reduce glare for the driver
You should stare at the sun so you do not fixate on the car
The driver may not see you, so slow, cover the brakes, and keep an escape
Glare only blinds motorcycles
questions.explanation: A driver looking toward you can still miss you, and glare makes that worse. Slow, cover the brakes, and have an out.

questions.q: Dusk makes a dark motorcycle hard to pick out at a cross street. Which habit helps you be seen?
options: Headlight off until full dark, and ride the door line of parked cars
Hide behind a bus so the bus is the only shape at the corner
Speed up because shorter time in the intersection means you were seen
Headlight on, brighter gear, and a lane position the side-street driver can see
questions.explanation: Be seen with the headlight, bright gear, and a visible position. Dusk is when drivers miss riders and then pull out.

questions.q: Backing from a driveway, a car shows only reverse lights and a trunk. What is the trained response?
options: Stare at the trunk emblem so you steer around the car automatically
Slow and be ready
Squeeze past the bumper on the paint
Lay the bike down if the reverse lights stay on
questions.explanation: A driver coming out of a driveway, including one who is backing, is a classic miss. Slow and be ready to brake. A backing driver often never sees a motorcycle.

questions.q: At a four-way stop you arrived first, but a car rolls in late from the left. What hazard remains?
options: You should share the intersection box by riding the lane line
You should fixate on the car's front tire until it stops rolling
The driver may still go and miss you, so cover the brakes and keep an out
Arriving first means you can ignore the car and accelerate away
questions.explanation: Intersection conflicts do not vanish because you had the turn. Drivers miss motorcycles. Slow, cover, and keep an escape.

questions.q: A car ahead slows with a left blinker at a driveway, and you are close behind. What have you lost?
options: Nothing, because a one-car gap is the course maximum
Only the chance to ride in the car's blind spot, which you wanted
The need to set up for any gravel the driveway spills into the lane
Escape space ahead
questions.explanation: Following too close removes your escape. Open the gap before a turning car or a driveway conflict traps you. You cannot smoothly handle the slow turn or what it hides.

questions.q: Group riders bunched a few feet apart are nearing a signal. What hazard does the bunch create?
options: It erases each rider's escape space and can hide riders from turning drivers
It is the staggered formation the course wants inside one lane
It lets the group share the lane side by side with cars
It replaces the need for headlights
questions.explanation: Following too close removes the escape. In a group you still need time and space, and you still need to be seen.

questions.q: Using the horn at a driver who is creeping out is useful only if you also do what?
options: Lay the bike down if the horn does not stop the car
Slow, cover the brakes, and keep an escape
Speed up, since a horn legally forces the driver to yield
Stay in the blind spot and honk until the light changes
questions.explanation: Do not assume you were seen just because you made noise or the driver looked. Slow, cover the brakes, and have an out. The horn does not prove they saw you.

questions.q: A right-turning car from the cross street swings wide toward your lane. How do you respond?
options: Lock the front brake and swerve at the same time
Ride the painted stop line so you share the turn with the car
Slow, cover the brakes, and use escape space instead of staring at the bumper
Accelerate and lean under the car's mirror
questions.explanation: Intersection turns are where cars miss or crowd riders. Slow, cover the controls, look to the escape, and do not fixate on the car.

questions.q: An oncoming car starts a U-turn in front of you at a wide intersection. What is the immediate plan?
options: Hold speed because U-turns are not intersection crashes
Stare at the driver's window so the bike will miss the car
Brake-check the traffic behind you while you watch the U-turn
Slow, cover both brakes, and look for an escape rather than a deliberate slide
questions.explanation: A car turning across your path is the core intersection hazard. Brake readiness and an escape beat a planned lay-down.

questions.q: Parked cars line the curb and a driver is seated with hands on the wheel. Why does that matter?
options: The car may pull out, so slow and stay visible
A seated driver always sees every motorcycle in the door mirror
You should ride the paint beside that door to share the lane
You should stare at the side mirror until you have passed
questions.explanation: A pull-away from the curb is another miss. Be seen, stay out of the blind spot, and be ready to slow.

questions.q: Your lane is blocked by a fallen ladder, and a gap is open in the lane to your right with no car there. Where do you look?
options: Back at the traffic behind you until the ladder is passed
At the open gap you intend to use
At the ladder rungs until the front tire touches them
Down at the speedometer so you do not oversteer
questions.explanation: Target fixation pulls you toward the ladder if you stare at it. Look at the escape path and ride toward that space.

questions.q: A plastic bag floats up in front of your windscreen on a multi-lane road. What should your eyes do?
options: Follow the bag downward until it hits the front tire
Watch the bag
Leave the bag and look along the lane path you mean to keep
Lock onto the bag so you can swerve with the front brake applied
questions.explanation: Do not fixate on a small object. Look where you want to go. If a swerve would hit traffic, brake straight for a small hazard.

questions.q: Two hazards arrive together: a left-turning car and a tailgater. What should you protect first?
options: Space ahead so you can slow for the car without brake-checking the tailgater
Speed, by accelerating between the turning car and the oncoming lane
The lay-down, because two hazards mean you should slide
The blind spot beside the turning car
questions.explanation: Following too close removes your escape, and a tailgater makes that worse. Add space ahead rather than brake-checking or speeding off.

questions.q: Before a green light, you see gravel fanned across the intersection from a dump truck. When do you commit to a plan?
options: By aiming your eyes at the largest stones and leaning toward them
Before the tires reach the gravel, with speed already reduced and inputs ready to stay smooth
After the front tire is sliding, with a sudden brake and swerve together
Only if the gravel is deeper than the tire, and otherwise ignore it
questions.explanation: Gravel is a set-up hazard. Choose a slower speed and a steady path before you are on it, and do not stare at the stones.

questions.q: A steel rail line runs down your street for a block before it crosses. What must you not do on the way there?
options: Cover the brakes as you approach the intersection beyond the rails
Keep your eyes up along the path you mean to ride
Ride along the slot while you wait to invent a crossing plan at the last second
Set your crossing angle and speed while you still have room
questions.explanation: Set up for tracks before you are on them. Do not ride the slot, and do not delay the plan until the tire is in the groove.

questions.q: Reflective material on your jacket helps at night only if drivers have a line of sight. What defeats it?
options: Keeping the headlight on while you hold a visible lane position
Leaving two seconds or more of space ahead of you
Covering the brakes as you approach a side street
Riding in a blind spot or hidden behind a larger vehicle
questions.explanation: Being seen requires a position drivers can see, not only reflective gear. Get out of blind spots and do not hide.

questions.q: A driver ahead waves you to pass on the right inside the same lane. What is the hazard answer?
options: Stay in your lane space and do not share the lane
Accept the wave and ride the paint beside the car's doors
Pass through the car's blind spot
Lay the motorcycle down if the car drifts a few inches
questions.explanation: Do not assume a wave means the driver will leave you room. You are not sharing the lane, and a look or a wave is not proof you were seen. Be ready if the driver moves.

questions.q: Most intersection misses start with a driver who never identifies the motorcycle. What riding pattern answers that?
options: Plan on sliding the bike whenever a bumper moves
Be visible, slow, cover brakes, keep an out
Hide in the center of the lane behind the tallest car
Ride every blind spot so you can surprise the driver
questions.explanation: The common crash is a car turning left across a rider at an intersection. Visibility, a slower approach, covered brakes, and an escape are the response. Be visible, slow when a turn or pull-out is possible, cover the brakes, and keep an out.

questions.q: If your eyes stay glued to a pothole while a clear line sits two feet away, the bike will tend to
options: Stand up and track straight regardless of your gaze
Lock the front wheel without any lever input
Steer toward the pothole
Steer away from the pothole automatically
questions.explanation: Target fixation means you steer toward whatever you stare at. Look at the clear line, not at the hole. You ride where you stare.

questions.q: Cover both brakes when a side-street driver looks your way and rolls forward. Why both?
options: So you can lock the rear and ignore the front until the car stops
So engine braking alone can finish the stop
So you can brake hard while you swerve around the bumper
So you can brake now with front and rear together if the car enters
questions.explanation: Cover the controls near the conflict: fingers on the front brake, toe ready at the rear, so both brakes can work immediately.

questions.q: A tailgater flashes high beams because you slowed for a driveway threat. What should you refuse to do?
options: Brake-check them or speed away in anger and give up the space you need
Keep extra space ahead so you can still brake smoothly
Let them pass when a safe opening appears beside you
Stay ready for the driveway car that may still pull out
questions.explanation: Increase the gap in front when someone tailgates. Do not brake-check and do not race off. The driveway pull-out is still the hazard.

questions.q: An empty parking aisle opens beside you as a car noses out ahead. How can that aisle help?
options: It only helps if you stare at the car and ignore the aisle
It is escape space if you need to avoid the car
It is a blind spot you should ride in until the car stops
It is a place to lay the bike down on purpose
questions.explanation: An escape path is space beside or ahead of you. Use a clear aisle if it truly keeps you out of traffic, and look at that path.

questions.q: Small birds flush off the pavement in front of you with cars on both sides. What should you not do?
options: Keep your eyes on the open pavement you mean to ride
Stay loose on the grips while you slow
Swerve into a car for a small hazard, or stare at the birds and drift
Brake straight and stay upright if there is no safe swerve
questions.explanation: If a swerve for a small animal would put you into traffic, brake straight and stay up. Do not always swerve.

questions.q: Set up for three surface hazards the same way in time, even if the surface skill differs. Which three?
options: A lay-down, a locked front wheel, and a brake-check
Tracks, painted arrows, and gravel
Only ice, only at night, and only after the tire slides
Blind spots, tailgaters, and helmet fit
questions.explanation: Tracks, painted arrows, and gravel are hazards you set up for before the tires arrive. Do not decide in the middle of them.

questions.q: The plan if a crash is developing in a straight line with room to stop is which action, not a slide?
options: Staring at the threat until fixation solves it
Engine braking alone while you cover neither brake
A straight stop with both brakes, or a swerve
Laying the motorcycle down so you can slide into the car
questions.explanation: The plan is a straight stop or a swerve. Laying the bike down is a failure of those choices, not the technique to choose. A straight stop with both brakes, or a swerve if braking will not finish in time.

questions.q: Why is the center of a packed intersection a poor place to hide behind a taller car?
options: It is the most visible place for every driver who might turn
It guarantees an escape path of several seconds
It keeps you out of every blind spot by definition
Turning drivers cannot see you until too late
questions.explanation: Be seen. Do not hide in the stack. A position the driver can see, plus slowing and covered brakes, answers the classic miss. Left-turning and side-street drivers cannot see you until you pop out with no time left.

questions.q: A pickup waits on a gravel farm drive, front tires on the edge of the pavement. Which two setups overlap?
options: Slow and be ready for the pull-out, and set up for the gravel before you reach it
Accelerate across both the truck's nose and the gravel while braking hard
Ride the slot of a nearby rail line to avoid the truck
Stare at the truck grill and fight a gust that has not arrived
questions.explanation: A driveway pull-out is a classic miss, and gravel is a hazard you set up for early. Slow before you are on the loose stones.

questions.q: Once you have looked at a driver and the driver has looked toward you, the hazard is over. Why is that false?
options: Because blind spots disappear after any glance
A look is not the same as seeing you
Because eye contact legally ends your need to brake
Because the only remaining hazard is a purposeful lay-down
questions.explanation: Do not assume a driver who looks at you has actually seen you. Slow, cover the brakes, and keep an escape path.

questions.q: During an ordinary straight stop on dry pavement, where does most of the stopping power come from?
options: Engine braking only, because the levers are for curves
The clutch lever, pulled in so the motor stalls the bike
The front brake, about 70 percent, used together with the rear brake
The rear brake alone, with the front lever left untouched
questions.explanation: In a normal stop, most stopping power is the front brake, about 70 percent, and you still use the rear brake with it.

questions.q: On a dry, level road you need a smooth ordinary stop. Which control split matches the course?
options: Use the rear pedal only so the front tire cannot flat-spot
Downshift and ignore both brakes until the bike almost stalls
Stab the front lever and hold a locked front wheel
Use both brakes, with the front doing most of the work, about 70 percent
questions.explanation: Use both brakes together. The teaching figure is about 70 percent of the stopping power from the front.

questions.q: Most of the deceleration in a planned stop is produced by which brake?
options: The front brake, while the rear brake is still applied with it
The rear brake
Neither brake, if you are already in a low gear
The rear brake locked and held so the tire slides straight
questions.explanation: Most stopping power is at the front, about 70 percent, but the normal stop still uses both brakes.

questions.q: Using only the rear pedal for a normal stop from road speed leaves you with what?
options: A safe substitute that the course prefers to using both brakes
A much longer stop
The shortest possible stop
Automatic ABS pulsing even if the motorcycle has no ABS
questions.explanation: Do not leave the front brake out of a normal stop. About 70 percent of the stopping power is in front, used with the rear. You skipped the front brake that does most of the work.

questions.q: The front brake is powerful enough to do what if you grab it instead of squeezing?
options: Guarantee a stoppie the course wants you to hold
Make engine braking the only force you still need
Lock the front wheel without ABS
Replace the need to practice
questions.explanation: Squeeze the front brake smoothly. A grab can lock the front wheel. If it locks and you have no ABS, release immediately so it rolls, then reapply.

questions.q: About 70 percent is the teaching figure for which part of a normal stop?
options: The share of stopping power that comes from engine braking alone
The time you may legally ride in a car's blind spot
The lean angle you should use on wet painted arrows
The share of stopping power that comes from the front brake
questions.explanation: The course uses about 70 percent as the front brake's share of a normal stop, with the rear brake used at the same time.

questions.q: Squeeze the front lever and press the rear pedal together in a straight-line stop. Why together?
options: Because both brakes stop the motorcycle, even though the front does most of the work
Because the rear must lock before the front is allowed to work
Because engine braking will not begin unless both tires are sliding
Because a swerve should happen at the same moment as the hardest braking
questions.explanation: Use both brakes. The front supplies about 70 percent of the stopping power, and the rear still belongs in the stop.

questions.q: A normal straight stop from city speed should feel like which pattern?
options: A locked front wheel held all the way to the stop line
A progressive front squeeze plus a steady rear press, bike upright
A rear-brake stomp with the front lever left alone
A clutch-in coast with no brake until the last instant
questions.explanation: Normal stops use both brakes, upright, with most of the power from a smooth front squeeze, about 70 percent.

questions.q: Leaving the rear brake unused in every stop is a poor habit because
options: The rear brake is only for ice and must never be used on dry pavement
Skipping the rear is how ABS is designed to be pumped
You should use both brakes
The rear brake is illegal to use if the front brake works
questions.explanation: Use both brakes in a normal stop. The front does most of the work, and the rear is still part of the stop. The rear adds stability and stopping power.

questions.q: Downshifting without the brakes is not enough when a car pulls across you. Why not?
options: Engine braking out-stops both brakes on dry pavement
A low gear locks the front wheel in a controlled way
Downshifting replaces ABS
Engine braking is not a substitute for both brakes in an emergency
questions.explanation: In an emergency, use both brakes. Engine braking helps slow the bike but does not replace the front and rear brakes.

questions.q: Engine braking in a sudden stop is best understood as what?
options: A helper at most
The primary emergency technique taught for panic stops
A way to lock the rear on purpose and hold the slide
Proof you can swerve and brake hard at the same time
questions.explanation: Do not rely on the engine alone when you need to stop now. Apply both brakes. A replacement for the front and rear brakes.

questions.q: In a true emergency on a straight, clear path, which tools actually make the stop?
options: A locked rear brake held while you lean the bike over
Both brakes, front doing most of the work
The gearbox only, with the brake levers covered but unused
A deliberate lay-down onto the pavement
questions.explanation: Emergency stopping power comes from both brakes. Engine braking is not a substitute, and a slide is not the plan. The gearbox by itself.

questions.q: The rear brake in a normal stop should be used how, relative to the front?
options: Ignored until the motorcycle is fully stopped
Applied only after you have started a hard swerve
Pressed along with the front
Stabbed hard enough to lock and then held locked
questions.explanation: Use both brakes together. The rear is part of the stop even though about 70 percent of the power is at the front.

questions.q: Both brakes belong in the stop, but the front can do too much if you do what?
options: Squeeze progressively while the motorcycle stays straight
Release immediately if the front wheel stops rolling and you have no ABS
Practice the same stop in an empty lot
Grab and lock the front wheel instead of squeezing up to a firm pressure
questions.explanation: Threshold braking is firm pressure just short of lockup. A grab that locks the front, without ABS, means release now so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly.

questions.q: Weight shifts forward during a hard stop. How should your front-brake pressure respond?
options: Increase it as weight moves forward, short of lockup
Drop it to zero the moment the fork compresses
Lock the lever and hold it there so the tire slides
Move all the pressure to the rear pedal only
questions.explanation: Threshold braking is firm pressure just short of lockup, adjusted as weight shifts forward onto the front tire.

questions.q: Threshold braking means which pressure, on a motorcycle without ABS?
options: Pumping the lever rapidly no matter what the tire is doing
Firm pressure just short of lockup, adjusted as the weight moves forward
A locked front wheel held until the bike stops
Light engine braking with both brakes released
questions.explanation: Threshold braking is firm brake pressure just short of a skid, changed as weight shifts onto the front tire.

questions.q: Firm pressure just short of a skid is the goal when the motorcycle has no ABS. What are you doing?
options: ABS pumping, even though this motorcycle has no ABS
A rear-brake-only stop from highway speed
Threshold braking, and you ease or add pressure as the stop loads the front
A lay-down, because any firm pressure means you should slide
questions.explanation: Without ABS, brake firmly up to the edge of lockup and adjust as weight shifts forward. That is threshold braking.

questions.q: As the fork dives in a straight stop, more traction is available at the front. What should you do with that?
options: Release the front completely so the rear can do all the work
Lock the front on purpose to spend that traction as a slide
Start a swerve while the lever is at maximum
Use more front brake, still short of lockup
questions.explanation: Weight shift forward is why the front brake can do about 70 percent of the work. Squeeze it, and do not throw that traction away on a lockup. Use it with a controlled front squeeze, still short of lockup if you have no ABS.

questions.q: If the front wheel locks and the motorcycle has no ABS, what is the immediate move?
options: Release the lever immediately so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly
Hold the lever tighter so the slide stays straight
Pump the lever in fast chops while the wheel stays locked
Ignore it and stomp the rear brake harder
questions.explanation: A locked front wheel, without ABS, will not steer. Release immediately so it rolls, then reapply the lever smoothly.

questions.q: A locked front tire on a bike without ABS is fixed by which sequence?
options: Pull in the clutch and wait for engine braking to unlock the tire
Let the lever out now, feel the tire roll, then squeeze again smoothly
Clamp the lever to the bar until the motorcycle stops
Add more rear brake and keep the front locked in a lean
questions.explanation: Release the front brake immediately on lockup if there is no ABS, so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly.

questions.q: Release the front lever the instant the tire stops rolling, but only when which equipment is missing?
options: A clutch, because engine braking will unlock a sliding tire
A helmet, because lockup is only a gear problem
ABS, because with ABS you hold a firm pressure and let the system pulse
A rear brake
questions.explanation: No ABS and a locked front: release immediately, then reapply. With ABS, squeeze and hold, and do not release just because you feel a pulse.

questions.q: Reapplying the front brake after a no-ABS lockup should be what kind of motion?
options: A harder grab than the one that locked the wheel
A pump that keeps the tire skidding the whole time
A complete refusal to use the front brake again
A smooth squeeze
questions.explanation: After you release a locked front wheel so it rolls, reapply smoothly. Do not grab the lever again. Another sudden grab.

questions.q: Without ABS, the front tire chirps and the bars go light. What does that feedback mean?
options: It is at its limit; ease off, then reapply
You should squeeze harder and hold a full lock
You should swerve immediately while staying on the lever
You should take both hands off the bars
questions.explanation: If the front wheel locks without ABS, release immediately so it rolls, then reapply smoothly. Do not hold the lock or swerve while braking hard. The front is at the edge or past it, so ease off enough for the tire to roll and then reload smoothly.

questions.q: The front tire has stopped rotating in a straight panic stop and there is no ABS. Why release at once?
options: The rear brake cannot work until the front has slid for a full second
A locked front wheel cannot steer and can wash out from under you
A locked front wheel is the shortest stop the course teaches
Releasing would cancel the engine braking you are relying on
questions.explanation: Release a locked front brake immediately when there is no ABS so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly. Holding the lock can drop the bike.

questions.q: Holding a locked front brake all the way to a stop, with no ABS, is likely to cause what?
options: The same pulse you should freeze and ignore on ABS
A required stoppie that you should catch with the rear brake
A loss of steering and a front-end slide
A shorter, more stable stop than threshold braking
questions.explanation: Do not hold a locked front wheel. Without ABS, release immediately so the tire rolls, then reapply smoothly.

questions.q: Going straight on a good-traction surface, you accidentally lock the rear brake. What does the MSF manual say you can do?
options: Add a hard front-brake grab and swerve
Shift to neutral and coast to a stop
Lean the motorcycle to scrub off speed
Keep it locked until you have stopped
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped; even with a locked rear wheel, you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going in a straight line."

questions.q: Why can releasing a locked rear brake be dangerous?
options: If the rear is out of line with the front, the bike can high-side
Releasing the rear brake always locks the front wheel
It switches the ABS off for the rest of the ride
It makes the engine stall at any speed
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "if the rear wheel is out of alignment with the front, there is a risk of a high-side crash. This occurs when the wheels are out of alignment and a locked rear wheel is released."

questions.q: ABS on the motorcycle you are riding begins to pulse in a hard straight stop. What should you do?
options: Pump the lever the way older non-ABS car advice sometimes said
Lock your elbows and swerve while the brakes stay at maximum
Keep a firm squeeze and press, and let the ABS pulse without pumping it
Release both brakes the moment you feel the pulse
questions.explanation: With ABS, squeeze and press firmly and hold. Let the system pulse. Do not pump it and do not release when you feel the pulse.

questions.q: When the ABS pulses under your fingers, that feeling means what?
options: The brakes have failed and you should release them completely
You should pump the lever faster than the pulse
You should stand the bike up by swerving against the brakes
The system is working, so hold firm pressure instead of letting go
questions.explanation: Do not release when you feel the ABS pulse. Hold a firm squeeze and press, and let ABS work.

questions.q: Pumping the ABS lever during a panic stop is a mistake because
options: ABS should be held firmly so it can pulse by itself
Pumping is the only way ABS can build pressure
ABS works only if you release the lever between each pulse
Pumping shifts the stop onto engine braking
questions.explanation: Do not pump ABS. Squeeze and press firmly and hold. The pulse is the system, not a signal to release or to pump.

questions.q: Feeling the lever chatter in a hard stop on an ABS motorcycle should lead you to
options: Add a hard swerve while you keep maximum braking
Maintain firm pressure and trust the pulse until the motorcycle stops
Snap the lever out and leave it out for the rest of the stop
Switch to engine braking only
questions.explanation: The chatter is ABS. Do not release when you feel it, and do not pump. Hold firm pressure.

questions.q: A firm hold on both brakes is the ABS technique. Which rider habit cancels that?
options: Practicing the same stop in an empty lot
Using the front and the rear together
Letting go as soon as the lever pulses, or pumping the lever yourself
Staying upright in a straight line while the system works
questions.explanation: ABS wants a firm squeeze and press, held. Do not pump, and do not release just because you feel the pulse.

questions.q: Motorcycle ABS is not a reason to do what in an emergency?
options: Brake firmly in a straight line and let the system manage lockup
Leave more following space as speed rises
Practice stops where you cannot hit anyone
Release the brakes when they pulse, or pump them as if there were no system
questions.explanation: With ABS, apply the brakes firmly and hold. The pulse is normal. Releasing or pumping throws away the system.

questions.q: The pulse under your boot on an ABS rear brake should be treated how?
options: As a cue to keep pressing firmly
As a cue to stomp harder and hold a locked rear in a lean
As a failure that means you should use engine braking only
As a signal to swerve while the pedal stays buried
questions.explanation: Let ABS pulse. Do not release when you feel it, and do not pump. A firm press is the technique. To lift off or to stab again.

questions.q: Do not release the brakes just because ABS chatters. What should you do instead?
options: Lean the bike and keep the lever pulled in
Hold firm pressure and let it pulse
Pump quickly so the chatter goes away
Take your fingers off and coast
questions.explanation: When you feel ABS pulse, do not let go. Squeeze and press firmly and hold. Hold firm pressure and let the system keep pulsing until you have stopped.

questions.q: Hard braking while you try to swerve can do what to the motorcycle?
options: Charge the ABS even if the motorcycle has no ABS
Turn a rear-wheel lock into a recommended curve technique
Stand the bike up or slide the tire, so separate the brake from the swerve
Make the swerve sharper and safer than braking first
questions.explanation: Do not brake hard while you swerve. Braking and swerving together can stand the bike up or slide the tire.

questions.q: Swerving with the front brake still squeezed hard is likely to cause what?
options: A tighter, cleaner swerve than one made with the brakes released
Automatic threshold braking in the new direction
A better stop than braking in a straight line first
The motorcycle stands up out of the lean, or the front tire slides
questions.explanation: Brake first and then swerve, or swerve with the brakes released. Do not brake hard and swerve together.

questions.q: Brake first, then swerve, when an obstacle appears in a straight line. Why that order?
options: So you are not braking hard at the same moment the bike needs to lean
So the front tire can stay locked during the lean
So engine braking can replace the swerve entirely
So you can lay the bike down as the planned third step
questions.explanation: Separate braking and swerving. A hard brake during the swerve can stand the bike up or slide the tire.

questions.q: A combined hard stop and a hard lean is the wrong pairing because
options: A lean makes engine braking stronger than both brakes
Braking can stand the bike up or slide a tire
The course wants both at full force in every emergency
ABS requires a swerve before it will pulse
questions.explanation: Do not brake hard while you swerve. Brake, then swerve, or swerve only after the brakes are released. The brakes can stand the motorcycle up or slide a tire if you swerve at the same time.

questions.q: Standing the bike up in the middle of an attempted swerve often comes from what?
options: A loose grip during a truck gust
Using the rear brake gently in a slow parking-lot turn
Braking hard while trying to lean away
Looking at the escape path with the brakes released
questions.explanation: Hard braking while swerving can stand the bike up. Release the brakes to swerve, or finish the braking before you swerve. Braking hard while you are trying to lean the motorcycle away from the hazard.

questions.q: Sliding the front tire during a swerve is more likely if you do what?
