options: Straighten, brake, and only then move over with the brakes eased
Look through the escape instead of at the obstacle
Practice the maneuver at low speed in an empty lot
Keep a hard front-brake squeeze while you ask the tire to change direction
questions.explanation: A tire that is braking hard has less left for a lean. Do not brake hard and swerve together or the tire can slide.

questions.q: Separate the stop from the direction change. Which sequence fits the course?
options: Brake in a straight line first, or swerve only with the brakes released
Grab the front brake at the same instant you countersteer
Lock the rear and hold it through the swerve
Use engine braking as the only way to do both jobs
questions.explanation: Braking and swerving together can stand the bike up or slide the tire. Separate them.

questions.q: If you must swerve right now, what should the brakes be doing?
options: Replaced by a deliberate lay-down
Released, so the tires can lean instead of braking hard at the same time
Locked in front and held there for stability
Pulsing because you are pumping a non-ABS lever on purpose
questions.explanation: If you swerve, do it with the brakes released. If you brake hard, do that first, in a straight line, and then swerve.

questions.q: Straighten the motorcycle somewhat before a hard stop in a curve when you have the room. Why?
options: Straightening is only for gravel
You should never brake until the curve is completely finished, even with room
A hard stop is more stable once the bike is more upright
A hard stop is safer at full lean with the front brake grabbed
questions.explanation: If you have room in a curve, straighten somewhat before a hard stop. A hard brake at full lean is a poor plan.

questions.q: Room to stand the bike up a little exists before a tight corner's hazard. How do you use it?
options: Grab the front brake while you hold the full lean
Stomp and hold a locked rear all the way around the bend
Swerve and brake hard in one motion toward the hazard
Straighten somewhat, then make the hard stop more upright
questions.explanation: When there is room, straighten somewhat before a hard stop. Do not grab the front brake at maximum lean.

questions.q: Slowing gently inside a curve, because you cannot straighten yet, should be done how?
options: Smoothly and gradually, with less force than when upright
With a sudden handful of front brake at full lean
With a locked rear held until the apex
By shutting the engine off with the cut-off switch
questions.explanation: MSF manual: if conditions do not allow you to straighten first, "brake smoothly and gradually, but do not apply as much braking force as you would if the motorcycle were straight up." As you slow, reduce the lean and brake more firmly.

questions.q: Panic on the front lever in the middle of a lean is a common way to do what?
options: Activate a no-ABS pump routine the course prefers
Overload the front tire or stand the bike up
Meet the course standard for slowing in a curve
Replace a gentle use of the rear brake
questions.explanation: Do not panic-grab the front brake while leaned. If you must slow in the curve, be gentle and smooth, with more rear than that grab. Overload the front tire or stand the bike up, so avoid that grab.

questions.q: The gap ahead of you at higher speed is a braking tool. What is the course minimum in good conditions?
options: One second, because motorcycles stop in half a car's distance at any speed
Whatever fits between you and the bumper, as long as you can see paint
Four seconds is the maximum you are ever allowed to leave
At least 2 seconds, and more as speed, traffic, or conditions demand
questions.explanation: The MSF minimum following time is 2 seconds. Increase it as speed rises, because stopping distance grows much faster than speed.

questions.q: Two seconds is the minimum following time under good conditions. When should it be longer?
options: At night, and when the pavement is slippery
Only when you are practicing stoppies in traffic
Never, because 2 seconds is also the maximum
Only if you have ABS, and shorter if you do not
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "If the pavement is slippery, if you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front of you, open up a three-second or more following distance." At night: "Open up a three-second following distance or more."

questions.q: At night the following time should be longer than the sunny-day minimum because
options: ABS must be pumped at night and that takes less room
You see hazards later at night
Darkness shortens stops
The front brake loses the 70 percent share after sunset
questions.explanation: The minimum is 2 seconds in good conditions. At night, leave more time because you may identify the hazard late. You see hazards later, and stopping distance still grows quickly with speed.

questions.q: In a group, the following time behind the rider directly ahead should be at least how long?
options: Zero, if you are riding side by side in the same lane
Ten seconds is required between every rider at any speed
About 2 seconds
Half a second
questions.explanation: Leave about 2 seconds behind the rider directly ahead of you. The staggered offset is about one second. Add more in bad conditions.

questions.q: Bad weather calls for a following gap that is
options: Shorter than 2 seconds so you can use the car's tire tracks only
Unchanged, because rain does not affect braking distance
Replaced by engine braking with the brakes covered but unused
Longer than the 2-second minimum
questions.explanation: In bad weather, increase following time beyond 2 seconds. Stopping takes longer when traction drops. Traction and sight are worse.

questions.q: Rain adds to stopping distance. Which gap choice matches that fact?
options: More than the dry-pavement minimum of 2 seconds
Less than 2 seconds
A gap of a few feet, closed up behind a truck
No gap change, but a harder front-brake grab in every curve
questions.explanation: Bad weather means more following time than the 2-second minimum. Rain lengthens the stop and reduces traction.

questions.q: A one-second gap at road speed is too short because
options: The front brake needs less room as speed rises
The minimum is two seconds, and stops grow fast
One second is the required maximum in good weather
One second is the ABS pulse interval you must match
questions.explanation: Do not follow at one second. The course minimum is 2 seconds, and the gap must grow as speed rises. Even the minimum is 2 seconds, and stopping distance grows much faster than speed.

questions.q: A car ahead stops suddenly on a straight dry street. Which braking picture is correct?
options: A hard swerve with the front brake still at maximum
Engine braking only, because there is no time for the levers
A locked rear held while you lean away from the car
Both brakes, firm, with the bike upright
questions.explanation: Emergency stops use both brakes in a straight line. Do not brake hard and swerve at the same time. Both brakes, motorcycle upright, firm pressure, and no swerve until the brakes are released.

questions.q: Your motorcycle has no ABS and the front tire just stopped spinning. How fast should the lever come out?
options: Immediately, so the wheel can roll, followed by a smooth reapply
After you have slid for a full second, then hold whatever remains
Never, because a locked front is threshold braking
Only after you have also locked the rear and held it
questions.explanation: Without ABS, release a locked front brake immediately so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly.

questions.q: Your motorcycle has ABS and the same hard stop makes the lever buzz. How is that different?
options: You take your hand off and use only the rear pedal
You hold pressure and let ABS pulse
You release immediately
You pump the lever until the buzz stops
questions.explanation: ABS: squeeze firmly and hold, even when it pulses. No ABS: if the front locks, release immediately, then reapply smoothly. You hold the firm pressure and let ABS pulse, instead of releasing the way you would without ABS.

questions.q: Comparing the two machines, a buzzing lever means hold, and a silent locked front means release. What is the split?
options: Pump both kinds of brakes as fast as you can
Use engine braking in place of either system
Hold firm pressure on ABS
Release on both kinds of motorcycle the moment anything feels wrong
questions.explanation: Do not treat ABS and a non-ABS lockup the same way. Hold ABS. Release a locked non-ABS front immediately, then reapply smoothly.

questions.q: A downhill street still needs a real stop at the bottom light. What is not sufficient by itself?
options: Using the front and rear brakes together, adjusted for the extra speed the hill adds
Leaving a longer gap
Staying upright instead of swerving against the brakes
Rolling off the throttle and trusting engine braking to replace both brakes
questions.explanation: Engine braking is not a substitute for both brakes in an emergency, including a downhill stop. Use the brakes.

questions.q: Wet pavement makes a threshold stop arrive sooner. What changes in your pressure?
options: You reach the edge of lockup with less lever force
You grab harder than on dry pavement
You stop using the front brake and lock the rear instead
You pump ABS even though the motorcycle does not have it
questions.explanation: Threshold braking is firm pressure just short of lockup. On a wet road that point comes sooner, so adjust as the weight shifts forward.

questions.q: You are leaned over and a patch of gravel is still ahead, but you are not on it yet. What belongs to braking skill here?
options: A swerve with the front brake squeezed hard
Slow gently before you reach the gravel
A panic front grab at full lean once the tire is on the stones
A locked rear held through the gravel and the curve
questions.explanation: Set the speed before the hazard. If you have room, straighten somewhat before a hard stop. Do not panic-grab the front while you are leaned.

questions.q: Counting a following gap, you pass a sign two seconds after the car ahead. At a higher speed that same two seconds is
options: A substitute for using both brakes if the car stops
The minimum, which covers more road at speed
Too long, so you should close up until the gap looks the same in feet
Illegal, because the course maximum is one second
questions.explanation: Two seconds is the minimum following time. As speed rises, stopping distance grows much faster, so do not shrink the time gap. The minimum, not a reason to move closer, because the feet in that gap must grow as speed rises.

questions.q: Practicing a quick stop, you feel the front tire lock on a bike without ABS. The drill is not finished until you
options: Hold the lock and try to catch a stoppie
Swerve out of the lot while the lever stays in
Stand on the rear pedal and hold that lock through a turn
Release immediately, let the wheel roll, and reapply smoothly
questions.explanation: Practice the real skill in an empty lot: if the front locks and there is no ABS, release immediately and reapply smoothly. Do not stunt it.

questions.q: Practicing on an ABS motorcycle, the correct hard-stop habit is which one?
options: A firm squeeze and press, held, while the system pulses
A pump each time you feel the pulse
A release the instant the lever chatters
A front-brake grab in a tight circle to see if ABS holds the bike up
questions.explanation: With ABS, squeeze and press firmly and hold. Do not pump and do not let go when it pulses. Practice that in an empty lot, not as a stunt.

questions.q: You need to miss a board in the lane and you have already started a hard stop. What should you not add?
options: Eyes on the clear path rather than on the board
A swerve while the brakes are still applied hard
A straight finish to the stop if the board is inside the stopping distance
A later move sideways only after the brakes are released
questions.explanation: Do not brake hard while you swerve. Either stop straight, or release the brakes and then swerve.

questions.q: A curve has a wide straight section of your lane before the hazard. How should a hard stop be set up?
options: Stay at full lean and grab the front brake
Hold a locked rear while you keep the lean
Downshift only and save both brakes for the next corner
Straighten first, then brake hard upright
questions.explanation: If you have room, straighten somewhat before a hard stop. Hard braking belongs on a more upright motorcycle.

questions.q: No room to straighten, and the curve is already under you. The front lever should receive what?
options: No panic grab
A maximum squeeze equal to a straight-line emergency stop
Nothing at all, and no rear brake either, only a downshift
A pump, whether or not the motorcycle has ABS
questions.explanation: When you must slow in a curve, be gentle and smooth. More rear than a panic grab of the front.

questions.q: Using the front brake for about 70 percent of a normal stop still includes the rear because
options: The rear is only a backup if the front lever breaks
The 70 percent figure is the rear brake's share
ABS cancels the front brake and leaves only the rear
Both brakes are the technique
questions.explanation: About 70 percent front is the teaching figure, and you still use the rear brake with it. Use both brakes.

questions.q: Smooth reapply after a front-wheel release is the second half of which no-ABS skill?
options: Releasing a locked front, then squeezing again
Pumping the lever so the tire never rolls
Holding the first lock all the way through the stop
Swerving while the lever comes back in hard
questions.explanation: If the front locks and there is no ABS, release immediately so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly. Unlocking the front by releasing immediately, then squeezing again without another grab.

questions.q: Just short of lockup is a moving target during one stop. Why does the target move?
options: Engine braking fixes the target so you should not adjust the lever
Weight shifts forward
Weight shifts backward
ABS always moves it, even on a motorcycle that has no ABS
questions.explanation: Threshold braking is firm pressure just short of lockup, adjusted as weight shifts forward. The front can take more pressure and you adjust to stay at the edge.

questions.q: A rider pumps a non-ABS front brake in rapid chops and keeps the tire skidding. What is the better pattern?
options: A harder grab that holds the lock
A swerve added on top of the chops
Release so it rolls, then reapply smoothly
Faster chops so the skid never breaks
questions.explanation: Do not pump a locked non-ABS front. Release immediately so the wheel rolls, then reapply smoothly.

questions.q: Fog cuts your view of the brake lights ahead. The following-time rule that applies is
options: More than 2 seconds
Less than 2 seconds so you can see the car's bumper
Exactly the length of one car, no matter the speed
Whatever engine braking can cover without using the brakes
questions.explanation: In bad weather, leave more than the 2-second minimum. You need the extra time because you see the hazard later and may have less traction.

questions.q: You have ABS, a straight lane, and a vehicle stopped ahead. The lever starts to pulse near the end. Finish by
options: Pumping in time with the pulse
Swerving the last few feet with the brakes still hard on
Holding firm pressure through the pulse
Releasing both brakes so the pulse will not ruin the stop
questions.explanation: Do not release when ABS pulses. Squeeze and press firmly and hold. Let the system work. Holding the firm pressure through the pulse until you are stopped or the hazard is handled.

questions.q: Engine braking down a grade keeps the speed in check on a normal ride, but a sudden blockage still requires
options: A locked front held if the bike has no ABS
A swerve combined with maximum braking
A deliberate lay-down if the grade is steep
Both brakes, not just engine braking
questions.explanation: Engine braking is not a substitute for both brakes in an emergency. Use the front and the rear.

questions.q: The teaching figure of about 70 percent front assumes you are also doing what?
options: Applying the rear brake
Locking the front as proof of that percentage
Leaving the rear pedal for curves only
Replacing the front with a downshift
questions.explanation: About 70 percent of normal stopping power is the front brake, used together with the rear. Use both brakes. Treating the front as the only control.

questions.q: A curve, a hard stop, and enough lane to reduce the lean all come together. The skilled order is
options: Swerve toward the outside while the front brake is locked
Reduce the lean, then brake hard more upright
Brake hard first at full lean, then try to straighten
Lock the rear and hold the lean
questions.explanation: If you have room, straighten somewhat before a hard stop. Do not start that hard stop at full lean. Reduce the lean somewhat, then brake hard while the motorcycle is more upright.

questions.q: Following a rider directly ahead of you in clear weather, the timing floor is
options: About half a second so your headlight fills their mirror
Side by side, which counts as two seconds
Whatever keeps your front tire beside their rear tire
About 2 seconds, more when risk rises
questions.explanation: The minimum following time is 2 seconds behind the rider directly ahead. Increase it at night, in a group when the situation calls for more, or in bad weather.

questions.q: The oily, debris-filled part of a typical lane is usually which MSF position?
options: The painted lane line, which the course calls position 4
Position 2, the center third
Position 1, the left third
Position 3, the right third
questions.explanation: MSF numbers the lane as left third (1), center (2), and right third (3). The center often collects oil and debris, so a tire track is usually better.

questions.q: According to the current MSF manual, which part of your lane must always be avoided?
options: The center third
The left third
The right third
None of them
questions.explanation: MSF manual (18th edition): vary your lane position as conditions warrant, "keeping in mind that no portion of the lane need be avoided — including the center." The center collects oil drippings, but "unless the road is wet, the typical center strip permits adequate traction." Avoid big buildups of oil at busy intersections and tollbooths.

questions.q: MSF lane position 1 is which part of your lane?
options: The center third, where oil usually gathers
The right third, next to the shoulder
The opposing lane, just across the centerline
The left third of the lane
questions.explanation: Position 1 is the left third of the lane. Position 2 is the center, and position 3 is the right third. The left third, a common tire-track choice when it is clear.

questions.q: MSF lane position 3 is found in which part of the lane?
options: In the right third of your lane, often the right tire track
In the center, on top of the oil strip
On the centerline paint so you can share with an oncoming car
Beside a truck trailer, in the no-view zone
questions.explanation: Position 3 is the right third. It is a normal place to ride when that tire track is clean and it fits the situation.

questions.q: A dark stripe of oil shines in the center third on a warm day. Which path is the better default?
options: The painted lane line
The opposing lane
A clear left or right track
The oil stripe itself
questions.explanation: Avoid the oily center when you can. Ride a tire track, the left third or the right third, instead of the debris in position 2.

questions.q: You are entitled to the full lane. What does that rule forbid as a courtesy habit?
options: Moving between the left and right tire tracks as conditions change
Taking position 1 when a left-turning driver needs to see you
Leaving two seconds of space ahead of you
Riding the paint so a car can squeeze beside you in the same lane
questions.explanation: A motorcycle is entitled to the full lane. Do not ride the paint to share that lane with a car.

questions.q: A driver motions you onto the white lane line so they can pass inside your lane. What should you do?
options: Keep the lane instead of riding the paint to share it with the car
Accept the wave and ride the line
Move into the car's blind spot and stay there
Speed up and weave so you lose them in the traffic ahead
questions.explanation: Do not share a lane with a car, and do not ride the paint to make room. You are entitled to the full lane.

questions.q: Sharing one lane with a car, side by side, violates which national riding point?
options: You must filter wherever traffic is stopped
You do not give up the lane by riding the paint so two vehicles occupy it
You must always ride position 2 even when it is oily
You must pass every car one at a time inside the same lane
questions.explanation: Do not share a lane with a car. Stay in your lane. Filtering is not a national permission.

questions.q: The white line on your right looks like a place to let a car crowd past. Why refuse it?
options: Paint is the best traction in the rain
The line keeps you visible to a left-turning driver
Riding the paint to share the lane gives up the space you are entitled to
The line is position 1 and the required group-leader spot
questions.explanation: Do not ride the paint so a car can share your lane. The motorcycle is entitled to the full lane.

questions.q: Before you move from the left track into the lane on your left, which sequence fits the course?
options: Move first, then signal, then glance at the mirror
Mirror only, because a head check makes the motorcycle weave
Honk and change lanes without a signal if the gap looks empty
Signal, check the mirror, turn your head to check the blind spot, then move
questions.explanation: Before a lane change: signal, mirror, head check by turning your head, then move. Mirrors have blind spots.

questions.q: Mirrors have blind spots, so a lane change still needs what after the mirror check?
options: A head check, turning your head to see the space the mirror missed
A longer stare into the same mirror until you feel sure
A move onto the paint while you decide
A speed increase that closes the gap you meant to use
questions.explanation: Turn your head before you move. The mirror does not show the whole blind spot beside you.

questions.q: Signal, mirror, head check, then move is the lane-change order. Which step do riders skip most dangerously?
options: None, because mirrors show every car beside you
The head check, leaving a car hidden in the mirror's blind spot
The signal, which matters less than riding the lane line
The move itself
questions.explanation: Mirrors have blind spots. Turn your head and look before you change lanes. Signal and mirror come before that move.

questions.q: You signaled and the mirror looks empty, but a car is beside your hip. What failed?
options: The entitlement to the full lane, which requires you to share
Position 2, which should have been held in the oil stripe
The head check
Nothing, because an empty mirror means the lane is empty
questions.explanation: Before you move, turn your head. A mirror can miss the car in your blind spot. The look mirrors cannot replace.

questions.q: Turn your head before a lane change so you can see what?
options: The oil in the center of the lane you are leaving
The leader's hand signal only, with no need to see traffic
A path onto the paint where a car can share your lane
The blind spot the mirror does not cover
questions.explanation: A head check means turning your head to see the blind spot. Then move, after the signal and the mirror.

questions.q: Do not ride for long in the blind spot beside a car's rear quarter. What should you do instead?
options: Move forward or drop back into a place the driver can see
Stay there, because that spot is position 2
Ride the door line so you share the car's lane
Speed up and lose the car by weaving ahead
questions.explanation: A car's blind spot is a bad place to ride. Do not linger where the driver cannot see you in a mirror or with a glance.

questions.q: Lingering beside a truck's trailer is dangerous for which visibility reason?
options: That spot is the outside of every curve
The driver cannot see you there, and the trailer hides a huge space
The trailer is the cleanest tire track, called position 1
Trucks expect motorcycles to share the trailer lane
questions.explanation: Do not linger beside a truck's trailer. It is a blind area. Move where the driver can see you.

questions.q: You have matched a trailer's speed and your helmet is beside the trailer wheels. What is the position error?
options: You are in the left tire track
You should move onto the trailer paint and share that lane
You are lingering in the truck's blind area instead of moving ahead or back
You are correctly holding the staggered one-second offset
questions.explanation: Do not linger beside a truck trailer. Get out of the blind area by passing or dropping back when it is safe.

questions.q: What lane position does the MSF manual call a good choice for a curve?
options: Across the centerline, for the widest view
The center of your lane, from entry to exit
Side by side with another motorcycle
On the painted edge line the whole way
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "A good choice is to move to the center of your lane before entering a curve — and stay there until you exit. This permits you to spot approaching traffic as soon as possible." Change position for traffic, road conditions and the curve of the road.

questions.q: An oncoming car might cross the centerline in a blind curve. Your lane position should
options: Leave room for that car and still let you see, without leaving your lane
Move into the opposing lane early so you claim the space first
Sit on the centerline paint and share with whatever comes
Hide in the center behind a slower car
questions.explanation: Curve position should help you see and leave room for an oncoming car that crosses the center. Stay in your lane.

questions.q: The leader of a staggered group belongs in which track?
options: The left tire track, with the next rider in the right track
The center oil strip, with everyone directly behind in one file on that stripe
The right paint, sharing the lane with the second rider beside them
Beside the trailer of the truck the group is passing
questions.explanation: In a staggered group the leader rides the left track and the next rider rides the right track. Do not ride side by side.

questions.q: The rider just behind the leader in a stagger should be where?
options: In the opposing lane so the group can see farther
In the right track, about one second offset from the leader
Side by side with the leader in the same lane
In the leader's blind spot, one foot off the rear tire
questions.explanation: The next rider after the leader takes the right track with about a one-second offset. They are not beside the leader.

questions.q: About two seconds is the gap to which rider in a staggered pair of tracks?
options: The car in the next lane, which you should match bumper to bumper
The tailgater behind the group, whom you should brake-check
The rider directly ahead of you
The rider in the other track
questions.explanation: Keep about two seconds behind the rider directly ahead of you. The stagger offset to the other track is about one second.

questions.q: A one-second offset in a stagger is not permission to do what?
options: Use the left and right tire tracks
Leave about two seconds to the rider in your own track
Pass one rider at a time when a pass is needed
Ride side by side in the same lane with the other motorcycle
questions.explanation: Do not ride side by side in the same lane. A stagger uses the left and right tracks with a one-second offset, not a paired ride.

questions.q: When a staggered group passes a slow vehicle, the pass should be made how?
options: One rider at a time
Two riders abreast so they share the passing lane
By moving onto the paint and squeezing past inside the same lane
By the whole group speeding up together with no signals
questions.explanation: Pass one at a time. Do not ride side by side, and do not turn the pass into a shared lane with a car.

questions.q: Side-by-side riding in one lane breaks the stagger because
options: The one-second offset is measured bumper to bumper with a car
The formation uses offset tracks, about one second apart
The course requires every rider in position 2
Side by side is the required way to be seen at intersections
questions.explanation: Do not ride side by side in the same lane. Stagger: leader left, next rider right, about one second offset, about two seconds to the rider directly ahead. Paired handlebars.

questions.q: Following distance at least 2 seconds is the floor. Which situation pushes it higher?
options: Any time you want to share a lane
Only when you are lingering beside a trailer
Night, slippery pavement, or heavy traffic
A sunny day on an empty open road, where less than 2 seconds is required
questions.explanation: MSF manual: open up three seconds or more "if the pavement is slippery, if you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy", and at night.

questions.q: At night you can see less of what the car ahead may stop for. The position and gap answer is
options: Less than 2 seconds so their taillights fill your view
The painted line, shared with the car ahead
The truck's trailer flank, where their lights are brightest
More than 2 seconds, in a visible track
questions.explanation: Increase following distance at night beyond the 2-second minimum, and do not ride where you are hidden. More than 2 seconds of following time, in a visible tire track rather than a blind spot.

questions.q: Rain on the ride home means the following gap should
options: Open beyond 2 seconds
Close under 2 seconds so you can follow the car's dry patch in the oil stripe
Stay on the lane line where the paint gives a reference
Be replaced by riding beside the car in its blind spot
questions.explanation: In bad weather, leave more than 2 seconds. The center may also be slicker, so choose a cleaner tire track. Weather makes the stop less certain.

questions.q: Someone is tailgating you in the left third. The space you should add is where?
options: In the opposing lane, by speeding up to lose them
In front of you
Behind you, by brake-checking until they drop back
Beside you, by moving onto the paint and letting them share
questions.explanation: When you are tailgated, add space in front of you. Do not brake-check and do not speed up to lose them. You can slow without a sudden stop.

questions.q: A tailgater cannot pass because you are beside them in a narrow lane. When it is safe, you should
options: Brake-check them, then return to the blind spot
Share the lane by riding the paint until they squeeze through
Move over so they can pass, without speeding up to lose them in traffic
Speed up and weave so they cannot get by
questions.explanation: Move over when it is safe so a tailgater can pass. Add space ahead. Do not speed up to lose them.

questions.q: Losing a tailgater by accelerating through gaps is the wrong move because
options: Higher speed always shortens the stop you might need
The course wants you to brake-check first and talk later
You should share your lane so they can occupy it with you
You should add space in front and let them pass when it is safe
questions.explanation: Do not speed up to lose a tailgater. Add room ahead and move over when safe so they can pass. Race away.

questions.q: A driver ahead is preparing to turn left across your path. What does the MSF manual say to do?
options: Slow, and pick the lane position where that driver can see you
Stay in the center, stacked directly behind a tall van
Ride the right paint, shared with a car that is also turning
Wait beside a trailer in the next lane until the light changes
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "slow and select a lane position to increase your visibility to that driver. Cover the clutch lever and both brakes to reduce reaction time. As you enter the intersection, move away from the vehicle."

questions.q: Hiding in position 2 behind a taller car at a left-turn intersection is weak because
options: You should ride the paint and share with the car ahead
The turning driver cannot see you there
Position 2 is the most visible place in every intersection
The center is required whenever a car might turn left
questions.explanation: A visible lane position, often the left third, plus slowing, is better than hiding in the center behind another vehicle. The turning driver cannot see you, whereas the left track often shows you earlier.

questions.q: Slowing as you hold a visible left-track position near a left-turn threat does what a hidden center spot does not?
options: It replaces the head check on a later lane change
It is the staggered side-by-side formation
It shows you to the driver and gives you time to brake
It forces you to share the lane with the turning car
questions.explanation: Often the left track makes you visible to a driver who might turn left across you. Slow as well. Do not hide in the center stack.

questions.q: Stopped traffic fills two lanes ahead. Riding the paint between those lanes is acceptable when?
options: Whenever traffic is stopped
By leaving the roadway and riding the sidewalk until traffic moves
Whenever a driver waves, even if you must share their lane
Only where your state allows filtering
questions.explanation: Lane splitting or filtering is not a national right. Do it only where your state allows it; otherwise stay in your lane.

questions.q: A friend says motorcycles may always filter between stopped cars. What is the national answer?
options: Stay in your lane unless your state specifically allows that maneuver
The empty paint between cars is a lane you are entitled to share
You should leave the pavement and wait on the shoulder every time traffic stops
It is required in a staggered group so riders can pass one at a time
questions.explanation: Do not share a lane, and do not filter as a national habit. Do it only where your state allows it; otherwise stay in your lane.

questions.q: Filtering forward between lanes of cars is a state rule, not a national one. Until you know your state allows it, you should
options: Pass the whole line side by side with another rider
Stay in your lane rather than riding the gap beside the cars
Ride the paint
Linger beside the nearest trailer while you decide
questions.explanation: The national answer is to stay in the lane unless your state specifically allows filtering. Do not assume the maneuver is yours everywhere.

questions.q: The third rider in a stagger falls back into which place?
options: The center oil stripe, one foot behind the second rider
The opposing lane
The left track, two seconds behind the leader
Side by side with the leader, sharing the left third
questions.explanation: The rider directly ahead of the third rider is the leader in the left track. Leave about two seconds. The diagonal rider is only the one-second offset.

questions.q: A fourth rider in the same stagger should line up with whom?
options: The leader, side by side in the left third
A car in the next lane, bumper to door
The trailer beside the group, matching its speed
The second rider's track, two seconds back
questions.explanation: Riders in the same track keep about two seconds. The fourth rider follows the right-track rider, not a side-by-side pair.

questions.q: Curvy pavement is a reason for a group to leave the stagger and do what?
options: Form a single file with at least a 2-second gap, instead of riding side by side
Pull up handlebar to handlebar so everyone sees the same apex
Share each lane with a car through the bends
Drop to a one-second tailgate in the oily center
questions.explanation: On a curvy road, a single-file formation with at least 2 seconds is the better space cushion. Do not ride side by side.

questions.q: Entering a highway, the group should be in what order before it spreads back into a stagger?
options: Side by side on the ramp so two riders merge as one wide vehicle
Split across the ramp paint, sharing the ramp with cars
Stacked in the ramp's blind spot beside a merging truck
Single file, so each rider has room to merge, then stagger once everyone is on
questions.explanation: Use single file when entering or leaving a highway. Do not ride side by side through the merge. Stagger again once the group is safely on.

questions.q: Leaving a freeway, the formation that gives each rider a merge cushion is
options: Single file with at least 2 seconds
A stagger so tight that the bikes' bars overlap
Position 2 for everyone, on the oil, bumper to bumper
A filter between the cars that are also exiting
questions.explanation: Entering or leaving a highway is a time for single file and a real following gap. Do not share a lane and do not ride side by side. A side-by-side pair on the ramp.

questions.q: Passing a slow truck, two riders start to pull out together. What should the second rider do?
options: Ride the truck's trailer flank until both are ahead
Share the truck's lane by riding its paint
Wait and pass one at a time, after a signal, mirror, and head check
Stay side by side with the first passer through the whole pass
questions.explanation: Pass one at a time. A lane change still needs a signal, a mirror check, and a head check before you move.

questions.q: The rider ahead in your track passes a car. You should start your own pass when?
options: At the same instant, side by side
From the car's blind spot without a head check
By riding the centerline paint beside the car
After that rider is clear and you have checked
questions.explanation: Pass one at a time. Do not follow somebody's pass side by side. Check the blind spot yourself before you move. After that rider is clear and you have done your own signal, mirror, and head check.

questions.q: A lane change on a freeway still fails if you only look in the mirror because
options: The mirror's blind spot can hide a car beside you until you turn your head
Mirrors show the entire trailer no-zone and the next lane
A head check is only for group rides
You are entitled to move without looking if you own the full lane
questions.explanation: Mirrors have blind spots. Signal, check the mirror, turn your head, and only then move.

questions.q: Over your left shoulder, before you move left, you are looking for
options: The one-second stagger of a car beside your door
A vehicle the left mirror did not show in the blind spot
The oil stripe you intend to ride in the new lane
Permission to share the new lane by riding its paint
questions.explanation: Turn your head on the side you are moving toward. The head check covers the blind spot the mirror misses.

questions.q: You want the right lane. The order that matches the course is
options: Head check only, with no signal
Ride the line first and signal after you are beside the other car
Signal right, check the right mirror, look over your right shoulder, then move
Move right, then look, then signal if someone honks
questions.explanation: Signal, mirror, head check, then move. Do the head check on the side you are entering.

questions.q: A car is exactly where your mirror is blank, beside your left elbow. The lane change should
options: Go now, because a blank mirror means the spot is empty
Go now along the paint so you share that car's space
Go now and speed up to lose the car you cannot see
Wait until a head check shows that blind spot is empty
questions.explanation: Do not trust the mirror alone. Turn your head. If the blind spot is occupied, do not move into it.

questions.q: After you pass a car, returning to a tire track in the lane should not include
options: Lingering beside the driver's door in the blind spot
A clean move back once you are fully ahead and seen
A signal and a head check if you are changing lanes to return
Space ahead so you are not glued to the bumper you just passed
questions.explanation: Do not linger in a blind spot after the pass. Complete the pass and leave the driver a place to see you.

questions.q: The no-zone along a box trailer is a poor place to cruise because
options: It lets you share the trailer lane by riding on the paint
The truck driver cannot see you there, so do not linger beside the trailer
It is MSF position 1, the required highway track
It is the outside line for every right-hand curve
questions.explanation: Do not linger beside a truck's trailer. Move ahead or drop back into view. That flank is a blind area.

questions.q: You are about to be passed by a long truck. Where should you avoid settling?
options: Well back, with more than a tight gap
In a tire track of your lane rather than on the paint
Beside the trailer, matching its speed in the driver's blind area
Ahead of the truck, in your own lane, where the driver can see you
questions.explanation: Do not linger beside the trailer while the truck passes or while you pass it. Blind space beside a trailer is a bad place to ride.

questions.q: Sand and a dark oil film sit in the middle third after a light rain. Your path should
options: Move to a cleaner left or right tire track before you are on that film
Stay in position 2
Ride the painted arrow in the center while you brake
Split the lane with the car ahead, one wheel on the paint
questions.explanation: The center often collects oil and debris, and the first rain makes that worse. Choose a tire track before you reach the slick middle.

questions.q: A patched seam and loose gravel occupy the right tire track. The lane choice that still respects the lane is
options: The center debris stripe, held no matter what is in it
The clear left third, inside your lane
The opposing lane
The right paint, shared with the gravel and a car
questions.explanation: Pick the cleaner tire track inside your lane. You are entitled to the full lane, and you do not need to ride a dirty track or the paint. The clear left third, position 1, without crossing into the opposing lane.

questions.q: Parked cars fill the curb on your right. A useful lane position is
options: The opposing lane
A car's blind spot in the travel lane beside you
Far enough left to avoid an opening door
The right paint, in the door's arc
questions.explanation: Use your lane. Move away from likely door swings toward a clearer part of the lane, and do not ride the paint or the opposing lane. Far enough left in your lane to avoid an opening door, still inside the lane.

questions.q: A blind left-hand curve puts oncoming traffic on your right side of the centerline. Room for a car that crosses that line comes from
options: A position more toward the right side of your lane
A position across the centerline in the oncoming lane
The painted centerline itself, shared with the oncoming car
A side-by-side pair that fills the lane from line to line
questions.explanation: Start toward the outside so you can see, and leave room if an oncoming car crosses the center. On a left curve that outside is toward the right side of your lane. Stay in your lane. Also the outside view line.

questions.q: Two motorcycles enter a tight curve abreast in one lane. The formation error is
options: A proper stagger
Position 1 and 3 used correctly at the same time beside each other
The required way to leave room for an oncoming car
Side-by-side riding, which a curve should replace with single file and real gaps
questions.explanation: Do not ride side by side. On a curvy road, single file with at least 2 seconds gives each rider room to see and maneuver.

questions.q: The one-second figure in a stagger is the offset to the diagonal rider. It is not
options: The following time to the rider directly ahead in your track
A real spacing idea the course uses
Shorter than the gap you keep to the rider in your own track
A reason to avoid riding handlebar to handlebar
questions.explanation: About one second is the stagger offset. About two seconds is the gap to the rider directly ahead of you. Do not confuse them and ride side by side.

questions.q: Keeping two seconds to the motorcycle directly ahead matters inside a stagger because
options: It allows you to share the lane with a car between the tracks
That is the rider you would hit if you only watched the diagonal one-second bike
The diagonal rider is the only one who counts
Two seconds is too long and collapses the formation into position 2
questions.explanation: The rider directly ahead of you, in your track, needs about a 2-second gap. The bike in the other track is the shorter offset, not your only cushion.

questions.q: Night riding in a group should stretch following time because
options: You should ride side by side so each rider's headlight covers a track
You should filter between cars to stay with the group
The 2-second minimum grows when it is dark, even if the stagger pattern stays the same
Darkness lets you close to under a second and still see
questions.explanation: At night, leave more than a bare minimum. In a group, still keep about 2 seconds to the rider directly ahead, and add more when the dark reduces what you can see.

questions.q: A car is following the last rider too closely. That rider's best space change is
options: A brake-check to punish the car
A sprint through traffic to lose the car
A shift onto the paint so the car can share the lane
More room in front, plus a move over when safe so the car can pass
questions.explanation: When you are tailgated, add space ahead of you and move over when it is safe so the driver can pass. Do not speed up to lose them.

questions.q: A driver is following you closely and you need to slow down. What does the MSF manual suggest?
options: Flash your brake light before you slow
Speed up until they fall back behind you
Brake hard with no warning
Move onto the lane line
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "If you are being followed closely, it's a good idea to flash your brake light before you slow. The tailgater may be watching you and not see something ahead that will make you slow down." The better fix for a tailgater is to let them pass.

questions.q: Speeding up to drop a tailgater in a crowded lane usually
options: Is safer than a 2-second gap
Removes your own escape space
Is the course method
Counts as moving over so they can pass
questions.explanation: Do not speed up to lose a tailgater. Keep extra space in front and let them pass when it is safe. Removes your own escape and is not the way to handle the follower.

questions.q: Position 2 at a left-turn intersection is the weak choice when it means
options: You are hidden where the turning driver can't see
You are in the left tire track where you can be seen
You have slowed and covered the brakes
You have left a 2-second gap ahead
questions.explanation: The center can hide you behind another vehicle. For a left-turn threat, a visible track, often the left third, is the better position. You are stacked in the center where the turning driver cannot pick you out.

questions.q: Between two lanes of stopped cars, the gap looks wide enough for your bars. National guidance says
options: Take the gap side by side with another motorcycle
Stay in your lane unless your state specifically allows you to filter there
Take the gap whenever cars are stopped, with no need to know your state's rule
Take the gap only after another rider waves you between the cars
questions.explanation: Filtering is not yours as a national right. Do it only where your state allows it; otherwise stay in your lane.

questions.q: Your state law is unclear and traffic is stopped. The safe national default is
options: Assume the gap between the cars is yours until someone objects
Leave the lane and ride the shoulder even where your state would allow the maneuver
Remain in the lane you are in
Ride the paint
questions.explanation: If you do not know that your state allows filtering, stay in your lane. Do not treat the maneuver as a national permission. Moving between cars.

questions.q: A rider tells you to ignore a state that allows filtering and never ride between lanes. What should you do instead?
options: Ride the shoulder past the line of cars every time traffic stops
Pair up side by side and pass the line as one wide vehicle
Move onto the paint and share a lane with the nearest car
Do it only where your state allows it
questions.explanation: Filtering is not a national right. Do it only where your state allows it; otherwise stay in your lane.

questions.q: Moving traffic, not just stopped cars, tempts you to ride the dashed line between lanes. Unless your state allows that maneuver, you should
options: Stay in your own lane and not share the line
Ride the line
Ride the line everywhere
Linger in the blind spot while you use the line
questions.explanation: Do not share a lane or ride the paint between lanes unless your state specifically allows the maneuver. Otherwise stay in your lane.

questions.q: Entitlement to the full lane means you may
options: Ride the dashed line between cars as if the lane lines were part of your lane
Use the left, center, or right third as the situation requires, without inviting a car beside you
Force a car to occupy the lane with you by riding the paint
Cross the centerline whenever the outside of a curve is over there
questions.explanation: The full lane is yours. Choose position 1, 2, or 3 inside it. Do not ride the paint to share it, and do not give the lane up.

questions.q: A metal plate and an oil spot both sit in the center third. The position move is
options: Brake hard on the plate once your tire is on it
Lean the bike over on the oil while you look at it
Share the plate with a car by riding the lane line
Pick a tire track around them early
questions.explanation: Set your lane position before the bad surface. The center collects this debris. Move to a cleaner track without leaving your lane. Choose a tire track around them while you are still approaching, inside your lane.

questions.q: Head check means more than moving your eyes inside the helmet. It means
options: Turning your head far enough to see the blind spot beside you
A longer look in the mirror you already used
Watching the rider ahead and skipping your own look
Looking down at the lane paint you plan to share
questions.explanation: Before a lane change, turn your head. Mirrors do not cover the blind spot, and a small eye flick is not a head check.

questions.q: The signal comes before the move so that
options: The blind spot becomes the safest place to wait
Drivers know your plan while you still check
You can skip the head check once the lamp is on
You may ride the paint during the signal
questions.explanation: Signal first, then mirror, then turn your head, then move. The signal does not replace the look into the blind spot. Drivers know what you intend while you still have time to mirror-check and head-check.

questions.q: A group leader who keeps racing ahead forces the tail to
options: Ride side by side to shorten the group
Share lanes with cars so the group becomes shorter
Either crowd the gap or ride beyond skill
Ride the gaps between cars to catch up, without knowing whether your state allows it
questions.explanation: Keep the formation's space. About two seconds to the rider directly ahead is the cushion. Do not collapse it to catch a leader, and do not ride side by side. The leader should leave a pace the 2-second gaps can hold.

questions.q: You are the leader and you see the group string out. The position fix is
options: Accelerate so the gaps shrink under one second
Wave everyone forward side by side
Move the group onto the centerline paint
Ease off so riders can catch up
questions.explanation: If riders fall behind, slow so they can close up safely. Keep about two seconds to the rider directly ahead and do not pull them into a side-by-side pack. Ease off so riders can catch up without speeding, then keep the stagger and the gaps.

questions.q: A right-side merge is coming. Your lane position before the merge should
options: Leave you visible and out of the merging driver's blind spot, with space ahead
Hide you beside a trailer in that merge
Put you on the paint so the merging car can share your lane
Put you in position 2 behind a tall truck that blocks the ramp view
questions.explanation: Be where the merging driver can see you. Do not linger in a blind spot, and keep space ahead rather than hiding in the center.

questions.q: In heavy rain the stagger can stay, but the gaps should
options: Turn into side-by-side pairs on the paint
Move everyone into the center for a smoother line
Grow to three seconds or more on the slippery pavement
Shrink so the group punches through the rain together
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "If the pavement is slippery... open up a three-second or more following distance."

questions.q: A truck's wind is pushing you while you ride beside its trailer. The position cure is
options: Stay beside the trailer until the wind stops
Move onto the trailer's lane line and share that lane
Lock your arms and hold the blind spot
Get ahead or drop back
questions.explanation: Do not linger beside a truck trailer. Wind and the blind area are both reasons to move forward or back into a visible, stable place.

questions.q: Your mirror shows a car, and a head check shows another one the mirror missed. You should
options: Speed up and slide between them side by side with a partner
Hold your lane until that blind spot is actually empty
Move anyway, because the mirror was enough
Move onto the paint between those two cars
questions.explanation: The head check exists because mirrors have blind spots. If the look shows a car, do not move.

questions.q: Single file on a highway ramp is preferred so that
options: The group should move between cars on the ramp even if the state has not allowed that maneuver
The leader can ride the ramp's painted edge
Each rider has room to merge without handlebars beside another motorcycle
Two riders can share the ramp lane with a car
questions.explanation: Enter and leave highways in single file. Side-by-side riding takes away the space cushion you need on a ramp.

questions.q: A group of three is side by side in one lane at a red light. The fix before the light changes is
options: Return to a stagger or a single file inside the lane
Stay abreast, because a red light requires side-by-side riding
Move onto the crosswalk paint and share it with cars
Filter to the front if the state has not spoken on the maneuver
questions.explanation: Do not ride side by side in the same lane. Use the stagger, or single file when you need more room. A row of handlebars.

questions.q: You are in the right track and the rider directly ahead is also in the right track. The gap to count is
options: Whatever fits if you pull up beside the left-track rider
About 2 seconds to that rider
One second, because every group gap is the offset
Zero, because the left-track rider is between you in time
questions.explanation: The rider directly ahead of you gets about 2 seconds. The other track is only the one-second stagger offset.

questions.q: An oncoming truck crosses the center slightly in a curve. The room you wanted was created by
options: Sharing the centerline paint with the truck
A hard lean onto the center oil while you stare at the truck
A lane position inside your lane that did not put you on the centerline
Riding in the opposing lane to see the truck sooner
questions.explanation: Leave room for an oncoming vehicle that crosses the center, and get that room without leaving your lane or riding the paint.

questions.q: Lane position numbers help you talk about the lane. Position 1, 2, and 3 are
options: Center, left, and the opposing lane
The paint, the tire track, and the sidewalk
Blind spot, trailer flank, and filter gap
Left third, center third, right third
questions.explanation: MSF position 1 is the left third, position 2 is the center, and position 3 is the right third.

questions.q: A driver is tailgating and the left lane is open for them to pass. You should
options: Ride the left paint and share your lane as they come by
Move right when safe and add space ahead
Speed up and block the left lane so they stay behind
Brake-check, then move into their blind spot
questions.explanation: Move over when safe so a tailgater can pass. Add space ahead. Do not speed up to lose them and do not share the lane. Move right when it is safe so they can pass, and keep extra space in front of you.

questions.q: Stopped cars occupy the lane to your left and your right. You are between them only if
options: The cars are stopped
A passenger waves you forward
You are in a group and must pass one at a time between the cars
Your state allows that filtering
questions.explanation: Stay in your lane unless your state specifically allows filtering. Stopped traffic does not create a national right to ride between lanes. Otherwise you should still be inside one lane.

questions.q: Diagonal riders in a stagger are about one second apart so that
options: They can filter between cars as a pair
The following gap to the rider directly ahead can shrink to nothing
Each motorcycle has an offset cushion and is not handlebar to handlebar
They can share one tire track at the same time
questions.explanation: The one-second offset keeps the stagger from becoming side-by-side riding. You still keep about two seconds to the rider directly ahead.

questions.q: A curve, poor pavement, and a highway exit all share which group-position choice?
options: A three-abreast row inside one lane
Everyone on the paint so cars can flow through the group
A move between the exiting cars, done whether or not your state allows it
Single file with at least a 2-second gap, instead of a tight side-by-side pack
questions.explanation: MSF prefers single file, minimum 2 seconds, on curvy roads, poor surfaces, and when entering or leaving highways. Do not ride side by side.

questions.q: You finished a pass and the car you passed is now in your mirror, not beside you. That means
options: You are out of its blind spot
You should drop back beside the door to stay seen
You should ride the lane line in case they want to share
You should brake-check to announce that the pass is over
questions.explanation: Do not linger beside a car. Once you are clearly ahead, take a normal lane position and keep a following gap to whatever is in front of you. You are out of the blind spot and can hold a normal tire track with space ahead.

questions.q: Mirrors first, then a real head turn. Skipping the turn is how riders
options: Meet a national duty to ride between lanes before you change lanes
Move into a car that was sitting in the blind spot the whole time
Correctly claim a full lane on the paint
Perform the one-second stagger offset
questions.explanation: Signal, mirror, head check, then move. The head check is what finds the vehicle the mirror missed.

questions.q: When the rider directly ahead of you is in your track, two seconds is the cushion even if
options: A tailgater wants you to close up and speed away
The center oil stripe looks like a faster line
The diagonal rider is one second off to the side
You would rather ride side by side to shorten the group
questions.explanation: Do not let the one-second stagger offset replace the two seconds you owe the rider directly ahead. Add more at night, in weather, or when the group needs it. A diagonal rider is only about one second off to the side in the stagger.

questions.q: A round steel manhole cover sits in your tire track on a rainy street. How should you cross it?
options: Leaned over, with the front brake squeezed so the cover cannot slide you
Along its edge, riding the rim like a rail slot
With a foot down, dabbing at road speed for balance
Upright, without a hard brake or a hard lean while the tire is on the cover
questions.explanation: Manhole covers are slippery, especially wet. Cross them upright. Do not brake hard or lean hard while you are on the steel.

questions.q: Painted lane arrows are dark and wet in your path. Where should the braking happen?
options: Before the paint, lightly
On the arrow, with a hard front squeeze while you lean
Not at all, because wet paint has the same grip as dry concrete
After a locked rear slide that starts on the paint
questions.explanation: In the rain, painted arrows are slick. Brake lightly before the paint, and cross upright rather than braking or leaning on it.

questions.q: A wide stop line glistens in the rain just short of the intersection. The surface plan is
options: Ride along the line until the paint ends
Slow before it, then cross upright
Brake hardest when the tire is centered on the line
Lean the bike onto the paint to finish a turn
questions.explanation: Painted stop lines in the rain are slippery. Do the light braking before the paint, and stay upright as you cross. Ease speed before the line, then cross the paint upright without a hard brake on it.

questions.q: Steel plates cover a trench in your lane and the pavement around them is wet. What do you avoid on the plate?
options: A path you chose before the tire arrived
Eyes aimed ahead through the plate
A hard brake and a hard lean
An upright posture and a steady speed
questions.explanation: Steel plates are slippery, especially wet. Cross upright. Do not brake hard or lean hard on the steel.

questions.q: A white crosswalk is soaked and you still need to slow for a person who might step out. How do you time the brake?
options: Hard, in the middle of the wet paint, with the bike leaned
Only with a locked rear wheel held across the stripes
Not until you are leaned over on the last stripe
Lightly, before the paint
questions.explanation: Wet paint, including a crosswalk, is a poor place to brake hard or lean. Set the speed before the paint and cross upright. The tire is not braking hard while it is on the crosswalk.

questions.q: Trolley tracks run along the street and then bend across an intersection. What must you not do in the groove?
options: Stay upright as the tire crosses the rail
Ride along the slot
Cross near a right angle when the street lets you do that inside your lane
Slow and set the line before you reach the steel
questions.explanation: Do not ride along a trolley slot. Cross as close to 90 degrees as you can so the tire does not fall into the groove. The tire can drop in and track the rail.

questions.q: The rail slot is parallel to your lane for half a block. Your path should
options: Brake hard while the tire is trapped in the groove
Lean the bike so the tire rides the steel edge
Stay out of the slot; cross near 90 degrees
Drop the front tire into the slot and use it as a guide
questions.explanation: Do not ride along the slot. When you cross railroad or trolley tracks, get as close to a right angle as you can. Stay out of the slot and cross it near 90 degrees when you must go over it.

questions.q: Gravel sprayed across the lane from a side road is visible ahead. When do you slow?
options: Before the gravel, then stay steady
After the front tire is already sliding in the stones
On the gravel, with a front-brake grab and a sharp lean
Never, because gravel only matters on a corner
questions.explanation: Slow before gravel. Once you are on it, use a steady throttle and do not make sudden brake, steer, or throttle inputs.

questions.q: A dirty shoulder is the only place left to pass a hazard, and you can see the dirt early. The surface skill is
options: Dab a foot at speed to paddle through the dirt
Slow before it, then stay steady on the dirt
Accelerate onto the shoulder and brake hard in the dirt
Look down at the front tire the whole time you are on the dirt
questions.explanation: A dirty shoulder is like gravel. Slow before you get there, then steady throttle and no sudden inputs.

questions.q: The rear tire steps on loose stones you entered too fast. The recovery that matches the surface, not a stunt, is
options: Grab the front brake and swerve hard on the stones
Lay the motorcycle down so the stones cannot slide the tire
Steady the throttle and stop making sudden grabs at the bars or the brakes
Stomp the rear brake and hold the lock while you lean more
questions.explanation: On gravel, sudden inputs make the slide worse. You should have slowed before it. Now be steady: no sudden brake, throttle, or steering.

questions.q: Why are the opening minutes of a rain the slickest part of the storm?
options: Rain washes the oil away instantly and leaves bare, grippy asphalt
The oil sinks deeper and the paint becomes the grippiest surface
Water locks the tires in a way that rewards a harder lean
Rain floats oil up out of the pavement, and that film has not washed away yet
questions.explanation: The first minutes of rain float oil onto the surface. Reduce speed and lean less until that film has been washed off.

questions.q: Rain just started after a long dry spell, and the road looks shiny. How should the lean change?
options: Lean less, and reduce speed
Lean more, because a shiny road means the oil has already washed away
Keep the same lean and add a hard brake on the painted arrows
Drop a foot and drag it so the oil cannot slide the tire
questions.explanation: Early rain lifts oil. It is extra slick. Slow down and use less lean than you would on a dry, clean road.

questions.q: A summer shower begins while you are on a busy arterial that was dry and oily. The first response is
options: Ignore it, because only the first hour of a storm is safe and the first minutes are fine
Reduce speed and lean less while the oil is floating on the water
Speed up so you spend less time on the new rain
Move into the center stripe where the oil is thickest and brake there
questions.explanation: The opening minutes of rain are the slickest, not the safest. Oil floats up. Reduce speed and lean less.

questions.q: Grooved pavement makes the front end feel loose. What should you change, and what should you not do?
options: Brake hard and lean to stop the wandering feeling
Dab a foot along the groove at speed
Hold speed, loose grip, and look ahead
Look down at the front tire and fight the bars
questions.explanation: Grooved pavement can make the front feel loose. Hold a steady speed, use a loose grip, and look ahead, not down.

questions.q: Bridge grating starts to wiggle the front tire. The trained response is
options: A sudden front-brake squeeze to plant the tire
A hard lean to the next expansion joint
A look straight down through the grating
Steady speed, loose hands, eyes up the road
questions.explanation: Bridge grating can feel loose at the front. Do not chop the throttle or stare down. Steady speed, loose grip, look ahead. On the grate.

questions.q: You feel the bars twitch on a grooved bridge deck. Grabbing the bars tightly will
options: Make the twitch worse
Cancel the grooves
Be the same skill as threshold braking on dry paint
Let you dab a foot safely at highway speed
questions.explanation: On grooves or grating, a tight fight feeds the wiggle. Loose grip, steady speed, eyes ahead, not down.

questions.q: Wet leaves cover a shaded corner the way gravel would. You should treat them as
options: A loose surface: slow before them, then stay smooth with no sudden inputs
Dry pavement, because leaves add grip when they are wet
A place to lean harder so the tires cut through to asphalt
A place for a locked rear brake held through the corner
questions.explanation: Wet leaves behave like gravel. Slow before you reach them, then use a steady throttle and no sudden inputs.

questions.q: Mud tracked onto the road from a work entrance should be handled like
options: Grooves: stare down at the front tire
Gravel: reduce speed before the mud, then avoid sudden brake or steering inputs
Paint: brake hardest in the middle of the mud while leaned
Ice: dab a foot at speed and keep the throttle closed in a chop
questions.explanation: Mud behaves like gravel. Slow before it, then steady throttle and no sudden inputs.

questions.q: Sand spilled from a truck trails along the lane. The same rule as gravel says
options: Lean and brake together once the sand is under the front tire
Ride the sand lengthwise in a slot if one forms
Slow before the sand, then stay steady
Accelerate in the sand so the tire spins down to pavement
questions.explanation: Sand behaves like gravel. Set your speed before you arrive, then no sudden throttle, brake, or lean. Slow before the sand, then keep inputs steady instead of grabbing a brake in the sand.

questions.q: A shiny black patch on a cold morning may be ice. What input should you avoid?
options: An upright posture with your eyes ahead
A loose grip that does not fight the bars
Any sudden brake, throttle, or steering
A gentle, early reduction in speed made before the patch
questions.explanation: On ice or a shiny black patch, do not make a sudden input. Ease off, stay upright, and be ready with your feet without dabbing a foot at speed.

questions.q: Black ice in a shaded lane calls for feet that are
options: Down on the pavement, paddling, at the speed you are riding
On the pegs only after you have grabbed the front brake
Irrelevant, because ice wants a hard lean
Ready, but not dabbed down while you are still at speed
questions.explanation: Ease off and stay upright on ice. Have your feet ready, but do not dab a foot at speed.

questions.q: You are already on a shiny frozen patch. The move that keeps the tires under you is
options: Ease off smoothly and stay upright
A front-brake grab to get the weight on the front tire
A sharp lean to the drier-looking paint
A foot dabbed at speed for a third contact patch
questions.explanation: Do not make a sudden input on ice. Ease off, stay upright, and do not stick a foot down while you are moving at speed. A smooth ease off the throttle, motorcycle upright, no sudden brake or steer.

questions.q: Paint in the rain, a manhole, and a steel plate share which crossing rule?
options: Maximum lean, because a leaned tire cuts through water
A locked front wheel to scrub speed on the slick surface
A foot down at speed for balance
Upright, with no hard brake and no hard lean while the tire is on them
questions.explanation: Paint, manhole covers, and steel plates are slippery, especially wet. Cross them upright. Do not brake hard or lean hard on them.

questions.q: A metal bridge grate and a grooved concrete lane feel similar at the bars. The shared response is
options: Steady speed, loose grip, look ahead and not down
Chop the throttle and stare at the front tire
Threshold-brake at full force while you look at the grooves
Lean hard so the tire stops wandering
questions.explanation: Grooved pavement and bridge grating can make the front feel loose. Hold speed steady, loosen your grip, and look ahead.

questions.q: Autumn leaves are wet in a pile at a stop, and you can see them early. Your speed should change
options: In the middle of the pile, with a front-brake grab
Not at all, because wet leaves are grippier than asphalt
After a hard lean that starts on the leaves
Before the leaves, with no sudden brake once the tire is in the pile
questions.explanation: Treat wet leaves like gravel. Slow before them, then avoid sudden inputs while you are on them.

questions.q: A construction apron drops sand and mud onto the highway edge. If your path must use that edge, you
options: Slow before it, then ride steadily
Wait until the tire slides, then grab the front brake
Look down and fight every small slip with a bar yank
Dab a foot to ski through the mud at speed
questions.explanation: Sand and mud behave like gravel. The setup is a slower speed before you arrive and smooth inputs afterward. Slow before the mess, then ride it steadily instead of stabbing the brakes.

questions.q: Ice at an intersection and a wet painted stop line can both be in the same approach. The order is
options: Lean on the paint and dab a foot on the ice at speed
Ride the ice in a slot parallel to the stop line
Ease off early, stay upright, brake before paint
Brake hardest on whichever surface is shiniest
questions.explanation: Shiny ice wants no sudden input, an upright bike, and no foot dab at speed. Wet paint wants the braking done before the paint, upright.

questions.q: A shiny patch you think is just wet asphalt on a freezing morning should still be ridden as
options: Guaranteed dry grip, so lean more to test it
A tar snake, so you should brake hard on it
A puddle you should hit faster so the tire planes across
As possible ice: ease off and stay upright
questions.explanation: A shiny black patch may be ice. Do not make a sudden input. Ease off and stay upright. Do not dab a foot at speed.

questions.q: Gravel in a curve is a surface problem first. The timing of the speed change is
options: After the rear locks, held through the rest of the curve
Irrelevant, because gravel has the same grip as clean asphalt
Before the gravel
At the apex, with the front brake grabbed at full lean
questions.explanation: Slow before gravel. A sudden brake or lean on the stones is the sudden input you were supposed to avoid.

questions.q: Steady throttle on gravel means you are not
options: Riding at a speed you already reduced before the gravel
Looking ahead toward the cleaner pavement
Staying relaxed at the grips
Making sudden throttle, brake, or bar inputs
questions.explanation: Once you are on gravel or a dirty shoulder, keep the throttle steady and avoid sudden inputs. The slowing belonged before the surface change. Chopping the throttle, stabbing a brake, or yanking the bars while the tire is in the loose stuff.

questions.q: Oil rising in a new rain is a reason to change lean angle how?
options: Use less lean until the oil film has been washed away
Use more lean so the tire's edge finds dry pavement
Keep the dry-road lean and brake on the painted arrows
Lay the bike down so the oil cannot affect the tire
questions.explanation: The first minutes of rain float oil and make the road extra slick. Reduce speed and lean less.

questions.q: Looking down at bridge grating is the wrong eye habit because
options: The course wants your eyes on the tire any time the surface changes
You ride toward what you stare at, and the grate already makes the front feel loose
The grating is grippier if you watch each bar pass the axle
A downward stare is how you hold a steady speed
questions.explanation: On grooved pavement or bridge grating, look ahead, not down. Keep a steady speed and a loose grip.

questions.q: A loose grip on grooved pavement lets the front
options: Follow a tar snake more precisely
Dab the ground through the fairing
Wiggle without your arms feeding it
Lock so you can brake and swerve together
questions.explanation: Grooves can feel loose. A tight grip makes it worse. Loosen your hands, keep speed steady, and look ahead. Wiggle without your arms feeding the motion, while you hold a steady speed.

questions.q: A manhole cover is in the middle of a gentle bend and the pavement is wet. The lean you want on the cover is
options: None you can avoid
As much as the dry corner would use, held across the steel
A deeper lean
A lean combined with a locked front brake
questions.explanation: Manhole covers are slippery when wet. Cross upright. Do not add lean or a hard brake while the tire is on the cover.

questions.q: Two steel plates in a row cover a street cut. You should cross both of them
options: With a foot dabbed at speed on the first plate
Upright, without braking or leaning hard on either plate
Leaned, with the brake applied on the second plate
By riding the gap between the plates like a rail slot
questions.explanation: Steel plates are slick, especially wet. Cross them upright and do not brake or lean hard while the tires are on the steel.

questions.q: A turn arrow painted on the road is wet, and the lane also bends. Set the lean and the brake so that
options: You brake only after the tire is on the arrowhead
You ride the length of the arrow in a slide
You are upright on the arrow, with any real braking done before the paint
You are leaned on the arrow while the front brake is working hardest
questions.explanation: Wet painted arrows want an upright bike and the braking done before the paint, not on it.

questions.q: Stop-line paint is wet and a light is red ahead. The last firm braking belongs
options: On the paint itself, where the white surface looks flatter
In a lean that starts on the line
After you have put a foot down at speed on the line
On the pavement before the line
questions.explanation: Painted stop lines in the rain are slick. Brake before the paint, then cross upright.

questions.q: A crosswalk's white bars are raining and empty. Even with no pedestrian yet, you still
options: Avoid hard braking or leaning on them
Brake hardest on the bars
Lean across the bars to shorten the crossing
Ride along one bar until the intersection ends
questions.explanation: Wet painted crosswalks are slippery. Do not brake hard or lean hard on the paint. Do the slowing before it. Avoid a hard brake and a hard lean on those bars, and slow before them if you need to slow.

questions.q: City trolley rails sit in the street and your lane runs beside them for a block. Keep the tire
options: Leaned into the groove at speed
Out of the slot, crossing near a right angle
In the slot, so the rail steers the motorcycle for you
On the steel head of the rail while you brake
questions.explanation: Do not ride along a trolley slot. The tire can drop in. Cross near 90 degrees when you have to go over the rails. Out of the slot, and cross only when you can get close to a right angle.

questions.q: A railroad crossing has a raised lip and a groove. The groove is the part that
options: Improves grip if you brake while you are in it
Should be used as a lane position for several yards
Replaces the need to slow before the crossing
Can catch a tire at a shallow angle
questions.explanation: Cross rails as close to 90 degrees as you can so the tire does not drop into the slot. Do not ride along the groove.

questions.q: Gravel on a freeway ramp is visible from the top of the ramp. Your speed for the gravel should already be
options: Reduced before the stones, then held steady
Increased on the stones so you exit the ramp sooner
Cut by a front-brake grab that starts in the gravel
Managed by a foot dabbing the ramp at speed
questions.explanation: Slow before gravel, including gravel you can see on a ramp. Then no sudden inputs. Reduced before the stones, with the throttle steady once you are on them.

questions.q: The pavement edge crumbles into a dirty shoulder. If you must use that shoulder, the entry is
options: A locked rear wheel held down the shoulder
A speed set before the dirt, then a steady ride
A last-second swerve onto the dirt while the front brake is on
A hard lean that starts as the tire leaves the pavement
questions.explanation: A dirty shoulder is handled like gravel. Slow before you get there, then steady throttle and no sudden inputs. A slower speed chosen before the dirt, then a steady ride with no sudden yank or brake.

questions.q: Loose stone on a decreasing-radius corner is visible early. Braking for it belongs
options: As a held rear-wheel lock through the apex
Together with a swerve that starts on the gravel
Before the stones, on cleaner pavement
At full lean, after the front tire is in the stones
questions.explanation: Set up for gravel before you are on it. Do not save the brake for the moment the tire is already in the loose stone. Before the stones, while you still have cleaner pavement and can be gentle.

questions.q: A parking-lot aisle is covered with loose grit. Low speed does not cancel the surface rule, which is
