options: Grab the front brake in the grit
Lean the bike over in the grit to test the edge
Paddle with a foot at a fast pace through the aisle
Ease off before it, then roll through steadily
questions.explanation: Grit behaves like gravel. Slow before it. In a slow turn, a front-brake grab can also drop the bike, so stay smooth. Ease off before the grit, then roll through steadily instead of grabbing the front brake in it.

questions.q: Diesel sheen and the oil that rises in a new rain are both reasons to
options: Slow down and lean less
Lean more so the tire cuts the film
Brake on the nearest painted arrow
Ride the shiniest strip in the center
questions.explanation: Early rain floats oil, and a fuel sheen is slick in the same way. Slow down and use less lean. Do not brake or lean hard on the shiny film. Reduce speed and lean less while the surface is extra slick.

questions.q: After the rain has washed for a long time, the first-minute oil film is less of a threat, but during those first minutes you
options: Ignore painted stop lines
Still reduce speed and lean less
Lean harder than on a dry day to heat the tires
Brake on every tar snake you meet
questions.explanation: The opening minutes are the extra-slick part. Reduce speed and lean less until the floated oil has been washed away.

questions.q: A grooved concrete lane on a bridge and a metal grate on the next bridge want the same hands and eyes:
options: A hard front brake and a look down through the deck
Feet dabbing the grate
Loose hands, eyes ahead, speed held steady
Tight hands, eyes on the tire, speed chopped up and down
questions.explanation: Grooved pavement and bridge grating can feel loose at the front. Steady speed, loose grip, look ahead, not down.

questions.q: The front tire hunts left and right on rain grooves. Fighting that hunt with stiff arms
options: Is the required way to plant a grooved tire
Replaces the need to slow for the first minutes of rain
Lets you brake hard on the grooves at the same time
Feeds the motion
questions.explanation: When grooves make the front feel loose, do not fight the bars. Loose grip, steady speed, eyes ahead. Relax the grip, hold speed, and look up the lane.

questions.q: A metal grate bridge has a view straight down to the water. Your eyes should be
options: Ahead on the path you mean to ride
Down on the water so you can watch the tire
On the expansion joint only, until the bridge ends
Closed, so the wiggle does not startle you
questions.explanation: On bridge grating, look ahead, not down. Keep a steady speed and a loose grip while the front feels loose. Down through the grate.

questions.q: Wet leaves in the gutter line of a shaded street act like
options: Dry asphalt, so you lean more to cut through
A rail slot, so you ride along the leaf line
Ice that wants a foot dab at speed
Gravel: slow first, then stay smooth
questions.explanation: Wet leaves behave like gravel. Reduce speed before the leaves, then steady throttle and no sudden brake or steer. Gravel, so you slow before them and then avoid sudden inputs.

questions.q: A farm road has tracked mud in two strips. You treat those strips as
options: A gravel-like surface: slow before them, then stay smooth
Paint: brake in the middle of the mud while leaned
Grooves: stare down and grip the bars hard
A puddle you should enter faster
questions.explanation: Mud behaves like gravel. Slow before you reach it and do not make sudden inputs once you are on it.

questions.q: Beach sand has blown across a coast road in a thin sheet. Thin does not mean harmless. You
options: Lean onto the sand to find a clean strip under it
Slow before it and keep the throttle steady
Hit the sand faster so the sheet cannot move
Brake hard the moment the front tire hisses in the sand
questions.explanation: Sand behaves like gravel, even in a thin sheet. Slow before it, then no sudden inputs. Slow before the sand and keep the throttle steady instead of chopping it in the sand.

questions.q: A black, shiny lane in freezing shade, with no rain falling, should be ridden
options: Upright, eased off, with no sudden input
With a test lean to see if it is ice
With a hard front brake to load the front tire
With a foot skating on the surface at speed
questions.explanation: Treat a shiny black patch in the cold as ice. Ease off, stay upright, and do not dab a foot while you are at speed.

questions.q: Your feet come off the pegs on an icy bridge while you are still rolling at road speed. That dab is
options: Safer than staying upright and easing off
A mistake; keep them ready but do not touch down at speed
The required third contact patch on ice
How you steer when you must not use the bars
questions.explanation: On ice, feet can be ready, but do not dab a foot at speed. Ease off and stay upright with no sudden input.

questions.q: Wet paint, wet steel, and a wet manhole are a family of surfaces. The family rule is
options: Dab a foot whenever the surface shines
Cross upright, no hard braking or leaning
Lean hard, and brake hard
Ride along them lengthwise
questions.explanation: Paint, manhole covers, and steel plates get slippery when wet. Upright, no hard brake, no hard lean.

questions.q: A steel plate is dry but polished smooth by traffic. Dry does not make it innocent. You still
options: Lean on it more than on the surrounding pavement
Ride the plate's edge like a track slot
Cross upright with no hard brake or lean
Brake on it, because only wet steel is slick
questions.explanation: Steel plates are slippery, and wet makes them worse, but a smooth plate is still a poor place to brake hard or lean hard. Cross upright.

questions.q: Gravel, a dirty shoulder, wet leaves, mud, and sand share the timing rule
options: Brake only after the tire is sliding on it
Lean more as soon as the surface changes
Cross at 90 degrees and then ride the slot
Slow before it, then stay steady
questions.explanation: Those surfaces behave like gravel. The speed change happens before you arrive. After that, steady throttle and no sudden inputs.

questions.q: You are already on leaves you should have slowed for. The next input should be
options: Smoother, with no sudden inputs
A front-brake grab to end the mistake
A hard swerve combined with that grab
A foot dab at the speed you are carrying
questions.explanation: Wet leaves behave like gravel. If you are already on them, stop making sudden inputs. Steady the throttle and ride through. Smoother, not a sudden brake, lean, or throttle chop.

questions.q: Mud on a painted arrow combines two problems. The plan that respects both is
options: Accelerate and look down at the front tire
Slow first, stay upright, no braking on it
Brake on the arrow and lean through the mud
Ride the arrow lengthwise in the mud
questions.explanation: Mud behaves like gravel, and wet or muddy paint is slick. Set speed early, stay upright, and avoid sudden inputs on the bad surface. Slow before the mess, stay upright, and do not brake on the paint or stab the brake in the mud.

questions.q: First rain on a bridge mixes floating oil, possible early ice in the cold, and joints. The speed you want is
options: Higher, so you spend less time on the bridge
The same, with a hard brake on each joint
Managed by looking down at the deck
Lower, with less lean and no sudden input
questions.explanation: Early rain floats oil. Cold bridge decks can ice. Joints want an upright, angled crossing. Reduce speed and do not make sudden inputs.

questions.q: Grooved pavement that also has a tar snake in the heat asks for two different restraints:
options: Steady and loose on grooves, no brake on tar
A hard brake on both the grooves and the tar
Eyes down on the grooves and a lean along the tar
A foot dab on the tar and a tight grip on the grooves
questions.explanation: Grooves want steady speed, a loose grip, and eyes ahead. Hot tar wants a crossing without braking on the tar.

questions.q: A painted arrow is dry, but a steel plate sits in the same lane just beyond it. You still
options: Ride the plate edge in a slot
Cross the plate upright, no hard brake or lean
Brake on the plate
Lean on the plate to finish the turn the arrow marks
questions.explanation: Steel plates are slick even when you already slowed for something else. Cross upright. Do not brake or lean hard on the plate.

questions.q: Trolley tracks curve with the street. Following the curve by staying in the slot is
options: The preferred line
Safe if you brake hard in the slot
Required in the rain only
The failure mode
questions.explanation: Do not ride along the trolley slot, even when the street curves with the rail. Cross as close to 90 degrees as you can. Get out of the slot and cross near a right angle when you leave it.

questions.q: A dirty shoulder on the outside of a curve is not an escape you take at the same speed. If you use it, you
options: Slow before the dirt, then keep inputs steady
Swerve onto it while braking hard
Lean harder as the pavement ends
Look down at the shoulder and fight the bars
questions.explanation: A dirty shoulder behaves like gravel. Slow before you get there. Sudden brake or steering inputs on the dirt make it worse.

questions.q: Chip-seal stones and fresh loose gravel behave alike under a tire. The rider's timing is
options: A look down at the stones until they end
Slower before the loose stones, then a steady throttle on them
A maximum brake once the stones are under the front tire
A deeper lean on the stones than on smooth asphalt
questions.explanation: Loose stone, like gravel, wants the speed set before you arrive and no sudden inputs afterward.

questions.q: Rain began thirty seconds ago on an oily downtown street. Lean angle should
options: Stay at the dry maximum and move onto the paint
Be replaced by a foot dab
Decrease, along with speed, while that oil is floating on the surface
Increase, because water cools the tires into more grip
questions.explanation: The first minutes of rain float oil and make the street extra slick. Reduce speed and lean less.

questions.q: You need to stop near a wet steel plate, not on it. The stop is placed
options: On the plate, where the steel looks flat and stable
In a lean that crosses the plate
After a slide that starts on the plate
Before the plate
questions.explanation: Steel plates are slippery, especially wet. Do not brake hard on them. Finish the firm braking on the pavement before the plate, and cross upright.

questions.q: A manhole, a painted arrow, and a stop line are all in one wet block. The repeated mistake to avoid is
options: Braking or leaning hard on each one
Slowing before the first slick patch
Staying upright as you cross them
Looking ahead to the next one
questions.explanation: Paint and manhole covers are slippery when wet. Brake before them, cross upright, and do not lean hard on them. Braking or leaning hard on each of those slick surfaces.

questions.q: Ice in a wheel track and dry pavement beside it still do not invite a sudden swerve at speed. You
options: Lock the rear and hold it on the ice
Ease off and stay upright over the ice
Yank the bars at the ice and grab the front brake
Dab the ice with a foot while you lean to the dry side
questions.explanation: On ice, do not make a sudden input. Ease off, stay upright, and do not dab a foot at speed. A yank is a sudden input. Ease off and stay upright over the ice rather than yanking toward the dry patch.

questions.q: Bridge grating in a crosswind adds a loose front end to the gust. Your grip should
options: Come off the bars entirely
Squeeze the front brake so the tire plants in the grate
Stay loose, with speed steady and eyes ahead
Lock up so the grate cannot move the tire
questions.explanation: Grating makes the front feel loose, and a gust makes that worse. Loose grip, steady speed, look ahead. Do not fight the bars or brake hard on the grate.

questions.q: Leaves in a wet pile hide the paint of a turn arrow. You cannot treat the pile as grip. You
options: Ride along the arrow under the leaves
Slow before the leaves and stay smooth
Lean on the pile so the arrow's paint can steer you
Lock the front brake in the leaves
questions.explanation: Wet leaves behave like gravel, and the paint under them is slick. Slow before the pile and stay smooth and upright.

questions.q: A rail crossing in the rain adds slick steel to the slot risk. Besides the angle, you also
options: Lean on the wet rail to cut through the water
Ride the slot so the rain cannot push the tire out
Dab a foot on the rail at speed
Stay upright and do not brake hard on the wet rails
questions.explanation: Cross as close to 90 degrees as you can so the tire misses the slot. Wet steel is also slick, so do not brake or lean hard on the rail.

questions.q: Gravel on an otherwise clean corner is not answered with a maximum straight-line brake once you are in it. It is answered by
options: The speed you took off before the gravel, and steady inputs while you are on it
A locked front wheel held in the gravel
A swerve and a hard brake at the same time on the stones
Engine braking alone after you have already grabbed the front brake
questions.explanation: Slow before gravel. Sudden braking on the stones is the sudden input the surface does not want.

questions.q: The dirty edge of the pavement is where a car's tires do not sweep. If you ride that edge, remember it may hold
options: A rail slot you should follow
Paint that is grippier than the tire tracks
Gravel and debris, so slow and stay smooth
The best rain grip, so lean more there
questions.explanation: The unswept edge can be a dirty shoulder. Treat it like gravel: slow before it, then steady throttle and no sudden inputs.

questions.q: On freezing pavement the rear tire starts to slide from a sudden throttle chop. The surface lesson is
options: Do not make that sudden input
Chop harder so the slide finishes
Grab the front brake to stop the slide
Dab a foot at speed and lean away
questions.explanation: Ice and shiny black patches want no sudden input. Ease off smoothly, stay upright, and do not dab a foot at speed.

questions.q: A grooved on-ramp makes the front feel vague. The speed and the eyes should be
options: A lean that follows one groove
Steady, eyes ahead, with a loose grip
Changing constantly, with the eyes on the front tire
A hard brake in the grooves while you look down
questions.explanation: Grooved pavement: steady speed, loose grip, look ahead, not down. Do not fight the loose feeling with a sudden brake.

questions.q: Wet leaves over a manhole are two slick layers. Cross them
options: By riding the manhole rim
With a foot on the cover at speed
Upright, after slowing, no hard braking
Leaned, with the brake on the cover
questions.explanation: Wet leaves behave like gravel, and a manhole is slippery. Slow before them, stay upright, and do not brake hard on the cover.

questions.q: Moving the gearshift on a standard motorcycle is the job of which foot?
options: The left hand, after you take it off the clutch lever
Either foot, because the lever can be reached across the engine cases
The left foot, following the usual one-down pattern with neutral between first and second
The right foot, sharing the same pedal as the rear brake
questions.explanation: You shift with the left foot. A typical gearbox is 1-N-2-3-4-5. Neutral sits between first and second, not above the top gear.

questions.q: Flat wrists matter on the throttle for which reason?
options: The right wrist should hook under the brake lever for the whole ride
A wrist bent downward can roll the throttle open when the bike hits a bump
A sharply bent wrist is required so the grip cannot snap shut
Wrists should rest on the mirror stalks while the palms steer
questions.explanation: Keep your wrists flat. A bump that folds a bent wrist into a roll-on is an accidental acceleration. A flat wrist lets the grip stay where you set it.

questions.q: Before a ride, the T in T-CLOCS sends you to inspect which parts?
options: The toll tag and the paperwork in a tail bag
Traffic flow, because T-CLOCS is a mental strategy instead of a check
Tires and wheels, including pressure, tread, and the fasteners that hold the wheels on
Only the tail lamp
questions.explanation: T is tires and wheels. Check pressure cold with a gauge, and look for cuts, nails, and loose spokes or axle hardware before you leave.

questions.q: During the controls portion of T-CLOCS, what are you checking?
options: Only the paint on the fuel tank and the color of the levers
Cornering lines, which you practice after the engine is already hot
Cargo straps alone, skipping the brakes and the clutch
Levers, pedals, cables, hoses, and a throttle that snaps shut
questions.explanation: C is controls. Levers and pedals should move freely, cables should not be frayed, and the throttle must snap closed when you release the grip.

questions.q: Lights and electrics, the L in T-CLOCS, include which check?
options: Headlamp, brake lamp, turn signals, and horn all work before you move
Lean angle, measured with a gauge while the bike is on the stand
Only the license-plate lamp, and only after you are in traffic
Lane position, because L is a step in the SEE strategy
questions.explanation: L is lights and electrics. A dead brake lamp or a dark turn signal hides what you are about to do. Confirm them in the driveway.

questions.q: Engine oil and the coolant, if the bike is liquid cooled, belong where in T-CLOCS?
options: Nowhere in the list
Under O, checked the way the owner's manual describes
Under T, which is only about tire shine and valve caps
Under S, which is the speedometer cable and nothing else
questions.explanation: O is oil and fluids. Check oil, and coolant on a liquid-cooled bike, as the manual says. Do not invent a grade or a made-up level mark.

questions.q: A chassis check, the second C in T-CLOCS, is aimed at what?
options: The passenger's jacket zipper and glove fit
The clock and the radio presets on the dash
Frame, suspension, chain, and fasteners
Only the decals
questions.explanation: The second C is chassis. A loose chain, a weeping fork seal, or a fastener that has backed off is easier to catch before it becomes a handling problem. The frame, suspension, drive chain or belt, and critical fasteners.

questions.q: Side and center stands are the last letter of T-CLOCS. What should you confirm?
options: The speed you plan to ride, which you set by leaving the choke on
Sunglasses only, because the final S replaces eye protection
That the stand is down and dragging, which proves the interlock works
The side stand springs up and stays up before riding
questions.explanation: S is stands. The side stand should retract and stay up. A center stand, if the bike has one, is for parking, not for riding away while it is still down. The side stand springs fully up and stays up, and you do not start off with a center stand down.

questions.q: Walking through T-CLOCS is meant to happen at what point?
options: Before you ride, especially after it sat
Only after a crash
Once a year when the registration sticker is due
Only when a passenger asks
questions.explanation: T-CLOCS is the pre-ride inspection: tires, controls, lights, fluids, chassis, and stands. Problems are cheaper to fix in the driveway than in a lane of traffic. Before you ride, including the first start of the day and after the bike has been sitting.

questions.q: Search, Evaluate, and Execute is the meaning of which Basic RiderCourse strategy?
options: SEE, the strategy MSF teaches for finding a hazard and acting on it
SIPDE, treated as if it were the same three words as SEE
T-CLOCS, the pre-ride list of parts on the motorcycle
A horn pattern of three blasts used only in a group
questions.explanation: MSF uses SEE: Search, Evaluate, Execute. SIPDE is a different system. Do not rename SEE or call SIPDE the MSF meaning of SEE.

questions.q: An active Search, the first step of SEE, asks you to look where?
options: At the front tire
Ahead, to the sides, and in the mirrors, including a space you could use as an escape
Only at the instrument cluster until the next intersection arrives
Only inside your own lane, ignoring cross traffic and driveways
questions.explanation: Search is a scan of the road ahead, the sides, the mirrors, and the space you might need. A glance at the gauges is brief, then your eyes go back to traffic.

questions.q: Evaluating a hazard under SEE means you do what before you move the controls?
options: Pick the fastest line even when it uses the oncoming lane
Ask a passenger to choose which car is allowed to matter
Judge which hazard is most urgent and choose a response
Wait until after a collision to decide who was more visible
questions.explanation: Evaluate is the decision. Predict what the driver, the debris, or the surface will do, then choose a smooth change in speed, position, or communication.

questions.q: Executing the decision in SEE should look like which action?
options: A maximum-brake stop at every shadow, whether or not it is a hazard
Freezing on the bars with the throttle chopped until the road is empty
Holding the horn down from one intersection to the next
A smooth change in speed, lane position, or a signal you already chose
questions.explanation: Execute is the action you selected. Make the speed change, the position change, or the signal smooth. A late grab or a swerve into another lane is not a finished plan.

questions.q: After the turn is finished and the signal is still blinking, you should
options: Weave once, because a weave is the self-cancel feature
Cancel it right away so you are not advertising a turn you will not make
Leave it on so traffic behind gives you a full extra lane for a mile
Tap the brake in a rhythm
questions.explanation: Many bikes will not self-cancel. Turn the signal off as soon as the maneuver is done. A leftover blink is false information.

questions.q: A short horn blast while you ride is appropriate in which situation?
options: You would rather honk than use either brake as a car turns across you
You hold it down for the full length of a freeway merge
A driver is drifting toward you and needs to notice the motorcycle
You want to greet a friend or comment on another rider's jacket
questions.explanation: The horn is a tool to be noticed, not a toy and not a brake. One clear blast can break a driver's fixation. It does not replace slowing down or leaving yourself an escape.

questions.q: High beam is a tool with which proper use?
options: Leave it on behind other vehicles so their mirrors stay glaring
Aim it at oncoming drivers until they change lanes
Tape the switch on
Seeing farther on empty roads, then dimming
questions.explanation: High beam helps you see and, as a brief flash, helps you be seen. Do not blind the driver ahead or the one coming toward you. Go back to low beam when others are near. See farther on a dark empty road, or flash briefly to be noticed, then return to low beam.

questions.q: Daytime headlight use on a motorcycle is recommended because
options: A lit headlamp makes the bike easier for drivers to pick out of traffic
Daytime use is discouraged
The lamp should stay off except inside a tunnel
Only a black motorcycle needs a headlamp, and other colors count as lights
questions.explanation: Ride with the headlight on during the day. Many bikes light it for you, but you still confirm the lamp works in T-CLOCS. A dark front end is easy to miss.

questions.q: If the throttle sticks open while you are moving, which pair of actions comes first?
options: Switch on the high beam
Stamp the shifter through every gear until the engine stalls on its own
Pull the clutch in and shut the engine off with the cut-off switch, then brake to safety
Open the choke
questions.explanation: Pull the clutch so the rear wheel is not being driven, hit the cut-off, and brake toward a safe place. Know that switch before the ride when you need it.

questions.q: Changing lanes starts with which order of mirror and head check?
options: The move first, then a glance in the mirror after you are already over
Mirrors first, then a head check toward the blind spot
A head check
Mirrors only, because a careful adjustment shows the blind spot
questions.explanation: Check the mirrors, then turn your head. Mirrors do not cover the wedge beside your shoulder. The head check is what finds a car sitting there.

questions.q: Mirrors leave a blind spot, so relying on them alone is unsafe because
options: A motorcycle mirror is only for watching a passenger
The glass goes black whenever the headlight is on
A vehicle beside your shoulder can be invisible in the glass
Mirrors reverse left and right and only show the lane you already left
questions.explanation: Even a well-aimed mirror cannot see the area just behind and beside you. Turn your head toward the lane you want before you commit the bike.

questions.q: Cover the front brake in which situation, without actually dragging it?
options: For an entire highway trip, with enough pressure to keep the pads touching
Only after the front wheel has already locked
Never, because a finger near the lever always means a skid
When a hazard is developing ahead and you may need to stop sooner
questions.explanation: Cover the brake when a car may turn, a light may change, or another hazard is ahead. Covering means your fingers are ready. It does not mean riding for miles with the lever pulled in.

questions.q: Neutral on a typical motorcycle gearbox sits where?
options: Below first, a full click under the bottom gear
Between third and fourth on every modern street bike
Between first and second, in the 1-N-2-3-4-5 pattern
Above the highest gear, one click past fifth or sixth
questions.explanation: The usual pattern puts neutral between first and second. You find it with a light shift. Do not invent a pattern that puts neutral somewhere else.

questions.q: Selecting neutral from first gear at a stop is done how?
options: By stamping the lever up through every higher gear and back down
By twisting the throttle until the neutral light is forced on
By holding the horn, which drops the box into neutral
With a light half-click upward until neutral is found
questions.explanation: From first, a gentle lift finds neutral. Forcing the shifter through the whole gearbox just to park is unnecessary on a normal 1-N-2-3-4-5 transmission.

questions.q: Stamping the shifter through every gear just to park is unnecessary because
options: Neutral is one small step from first
Neutral only exists above the top gear
The lever's hard stop at the top of the box is always neutral
Shutting the fuel off in fifth makes the gearbox choose neutral
questions.explanation: You find neutral; you do not ram the lever through every gear. On a typical box it is a half-step up from first. Parking in gear on the stand is another normal choice.

questions.q: An ordinary straight-line stop should use which brakes?
options: The rear brake only, saving the front brake for a skid
The front brake only after the rear tire has been held in a lock
Neither brake, coasting in neutral to the stop line
Both the front and the rear, squeezed and pressed together smoothly
questions.explanation: Use both brakes even on a normal stop. The front does most of the stopping, and the rear helps keep the stop stable. Apply them smoothly together.

questions.q: Slowing with only the rear brake for a routine light is weaker than
options: Adding the front brake and using both brakes together
Locking the rear wheel and holding the skid for every ordinary stop
Pulling the clutch and coasting in neutral from a block away
Dragging a boot
questions.explanation: A rear-brake-only stop is longer and easier to skid. The normal technique is both brakes, smoothly, with the front doing most of the work.

questions.q: Stopped at a light on level pavement, which foot position matches the usual technique?
options: Both feet paddling so you can release the brakes early
Left foot down, right foot on the rear brake, transmission in first with the clutch in
Both feet on the pegs and neither brake ready
Right foot down and the left foot resting on a rear-brake pedal that is not there
questions.explanation: The usual stop is left foot down and right foot holding the rear brake, bike in first, clutch pulled in. You can move as soon as the way is clear.

questions.q: While the bike is moving, the balls of your feet should rest where?
options: Tucked under the engine cases
Parked on top of the brake pedal and the shift lever for the whole ride
On the footpegs, ready to reach the shifter or the rear brake
Dragging on the pavement to stabilize the bike at road speed
questions.explanation: Ride on the pegs. From there you can lift to shift or move onto the rear brake when you mean to. A foot left on a pedal drags a brake or wears the shifter.

questions.q: A smooth upshift, once you are rolling, follows which order?
options: Look down, stomp the lever with the clutch still out, and chop the throttle
Hold the front brake, click up two gears, and dump the clutch
Roll the throttle wide open, then force the lever while the clutch is engaged
Roll off, pull the clutch, lift the shifter one gear, ease the clutch out, and roll on
questions.explanation: Upshift by easing the throttle, pulling the clutch, selecting one gear, and releasing the lever smoothly. Keep your eyes up. You do not need to watch your boot.

questions.q: As the bike comes to a stop, when should the clutch be fully in?
options: Never, because stops are done in top gear with the clutch out
After you have coasted the last block in neutral
Before the engine stalls, while both brakes finish the stop
Only after the engine has already stalled and the light has changed
questions.explanation: Pull the clutch in as you finish the stop so the engine keeps running. Keep using both brakes. You want first gear and a running engine when it is time to go.

questions.q: Downshift while you slow so that at the next corner or light you are
options: In neutral, because neutral is the safest gear for every approach
Still in top gear, with the clutch slipping to pretend you downshifted
Looking down at the lever to count the gears you have left
In a gear that matches your speed, ready to roll smoothly
questions.explanation: Brake with both brakes and shift down as speed falls. Arrive in a useful gear. Do not coast in neutral and do not stare at the shifter while you do it.

questions.q: Forcing the shift lever through two gears at once, as a habit, is less precise than
options: Lifting or pressing one gear at a time and easing the clutch out to match
Ignoring the clutch and stabbing the lever until it stops moving
Holding the front brake so the gearbox will skip to the gear you want
Using the choke as a gear selector on a warm engine
questions.explanation: Basic shifting is one gear per click, with the clutch and a smooth throttle. Forcing the lever is how riders miss neutral or end up in a gear that does not match their speed.

questions.q: Practice finding the engine cut-off while you are stopped so that later you can
options: Use it as the main brake in place of the front lever
Leave it in the off position whenever you ride, as a safety feature
Replace the need to check that the side stand is up
Reach it with your right thumb without taking your eyes off the road
questions.explanation: The cut-off is on the right. Rehearse finding it in a driveway. In a stuck-throttle moment you will not have time to look down and hunt for it.

questions.q: Confirm the headlamp works as part of the lights check because
options: A motorcycle with the lamp off is harder for drivers to see, even in daylight
The lamp should be switched off in the day to save the bulb for night
A working headlamp replaces the need for a head check
The high beam is the only filament you ever need to test
questions.explanation: Turn the headlight on and look. Daytime running light is part of being noticed. If the lamp is out, fix it before you depend on it in traffic.

questions.q: Check the brake lamp during T-CLOCS by operating which controls?
options: The shift lever, which should flash the lamp once per gear
The front lever and rear pedal, one at a time
Only the horn
The choke, which lights the brake lamp on a cold start
questions.explanation: Squeeze the front lever and look, or use a reflection or a helper. Then press the rear pedal. Either control should light the brake lamp. A dark lamp hides your slow-down.

questions.q: Tap the horn once in the driveway as part of the pre-ride check so you know
options: Holding the button down is how you cancel a turn signal
A silent horn is acceptable if the headlamp is very bright
The horn works when you later need a driver to notice you
The horn is loud enough to replace both brakes
questions.explanation: The horn is a notice tool. A short test before you ride tells you it works. It is not a toy, and it is not a substitute for brakes or for an escape path.

questions.q: The throttle should prove what during the controls check before you ride?
options: It stays at the last position until you pull it closed by hand
It only closes if the choke is left on
It should feel sticky
It snaps fully shut by itself when you let go of the grip
questions.explanation: Roll the grip and release it. It must snap closed. A throttle that sticks open is a do-not-ride defect. Do not plan to close it by hand in traffic.

questions.q: A frayed clutch cable, found while you check controls, means you should
options: Not ride until the cable is replaced
Ride carefully and shift without the clutch for the rest of the season
Spray it with chain lube and ignore the broken strands
Tie the frayed end to the bar so the lever stays in the friction zone
questions.explanation: Cables should be free and not frayed. A clutch cable that lets go can strand you or leave the bike stuck in gear. Fix it before you ride.

questions.q: A front-brake lever that pulls all the way to the handgrip is a sign to
options: Pump the lever until it feels normal and then ignore it
Stay parked, because spongy brakes or a lever that reaches the bar need service
Ride to the next town and bleed the system only if the lever gets worse
Switch to the rear brake alone and treat that as a complete brake system
questions.explanation: A lever that comes to the bar, or a spongy feel, means the brakes are not ready. Brake fluid and pads need service. Do not ride the bike that way.

questions.q: Cycle each turn signal during the lights check, then cancel it, because
options: A signal that stays on is helpful and should be left that way
The signal switch is also the engine cut-off and should stay in the middle
You need to know the lamps work and that you can switch them off yourself
Signals cancel automatically on every bike
questions.explanation: Left and right lamps should flash, and you should be able to turn them off. Many motorcycles will not cancel a signal for you after a turn.

questions.q: Coming down from second gear toward neutral should be done with
options: A hard stamp that skips neutral on purpose every time
The choke pulled out, which selects neutral on a warm engine
Both brakes locked so the gearbox will drop two gears at once
A gentle press
questions.explanation: Neutral is the light step between first and second. A gentle shift finds it. Smashing the lever drops you into first or misses the gap. You can feel the half-step instead of slamming into first.

questions.q: Higher gears still follow the same map on a typical bike, which is
options: Neutral only between first and second, then third, fourth, and fifth up from there
A second neutral placed between third and fourth for highway cruising
Neutral above the top gear on every 1-N-2-3-4-5 transmission
First gear at the top of the pattern and fifth at the bottom
questions.explanation: Remember 1-N-2-3-4-5. Some bikes add a sixth gear above fifth. Neutral does not move. You still find it between first and second.

questions.q: Hunting for neutral while the bike is leaned over in a curve is a bad idea because
options: A mid-corner neutral selection is how you tighten a line
You should be looking through the turn
Neutral makes the bike lean more safely than any gear
The shift lever only finds neutral when the bike is leaned
questions.explanation: Curves are for vision, lean, and a steady or gently rolling-on throttle. Find neutral when you are stopped or straight and stable, not while you are leaned in a turn. You should be looking through the turn with the clutch out and the throttle steady.

questions.q: Set the mirrors while you are stopped, and still plan to head-check, because
options: Mirrors should be aimed at your elbows
You adjust mirrors by weaving so you can see while you move over
No mirror adjustment removes the blind spot beside your shoulder
A perfect mirror setting makes a head check illegal
questions.explanation: Aim the mirrors before you leave so they show as much as they can. Then still check the mirrors and turn your head before a lateral move. The blind spot remains.

questions.q: Fingers ready at an intersection should rest so that
options: The lever is held at the bar the whole time you wait and then while you cruise
The clutch is slipped for the entire approach from highway speed
Both hands come off the grips so you can point at the cross traffic
You can squeeze the front brake quickly without already dragging the pads
questions.explanation: Cover the front brake when a hazard is ahead. That shortens reaction time. It is not the same as riding the brake or holding the clutch in the friction zone down a fast road.

questions.q: A progressive squeeze of the front brake, instead of a grab, is the normal technique because
options: Smooth pressure uses the tire without locking the wheel on a routine stop
A sudden grab is always safer and should be used for every light
The front brake should be stabbed and released over and over
Smooth pressure is only for the rear pedal, never for the lever
questions.explanation: Squeeze the front brake so weight transfers forward and the tire keeps rolling. Use the rear brake with it. A grab is how a rider locks the front wheel on a stop that did not need a skid.

questions.q: Grabbing a handful of front brake on dry pavement in a straight line can
options: Be required before the clutch is pulled in at a red light
Lock the front wheel, so release it at once
Be the preferred finish for every gentle slowdown
Replace the need to use the rear brake on a normal stop
questions.explanation: Normal stops are a smooth squeeze of both brakes. If the front wheel does lock, release the lever immediately so the tire can roll, then reapply with less pressure. Do not hold a locked front wheel.

questions.q: Learn the actual controls of the motorcycle you will ride before traffic, because
options: Every motorcycle on the road uses the right foot as the clutch
The front brake is always a left-foot pedal, with no exceptions worth learning
You can swap levers by habit once you are already in a lane
A scooter or a bike with a nonstandard layout may not match the typical lever-and-pedal map
questions.explanation: This course teaches the standard layout: clutch left hand, front brake right hand, shift left foot, rear brake right foot. If your bike is different, learn that bike's controls before you join traffic.

questions.q: Locate every primary control by feel while you are parked so that
options: You can use every control without looking
You never need a T-CLOCS check again
You can ride with the owner's manual open on the tank
Looking at the levers becomes the main search in SEE
questions.explanation: Sit on the bike and find each control with your eyes up. The front brake, clutch, both feet, the throttle, and the cut-off should be automatic before you need them in traffic.

questions.q: A signal left blinking after a lane change tells other drivers what?
options: That you have checked your blind spot
Nothing, because other drivers cannot see a motorcycle's turn signal
That you are about to turn or change lanes again
That your headlamp is on
questions.explanation: Cancel the signal when the lane change is done, not only after a turn at a corner. Many bikes will not cancel it for you. A leftover signal is a lie about your next move. False if you have finished.

questions.q: Search includes the pavement ahead of the motorcycle because
options: You should look down at the front tire rather than at the surface farther ahead
Sand, oil, and debris are hazards you need to evaluate before you are on them
The only things worth searching are brake lights, never the surface
Pavement condition is part of T-CLOCS and is not part of riding
questions.explanation: Search is not only other vehicles. The road surface, intersections, and your mirrors are all in the picture. Seeing sand or a shiny patch early gives you time to evaluate and execute a smooth change.

questions.q: Evaluate includes the chance that a driver does not see you, so you should
options: Speed up on the theory that surprise is the same as being seen
Move into the driver's blind spot so you are closer and safer
Choose a response that still works if that driver pulls out or turns
Assume eye contact guarantees the driver will wait
questions.explanation: SEE asks you to predict, not to hope. If a driver might turn across you, the evaluation includes an escape: cover the brake, adjust speed or position, and be ready to execute the stop.

questions.q: A horn blast can be part of Execute, but it does not replace
options: The need to cancel a turn signal that is still on
A pre-ride check of the lights
Finding neutral between first and second
A change in speed or position when needed
questions.explanation: Communication is one tool. If the horn does not change what the other driver is doing, you still need the speed and position part of the plan. The horn is not a brake.

questions.q: Cancel the signal after you complete a maneuver so the next driver does not
options: Yield or turn on the basis of a blink you forgot to switch off
See your headlamp, which goes out when the signal is canceled
Notice that your side stand is up
Hear the horn, which only works while a signal is blinking
questions.explanation: A blinking signal is a message. When the turn or the lane change is over, end the message. Many motorcycles leave that job to your thumb, not to an automatic cancel.

questions.q: A turn signal that will not cancel, or will not light at all, belongs in the controls check because
options: A stuck signal means the clutch cable is adjusted correctly
You cannot afford to broadcast a false turn or to have no way to show a real one
Signals are optional decorations and a failed switch can be ignored
The engine cut-off flashes the lamps for you if the switch breaks
questions.explanation: Lights and controls are checked before the ride. If you cannot turn a signal off, do not ride around advertising a turn. If you cannot turn it on, fix it before you depend on it.

questions.q: Leaving the curb on a motorcycle should include which last look?
options: A look only at the neutral light, with the stand left down
A wave in the mirror without turning your head
A check of the choke, which should be on as you enter traffic
A mirror and head check, with the stand up
questions.explanation: Signal if you are entering traffic, confirm the stand is up, check the mirror, then head-check the blind spot. Ease out through the friction zone. Do not rely on the mirror alone.

questions.q: A sticky grip that does not snap shut fails the controls check. The safe choice is to
options: Use the choke as a backup throttle return
Stay parked until the throttle closes by itself
Ride if you can pull the grip shut by hand whenever you think of it
Tie the grip forward with a strap and leave for the trip
questions.explanation: A throttle that sticks open is a do-not-ride defect. The cut-off switch is the emergency response if it happens while you are moving. It is not a reason to leave the driveway with a grip you already know is sticky.

questions.q: False information from a turn signal left on is fixed by which habit?
options: Waiting for the lean of the bike to cancel it, which every motorcycle does
Leaving it on so drivers stay extra far behind you
Switching the headlamp off to reset the signal circuit
Canceling the signal yourself after every turn and every lane change
questions.explanation: Do not trust a self-cancel that many bikes do not have. Thumb the signal off when the maneuver is complete. Drivers should see a blink only when you are actually about to move over or turn.

questions.q: Both brakes belong in a gentle slowdown, not only in a panic stop, because
options: The normal technique is always both brakes, used smoothly
The front brake should be saved for curves and never used in a straight line
Engine braking alone is the complete way to stop for a light
The rear brake is only a parking brake and is not used while moving
questions.explanation: Practice both brakes on ordinary stops. The front does most of the work, the rear helps, and the squeeze stays smooth. A rider who never uses the front brake will not use it well when it counts. The habit is there when the stop is urgent.

questions.q: Shift one gear at a time on a typical 1-N-2-3-4-5 box, and find neutral by
options: Forcing the lever until it will not move and calling that neutral
Pulling the choke out to open a neutral gate
A light touch between first and second rather than a sweep through the whole pattern
Clicking past fifth, where neutral is required to live
questions.explanation: The pattern is first, neutral, then the higher gears. A gentle shift finds the neutral detente. You do not need to run the lever through every gear to park or to start.

questions.q: At road speed, pressing the right handgrip makes the motorcycle do what?
options: Lean and turn to the left
Stand straight up
Lock the front wheel
Lean and turn to the right
questions.explanation: At speed, press the handgrip on the side you want to turn. Press right to go right. The bike leans that way. That press is countersteering.

questions.q: Pressing the left handgrip at speed is the countersteer for which result?
options: A left lean and a left turn
A right lean, used only when you want to go right
A parking-lot U-turn, which uses the same press as highway steering
A taller ride height
questions.explanation: Press left to go left once you are at speed. The front end steers briefly the other way and the motorcycle leans into the turn you pressed for.

questions.q: Slow, look, press, and roll is the cornering order that begins with
options: Braking hard after the bike is already at full lean
Pressing the bar first and only then deciding on a speed
Rolling the throttle off to a closed position in the middle of the lean
Reducing speed before the motorcycle is leaned into the turn
questions.explanation: Slow before the turn, while the bike is still upright. Then look through to the exit, press the bar to lean, and roll on the throttle gently to stabilize the exit.

questions.q: Looking through a curve means your eyes go where?
options: To the exit, along the path you want the motorcycle to follow
Down at the front tire and the patch of pavement beside the boot
Back at the entrance
At the guardrail or the oncoming lane
questions.explanation: Look through the turn to where you want to go. The motorcycle follows your eyes. Staring at a hazard is target fixation, and it steers you toward that hazard.

questions.q: The press in slow, look, press, roll is which action?
options: A hard squeeze of the front brake once the lean has started
A smooth push on the handgrip on the side you want to turn
A shove of the handlebars away from the turn, used only in a parking lot
A lean of your body off the seat while the bars stay untouched
questions.explanation: Press the grip on the turning side. Press right, go right. The press is the basic skill. Hanging off the bike is not the Basic RiderCourse answer. The bike leans that way.

questions.q: Rolling on gently after the lean is set does what for the motorcycle?
options: Is the moment to chop the throttle and grab the front brake
Means you should accelerate hard before you can see the exit
Stabilizes the bike and helps it hold the line through the exit
Replaces the need to have slowed down before the curve
questions.explanation: Once you are in the corner, the throttle should be steady or gently rolling on. That settles the motorcycle. A closed throttle in the middle of the lean unsettles it.

questions.q: Target fixation on a guardrail in a curve tends to make you
options: Automatically lean the other way, away from whatever you stare at
Cancel the lean
Gain traction, because staring at a hazard widens the tire
Steer into the rail
questions.explanation: You go where you look. If you lock your eyes on the guardrail, the debris, or the oncoming lane, you are likely to ride there. Look through to the exit in your own lane.

questions.q: Staring at a pothole on the inside of a curve is dangerous because
options: Your line drifts toward the hole instead of toward the clear exit
The pothole becomes better traction if you look at it long enough
Vision only matters at parking-lot speed
The correct response is to close the throttle and brake while fully leaned
questions.explanation: Target fixation steers the motorcycle into the thing you stare at. Pick up the clear path with your eyes. Do not study the hole, the rail, or the paint.

questions.q: You entered a curve faster than you meant to, and you still have grip and ground clearance. The better response is to
options: Straighten up, then immediately brake hard and try to re-lean
Look through the exit and press the bar to tighten the lean
Chop the throttle shut and grab the front brake while you are leaned over
Put a foot down and drag it along the pavement
questions.explanation: If traction and ground clearance remain, look where you want to go and press to lean a bit more. Do not chop the throttle and grab the front brake in the middle of the lean.

questions.q: Grabbing the front brake in the middle of a lean is a poor rescue because
options: It tightens the line more safely than a smooth press on the bar
The front brake adds ground clearance when the bike is over
It can overload the front tire while the bike is leaned and cause a slide
It is the first step of slow, look, press, and roll
questions.explanation: Do the serious slowing before the turn, while you are upright. A sudden front-brake grab at lean is how riders lose the front tire. Look and press if you still have grip and clearance.

questions.q: Chopping the throttle shut mid-corner unsettles the motorcycle because
options: A closed throttle is the same as a gentle roll-on and should be held to the exit
The engine brake adds lean angle without using the bars
It is the recommended way to tighten a line on a decreasing-radius turn
A closed throttle in the lean upsets the bike instead of settling it
questions.explanation: Once you are in the corner, keep the throttle steady or roll it on gently. Snapping it shut is not a line-tightener. It unsettles the motorcycle.

questions.q: Using the oncoming lane as the apex of a left curve is unacceptable because
options: Moving left across the line gives you more room to brake while leaned
The path has to remain in your lane, even when the corner is tempting
The oncoming lane is the proper racing line for a basic street course
A painted center line is the best traction in a wet curve
questions.explanation: Outside-inside-outside is a path inside your lane. Do not borrow the oncoming lane for a nicer apex. A car can be there even if you did not see it when you turned in.

questions.q: A decreasing-radius turn asks for more speed reduction because
options: You should brake hardest at the tightest point while fully leaned
The throttle should be chopped as soon as the radius starts to shrink
The corner tightens, and the early wide section can hide how sharp the end will be
Decreasing radius means the corner opens up
questions.explanation: Slow more before a turn that tightens. You set that lower speed while the bike is upright. Do not discover the tight part and then grab the front brake at full lean.

questions.q: A blind crest in a curve deserves extra slowing because
options: Crests always open into a straight, so speed can stay high
The correct fix is to move into the oncoming lane for a better view
You should close the throttle only after the crest, while leaned
You cannot see the rest of the corner, which may tighten or hold a hazard
questions.explanation: If you cannot see the exit, you cannot assume the corner stays gentle. Take off more speed before the crest. Look as far as the hill lets you, and do not apex across the center line.

questions.q: You cannot see through a corner blocked by a hill or by trees. The setup should be
options: A slower entry, chosen before the lean, for a corner you have not fully seen
The same entry speed you would use if the whole exit were visible
A move onto the painted line so the bike has a guide to follow
A closed throttle and a front-brake grab once you are committed to the lean
questions.explanation: Slow more when the rest of the corner is hidden. Blind curves and blind crests are not places to carry extra speed and hope. Do the slowing while you are still upright.

questions.q: A painted line in a curve is a poor place to brake or to lean hard because
options: A wet line dries first and should be used as the braking point
Paint offers less traction than the bare pavement, and wet paint is worse
Paint is the highest-grip part of the lane and is the preferred apex
Braking on the line while leaned is safer than braking while upright
questions.explanation: Do not brake hard or lean hard on a painted line in a curve, especially when it is wet. Choose a path on the clearer pavement in your lane, and do that choosing early.

questions.q: Wet lane paint on the inside of your curve should be treated as
options: The required path
A good place to chop the throttle and squeeze the front brake
A slick patch to avoid leaning or braking on
Extra grip, because water cools the paint and makes it sticky
questions.explanation: Painted markings are slippery, and rain makes them worse. Keep the hard lean and the braking off the paint. Adjust the path while you still have room. As an apex target.

questions.q: Debris lying in your curve is best handled by a path change made when?
options: At the last moment, with a hard lean directly across the debris
By closing the throttle and braking at full lean on top of the debris
By moving into the oncoming lane without a look
Early, before you are on it
questions.explanation: See the sand, gravel, or leaves early. Adjust while you can. If you must cross the patch, try to be upright over it, keep the throttle steady, then resume the lean.

questions.q: Crossing a gravel patch that sits in your curve works best if you
options: Straighten over it, then lean again after
Add lean and brake as the front tire reaches the stones
Chop the throttle the instant the gravel starts
Stare at the gravel so the bike will avoid it automatically
questions.explanation: A leaned tire on loose gravel is easy to slide. Get upright if you can, cross with small, smooth inputs, and pick the lean back up after the patch. Look at the clear pavement, not at the stones. Straighten the bike over the patch, hold a steady throttle, then lean again once you are clear.

questions.q: The basic countersteer skill the course wants is the bar press, not
options: Looking through the curve before you commit to the lean
Slowing while the motorcycle is still straight
Hanging your body off the inside of the bike like a racer
Pressing the handgrip on the side you want to turn
questions.explanation: Press the grip to lean. Body position can wait. Do not treat hanging off, or leaning your body opposite the bike, as the basic meaning of countersteering.

questions.q: Leaning your torso off the seat is not the beginner substitute for
options: A head turn toward the exit of the curve
A speed reduction completed before the lean
Staying inside your own lane on the outside-inside-outside path
A deliberate press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn
questions.explanation: The press is the skill that leans the motorcycle at speed. Hanging off is not the Basic RiderCourse answer, and leaning your body opposite the bike is not what countersteering means.

questions.q: Once the motorcycle is leaned and the line is started, the throttle should be
options: Steady, or gently rolling on, through the exit
Snapped shut and held closed until the bike is upright
Used in place of looking, so vision no longer matters
Chopped every time you want a tighter radius
questions.explanation: A steady or gently open throttle settles the bike in the corner. Closing it in the middle of the lean unsettles the motorcycle. Do the big speed change before the turn.

questions.q: Mid-corner engine braking from a fully closed throttle is a poor habit because
options: It is safer than having slowed down while the bike was upright
It unsettles the leaned motorcycle instead of holding a stable line
It is the roll in slow, look, press, and roll
It increases ground clearance automatically
questions.explanation: Roll on gently or hold a steady throttle once you are in the curve. A closed throttle mid-corner is not a precision tool. It upsets the bike you are trying to keep on line.

questions.q: Serious braking for a curve belongs at which moment?
options: On the painted line
After you have already had to press extra lean
Before the turn, while the motorcycle is still upright
At the apex, with the front brake squeezed hard at full lean
questions.explanation: Slow, then look, press, and roll. Use both brakes while you are straight, get down to the entry speed, and release the brakes before the significant lean. Do not save the braking for the middle of the curve.

questions.q: Adding a sudden brake after the lean has started is the opposite of
options: Pressing the inside grip to tighten the line when you still have grip
Looking at the exit instead of at a roadside hazard
Staying out of the oncoming lane
Setting the speed first and keeping the throttle steady or gently on
questions.explanation: If you need a large speed cut, make it before the lean. A sudden brake in the middle of the corner, especially a grabbed front brake, is how a too-fast entry gets worse.

questions.q: Hard parts of the motorcycle are already touching down in the lean. More press will not create
options: Ground clearance you have already used up
A license to cross the center line for a wider arc
A reason to hang off as the basic fix taught in the course
Better grip on a wet painted line
questions.explanation: Press to tighten the lean only if you still have traction and ground clearance. If something is already dragging, you are at the limit. The fix was a slower entry. Do not chop the throttle and grab the front brake.

questions.q: You still have pavement grip and the pegs are clear of the road. Tightening the line is done by
options: Aiming at the oncoming lane so the radius can open up
Looking through the turn and pressing the grip on the side you want to go
Closing the throttle completely and squeezing the front brake hard
Moving your body onto the outside of the seat and calling that countersteering
questions.explanation: With grip and clearance left, press the bar. That is the countersteer. Keep the throttle from being chopped, and keep the path inside your lane.

questions.q: A right-hand curve at road speed begins with which hand input?
options: A turn of the bars to the left, the way you would in a slow U-turn
A lean of your body to the left while the bars stay neutral
A press on the right handgrip
A press on the left handgrip, which leans the bike left
questions.explanation: Press right, go right. The motorcycle leans right. Do not reverse the press, and do not replace it with hanging off the left side.

questions.q: A left-hand curve at road speed begins with which hand input?
options: A press on the right handgrip, saved for left turns only
A hard front-brake application as the lean starts
Steering into the oncoming lane before you press anything
A press on the left handgrip so the motorcycle leans left
questions.explanation: Press left to go left at speed. Combine it with a look through your own lane and a speed you already set. The oncoming lane is not part of the turn-in.

questions.q: Your head in a curve should turn toward the exit rather than
options: Staring at the center line so the bike will follow the paint
Dropping your eyes to the tank or front tire
Looking through the turn
Watching the mirror until the apex
questions.explanation: Turn your head and look through the curve. Where you look is where you steer. The tank and the tire are poor targets. The exit in your lane is the target. Dropping your eyes to the tank, the front tire, or the edge right beside the boot.

questions.q: Watching the front tire through a curve pulls your attention
options: Off the bike, which automatically tightens the line without a press
Onto the oncoming lane
Too close, so you miss the exit and any debris farther along the lane
To the correct place
questions.explanation: Look farther along the path you want, not down at the contact patch. A near look makes the curve feel rushed and feeds target fixation on whatever is beside the wheel.

questions.q: An S-curve asks you to pick up the next bend with your eyes as
options: You stare at the first apex until the bike has passed it and only then look up
You use the oncoming lane to straighten both bends into one
You brake hard in the transition while the bike is leaned
You finish the first arc
questions.explanation: Look through the turn you are in, then move your eyes into the next one. Do not get stuck looking at the first apex, the rail, or the center line. Keep each path in your lane.

questions.q: When you can see several curves ahead, set your entry speed for
options: The tightest corner you can actually see
The fastest section
A constant speed that ignores a blind crest in the middle
The oncoming lane's width, which you may use if your lane looks slow
questions.explanation: Search as far as you can see and evaluate the tightest visible radius. Slow for that curve before you lean. A decreasing radius or a blind crest means you slow even more. For the gentle one in front of it.

questions.q: Releasing the brakes before the meaningful lean lets the tire
options: Stand the bike up
Take the turn without an extra braking load
Lock, which is the goal of a leaned entry
Slide onto the painted line, where grip is better
questions.explanation: Do the braking upright, then release and lean. Combining a hard brake with a big lean overloads the tire. If you were too fast and still have grip and clearance, press rather than grab. Take the cornering load without a sudden extra braking load at the same time.

questions.q: Selecting the gear for a curve should happen
options: By slipping the clutch all the way around the curve
In neutral, so the bike rolls freely with a closed throttle
Before the lean
At the apex, with your eyes on the shift lever
questions.explanation: Arrive in the gear you need. Shift while you are straight, along with the slowing. In the corner, look, press, and keep the throttle steady or gently on. Do not coast through in neutral. You are not hunting the shifter in the middle of the turn.

questions.q: Holding the motorcycle with your knees against the tank is basic stability, and it is not
options: A reason to keep your feet on the pegs
Compatible with looking through the exit
Useful while you press the handgrip
The thing that makes the bike turn
questions.explanation: Stay connected to the bike with your knees. The turn itself, at speed, still comes from the press on the bar. Do not make hanging off the basic answer.

questions.q: A wet curve gets its slower entry while you are upright because
options: Available grip is lower
Rain adds traction and lets you lean farther than on a dry day
Wet paint becomes the best surface for a hard brake at the apex
You should wait to slow down until you are fully leaned in the rain
questions.explanation: Slow more before a wet curve. Keep the hard lean and the braking off paint and metal. Once you are in the corner, stay smooth on the throttle instead of chopping it. The same lean or the same speed is less forgiving.

questions.q: Gravel spilled on the outside of your lane in a curve is a reason to
options: Close your eyes briefly so you do not fixate, then hold your exact line onto the gravel
Change path early and avoid a late leaned swerve onto the stones
Aim at the gravel and brake when the front tire arrives
Move into the oncoming lane as the standard detour
questions.explanation: Adjust before the patch. A last-second swerve while leaned is a good way to cross the gravel at the worst angle. Upright over it if you must cross, then resume the lean.

questions.q: You realize the curve is a decreasing radius only after you have turned in. If grip and clearance remain, you should
options: Stand the bike up and use the oncoming lane as a runoff
Stare at the outside edge so the bike will tighten by itself
Look farther through the tightening exit and press to increase the lean
Chop the throttle and grab a handful of front brake at full lean
questions.explanation: A tightening corner is why you should have slowed more on the way in. If you are already there and the tires and the ground clearance still allow it, look and press. Do not panic-brake in the lean.

questions.q: The first half of a decreasing-radius corner often looks easier than the second half, so you should
options: Enter fast and plan to brake at the tightest point while leaned
Treat every tightening corner as if it opens up
Apex in the oncoming lane where the radius feels larger
Choose the entry speed for the tighter part you are approaching
questions.explanation: Slow more before a corner that gets tighter. The gentle beginning is not the corner you are riding. Set the speed early, while the motorcycle is upright. For the easy part.

questions.q: A crest that hides the next part of the curve should change your plan by
options: Taking more speed off before you commit
Maintaining speed, since what you cannot see cannot be sharp
Moving left of the center line to see around the hill sooner
Closing the throttle only after the bike leaves the ground or the crest
questions.explanation: You cannot see the rest of the corner beyond a blind crest. Slow more first. Look as far as the road lets you, stay in your lane, and do not add a brake grab once you are leaned. The hidden part is unknown.

questions.q: Even a familiar curve can hide a stopped vehicle beyond a crest, so the entry should
options: Include a hard lean across the painted edge line
Leave you room to deal with what you have not seen yet
Be as fast as the last time you rode it empty
Use the oncoming lane
questions.explanation: Blind means you do not get to assume. Slow more, search as far as you can, and keep an escape inside your lane. Familiarity is not the same as a clear view.

questions.q: The center line is not a spare lane for your apex. On a left curve you still
options: Put the tires on the paint
Lean until the line is under the engine, then brake
Keep the inside of the path on your side of the line
Cross the line if no car is visible at the moment you turn in
questions.explanation: Your lane is the whole width you get. Outside-inside-outside happens inside it. The oncoming lane belongs to someone else, including someone you have not seen.

questions.q: A car that might be in the oncoming lane is a reason to
options: Stare at the car if it appears, even if that aim points you at it
Keep your apex clearly on your side of the center line
Apex earlier, farther across the line
Brake hard on the center-line paint while leaned
questions.explanation: Do not use their lane as your line. If a car does appear, look through your own escape path, not at the car's grille. Target fixation will steer you toward it.

questions.q: Standing the bike up in the middle of a curve so you can brake hard, then flopping back to a lean, is worse than
options: The recommended way to handle a decreasing radius
A good use of wet paint, which likes sudden load
Setting a lower speed before the turn
The definition of slow, look, press, and roll
questions.explanation: Panic transitions upset the tire. Slow before the curve. If you are already in it and still have traction and clearance, look and press. Do not chop, grab, stand up, and grab again. Having set a lower speed before the turn and pressing smoothly if you still have grip.

questions.q: A gentle roll-on through the second half of a curve that you can see through will
options: Be replaced, in the basic technique, by a closed throttle
Require a front-brake squeeze at the same time
Be a reason to look back at the entry instead of the exit
Help settle the suspension and drive you toward the exit
questions.explanation: That is the roll in slow, look, press, roll. The throttle comes on gently once the lean is established and you can see where the line goes. It is not a wide-open twist before the exit is visible.

questions.q: Sand washed across one part of a sunny curve should be crossed
options: By staring at the sand pile until the bike misses it
More upright, with a steady throttle, after you adjusted the path early
At maximum lean
With the front brake held on so the tire can bite the sand
questions.explanation: Treat sand like other debris in a curve. Move early if you can go around it inside your lane. If you must cross, be upright, stay smooth, look beyond the patch, then resume the lean.

questions.q: Wet leaves in a shaded curve are a surface problem you solve by
options: Using the leaves as the apex
Chopping the throttle and grabbing the front brake on the leaves
Slowing before them and not leaning hard or braking hard on top of them
Accelerating and adding lean as you reach the leaves
questions.explanation: Leaves, especially wet ones, are poor traction. Set a lower speed early, choose a clearer path if you have one in your lane, and keep your inputs smooth if you have to ride over them.

questions.q: A steel plate or a manhole cover in your curve should not be the place where you
options: Hold the bike as upright as the path allows, with a steady throttle
Look beyond the metal to the exit of your lane
Adjust your line early so the cross is shorter and straighter
Brake hard or hold a deep lean
questions.explanation: Metal is slippery, and wet metal is worse. Do not pick it as a braking zone or a deep-lean apex. Cross it more upright if you can, then continue the corner.

questions.q: If the bad patch fills your whole lane in the curve, the priority is to
options: Swerve into the oncoming lane at the last second without looking
Get upright over it, steady throttle, look ahead
Add lean until the patch is under the peg and then brake
Close your eyes so you cannot target-fixate
questions.explanation: You cannot always go around debris and stay in your lane. When you cannot, reduce the lean over the patch, avoid sudden brake or throttle chops, and pick the corner back up on the far side. Get as upright as you can over it, hold a steady throttle, and look to where you will resume the lean.

questions.q: Waiting until the front tire is on the debris to decide on a swerve usually means
options: Target fixation is avoided
The oncoming lane is automatically clear if you decide late
The swerve happens too late and while you may still be leaned
You get the best chance to cross the patch upright
questions.explanation: Search far enough ahead that a path change happens early. A leaned swerve onto gravel or wet paint is the opposite of getting upright over the bad spot.

questions.q: Countersteering can be described to a new rider as
options: Lean your body off the outside and keep your hands light and idle
Turn the bars hard into a walking-speed U-turn and call that the highway skill
Close the throttle whenever you want the bike to lean farther
Press the handgrip on the side you want to turn, and the motorcycle leans that way
questions.explanation: The basic sentence is press right, go right, and press left, go left, at speed. It is not hanging off, and it is not the low-speed technique of turning the bars into a tight U-turn.

questions.q: A small, early press at speed is enough to start a lean. You do not need to
options: Yank the bars to the steering stop
Look through the exit
Have slowed down before a tight or blind curve
Keep the tires off the wet paint
questions.explanation: The press is deliberate and smooth. A violent yank is not more skilled. Combine a controlled press with vision and with a speed you set before the turn. Yank the handlebars to the steering stop to prove the bike will turn.

questions.q: Holding a panic upright and a handful of front brake when a curve tightens is the mistake the press is meant to replace, if you still have
options: A reason to close the throttle completely at the same moment
Grip and clearance to lean a bit farther
A guarantee that the oncoming lane is empty
Wet paint under the tire, which adds the missing grip
questions.explanation: Look and press when the tire and the clearance can still give you a tighter line. If you are already out of clearance or the tire is sliding, more lean is not available. Either way, do not chop and grab in the lean. Traction and ground clearance to lean a little farther while you look through the exit.

questions.q: Putting a foot down in a road-speed curve does not tighten the line. The input that does is
options: A shift into neutral so the bike can lean freely
A stare at the roadside object you hope to miss
A press on the handgrip on the side you want to turn
A drag of the boot
questions.explanation: Keep your feet on the pegs. Press the bar, look through the turn, and keep the throttle steady or gently on. A foot on the pavement is not cornering technique.

questions.q: Dragging a knee or hanging off the seat is an advanced body position, so the basic course answer remains
options: Moving your weight to the outside of the turn and calling it countersteering
Braking deep into the lean as the first skill to master
Using the oncoming lane so body position does not matter
The press on the bar, after you have set your speed and your eyes
questions.explanation: Body position can wait. New riders learn to slow, look, press, and roll. Hanging off is not the skill that makes the motorcycle turn in this course.

questions.q: In a slow U-turn your eyes still matter. You should look
options: At the brake lever
Where you want the motorcycle to finish
At the ground beside the footpeg until the turn is over
Over your shoulder at the entrance the whole time
questions.explanation: Even at walking speed, you go where you look. Turn your head to the exit of the U-turn. Staring at the curb is target fixation at low speed. At the curb next to your front wheel.

questions.q: A rider who looks at the oncoming lane during a left curve is likely to
options: Gain a legal apex
Cancel the need to press the left grip
Drift toward that lane
Be pushed back to the right by the act of looking left
questions.explanation: Vision leads the bike. Look through the exit that stays in your lane. Looking at the oncoming lane, the ditch, or the rail pulls the line that way. Why the eyes belong on the path inside their own lane.

questions.q: The look and the press work together. A rider who looks through the exit and presses the correct grip will
options: Need to hang off before the press can do anything
Need to close the throttle or the lean will not start
Need to brake on the paint to finish the turn
Lean the motorcycle toward the path those eyes already chose
questions.explanation: Eyes first, then the press that leans the bike onto the path you are looking along. The throttle stays steady or rolls on gently. That is the middle of slow, look, press, roll.

questions.q: Entry speed for a curve you can see all the way through is chosen for
options: That whole visible arc
The straight that follows
The painted line's friction
The oncoming lane's extra width
questions.explanation: If you can see a constant curve, pick a speed that fits it and get there before you lean. You still do not brake hard on paint, and you still do not apex across the center line. Adjusted with a panic brake later. That whole visible arc, slowed while you are upright.

questions.q: A curve that starts gentle and then tightens is not a constant arc, so you should
options: Use the shoulder to invent a constant radius
Slow more, before reaching the tight part
Treat the beginning as the whole corner and accelerate
Wait to judge it until the tight part, then grab the front brake
questions.explanation: That is a decreasing radius. The early view flatters you. Take the extra speed off while you are straight. Look far enough to see the tightening if it is visible. Slow more than the gentle beginning suggests, before you are leaned into the tight part.

questions.q: Night does not change the shape of a curve you cannot see beyond your headlight. You should
options: Use the high beam on the painted line and brake there
Apex wider, into the oncoming lane, where the light reaches farther
Slow more, as for any blind curve
Ride the daylight speed
questions.explanation: If the headlight does not show the exit, the corner is blind. Slow before it. Stay in your lane, keep off the wet paint, and do not chop the throttle once you are leaned. Slow more, as you would for any blind curve, before you lean into what you have not seen.

questions.q: Braking while leaned over a wet edge line combines two problems:
options: Extra grip from the water and a safer place to stop
The recommended apex for a decreasing-radius turn
The roll-on that stabilizes the exit
Slick paint plus braking while leaned
questions.explanation: Do not brake or lean hard on a painted line, especially wet. Do the slowing on the better pavement, upright, and keep the line of the curve in the clearer part of your lane. Reduced traction from the paint and a brake load while the bike is leaned.

questions.q: The throttle's job after the press has set the lean is to
options: Stay steady or come on gently so the motorcycle stays settled to the exit
Snap shut so engine braking can tighten the radius
Replace looking, because a loud engine corrects target fixation
Be left closed until the bike is completely upright
questions.explanation: Slow is the step before the curve. Roll is the step in the curve. Once leaned, do not treat a closed throttle as the way to steer. It unsettles the bike.

questions.q: You feel the line drifting wide even though the tire still has grip and the peg is not down. Correct it by
options: Aiming at the shoulder or the oncoming lane, whichever is closer
Looking farther along your lane and pressing the inside grip a bit more
Grabbing the front brake to stand the bike up and then turning harder
Leaning your upper body off the outside and loosening your hands
questions.explanation: That extra press is countersteering. Use it while you still have traction and ground clearance. Keep the throttle from snapping shut, and keep the added lean inside your lane.

questions.q: A too-fast entry you survive is a reminder to change the next corner's
options: Vision, by watching the guardrail so you remember where it is
Throttle, by closing it earlier in the lean next time
Entry speed, taken off with both brakes while the bike is straight
Apex, by moving it into the oncoming lane
