questions.explanation: When the beam points at the sky, you are not seeing the road beyond the crest. Slow down and do not overdrive the dark side of the hill. The beam will not show the far side until you are on it.

questions.q: Road dips hide the bottom in a shadow the headlight skips over. What is the approach?
options: A hard lean through the shadow
Slower, so you can stop for the unseen bottom
Faster, so you fly the dip
The high beam left on behind a car in the dip
questions.explanation: A dip can hide a hole or an animal. If the light skips the bottom, slow until you can stop for what may be there. Do not use speed to jump the unknown. Slower, so the unseen bottom is still inside a distance you can stop for.

questions.q: Early dimming before a hilltop meeting is better than dimming as you pass. Why start early?
options: Because dimming early lets you ride faster
Because the low beam reaches farther than the high beam
Because they enter your beam before you see them clearly
Because the law requires the high beam only in driveways
questions.explanation: Dim as you approach, not at the last moment. Crests hide oncoming eyes until late. Your high beam should already be low so you do not blind them.

questions.q: Streetlights ending at the edge of town shrink the view in one moment. What do you change at that boundary?
options: Speed up because traffic is lighter
Switch to a dark shield
Turn the headlight off now that the streetlights are gone
Slow so you can stop inside the headlight's reach
questions.explanation: When the streetlights end, your headlight's patch is the road you can claim. Slow so you can stop within it. Do not take the dark as a reason to go faster. Slow down as the headlight becomes your only view, and be able to stop inside it.

questions.q: Moonlit pavement is not a substitute for the headlight. A rider wants the lamp off for the view. What do you keep on?
options: The headlight, and a speed to stop within it
Only the moon, if the road looks silver
A phone light in your left hand
The brake light only
questions.explanation: Keep the headlight on. Moonlight does not show you a stopping distance you can trust, and it does not make you obvious to a driver. Do not ride with a light in your hand. The headlight, and a speed that can stop inside its real patch.

questions.q: Failed bulbs that leave you on a parking light only are discovered in the driveway. What is the night plan?
options: Ride with the high-beam switch on even though the lamp is dead
Do not ride until a real headlight works
Ride the parking light if you stay in town
Ride the parking light behind a friend
questions.explanation: A parking light is not enough to see or to be seen as a headlight. If the headlight does not work, do not ride into the dark. Fix it first.

questions.q: Taillight outages discovered before a night ride mean drivers behind you get no lamp. What do you do?
options: Ride without it if you wear a light jacket
Ride without it and stay in the left lane
Fix the taillight before you ride at night
Ride without it if the brake light still works
questions.explanation: Be seen from the rear too. Do not start a night ride with a dead taillight. Reflective gear helps and does not replace the lamp.

questions.q: Brake-light failures at dusk mean a stop will not announce itself. What is the decision?
options: Ride if you pump the brake to make the headlight nod
Ride if you use hand signals only on the highway
Ride if a passenger holds a flashlight
Repair the brake light before night riding
questions.explanation: A dark brake light hides your stop. Fix it before you depend on it at night. A nodding headlight and a highway hand signal are not the repair.

questions.q: Blind spots beside a car at night are worse because the driver has less peripheral view. Where do you refuse to linger?
options: In the blind spot if you are faster than the car
In the blind spot
In the blind spot if your high beam is on
In the blind spot if you honk continuously
questions.explanation: A car's blind spot is a bad place at night as well as by day. Do not linger there. Be seen from a position the driver can actually use, and assume they still might not judge your speed. You pass or drop back rather than ride there.

questions.q: Intersections at night hide a driver who looks through your single headlight. How do you arrive?
options: With the headlight off so you do not distract them
In the oncoming lane to be more centered in their view
Ready to brake, covering the controls, without assuming you were seen
At a higher speed so you clear the crossing sooner
questions.explanation: Do not assume you were seen. Cover the controls, be able to stop, and keep the headlight on. Speed is not a substitute for being unseen.

questions.q: Left-turning cars at night are still the classic cross of a motorcycle's path. What is the prepared response?
options: Speed up to beat the turn
Swerve left across the center
Stare at their headlights while you hold speed
Slow, cover the brakes, and be ready to stop
questions.explanation: A driver may not judge a single headlight. Be ready to brake in a straight, stable way. Do not swerve into the oncoming lane, and do not lock your eyes on their lamps.

questions.q: Sunglasses still down at dusk make the headlight patch look smaller than it is. What do you switch to?
options: An open face with no eye protection
Clear eye protection, before it is dark
Darker sunglasses
A tinted shield and sunglasses together
questions.explanation: At night you need a clear face shield, not sunglasses or a dark tint. Change them while you can still see the buckle. Do not ride the dusk with night lenses that are actually day lenses. A clear shield or clear eye protection, before the light is gone.

questions.q: Group rides at night need more than a daytime stagger copied blindly. What spacing do you add?
options: Less space so nobody gets lost
The high beam on while you follow the rider ahead
A dark shield so the rider ahead's lamp does not bother you
More space than the daytime group, with every headlight on
questions.explanation: Increase following distance at night, including in a group. Keep headlights on, and dim your high beam when you are following. A dark shield is the wrong response to another rider's lamp.

questions.q: Dawn fatigue plus low sun glare is a reason to treat the morning like a risk, not a trophy. What do you do if your eyes are already fighting?
options: Stop at a safe place and rest
Speed into the sun so the trip ends
Flip a dark shield down and call the fatigue solved
Follow a truck at a one-second gap
questions.explanation: Fatigue is common when the night meets the morning. If you are blinking and the glare is taking the road, get off the bike and rest. A dark shield does not cure sleepiness.

questions.q: Wet leaves at night are a shiny patch your beam finds late. How do you ride over them?
options: In a lower gear with the clutch popped
Slow and upright, with no sudden lean or grabbed brake
Leaned over, so the edge of the tire cuts the leaves
With the front brake squeezed hard on the leaves
questions.explanation: Night hides the leaves until they are close. Slow before them and stay upright. Do not grab the front brake or snap a lean on a surface you can barely see.

questions.q: Gravel scattered on a night corner shows up as sparkle under the beam. What is the body position?
options: Braking hard with the bars turned
Accelerating hard to lighten the front over the stones
Upright, with speed already reduced, and no hard lean on the gravel
Leaned to the edge of the tire to finish the corner
questions.explanation: If gravel appears inside a night corner, you wanted to be slower and more upright. Do not add lean or a sharp brake once you are on it. Ease off and keep the bike up.

questions.q: Pushy cars behind you at night want a faster pace than your headlight supports. What do you give them?
options: A safe place to pass, without speeding up
Your braking distance, by speeding up
A brake-check
The oncoming lane, by moving left and holding
questions.explanation: Do not let a following driver choose a speed beyond your headlight. Keep the speed you can stop from, and let them pass when it is safe. Do not brake-check them.

questions.q: Pothole puddles at night hide the hole inside the shine. What speed is honest?
options: A walking pace in the opposing lane around every shine
A speed that can stop inside the headlight's reach
A speed that planes across every puddle
A speed copied from the car that just splashed through
questions.explanation: You cannot see the bottom of a night puddle. Ride so you can stop within the beam rather than hoping the shine is shallow. Do not swing into the oncoming lane as a habit. A speed that can stop inside the headlight, before the shine becomes a hit.

questions.q: Passenger loads at night add a longer stop to an already short view. What gap do you build?
options: A smaller gap so the passenger feels the car's lights
No gap change if the passenger wears reflective gear
A night gap even larger than your solo night gap
The solo night gap
questions.explanation: Night already demands more following distance. A passenger makes the stop longer. Add space and slow down before corners. Reflective gear helps you be seen and does not shorten the stop. The extra weight lengthens the stop.

questions.q: Clear shields on the helmet you meant to swap are still in the garage while a smoke shield is on your head. It is night. What do you do?
options: Ride the smoke shield if the streetlights are on
Ride the smoke shield with the high beam always on
Ride with the shield up and no eye protection
Go back for the clear shield before you ride
questions.explanation: Use a clear face shield at night, not a dark tint. Streetlights and a high beam do not replace a clear view of a short patch of road. Swap the shield first.

questions.q: Dusk sunglasses are still on as the sky goes gray. What is the simple gear change?
options: Switch to clear eye protection
Add a second dark lens
Take all eye protection off
Tint the headlight to match
questions.explanation: When the light fails, a dark lens fails with it. Put on a clear shield before night riding. Do not match the headlight to the sunglasses. Replace them with clear eye protection or a clear shield now.

questions.q: Rainy following gaps at night should compare how with a clear night gap?
options: They should match a dry daytime gap
They should close whenever the car brakes
They should be larger
They should be smaller
questions.explanation: Rain at night is glare, slick paint, and less sight. Slow a lot and add even more following distance than on a clear night. Do not use the car ahead as a roof. Glare and paint join the short view.

questions.q: Clear nights still have a fixed headlight patch. What does that patch forbid?
options: Only a speed that feels exciting
Only riding with a passenger
Only the use of reflective tape
Any speed that cannot stop in it
questions.explanation: Even on a clear night, overdriving the headlight means you cannot stop for what you cannot see. Reflective tape and a passenger do not extend the beam. Slow to the light you have. A speed that cannot stop inside the lit road.

questions.q: Shoulder stops at night need a place that is not the travel lane. Where do you put the bike if you must stop?
options: Off the roadway, where the bike is not in the lane
In the lane, with the headlight pointed at the sky
On a crosswalk
Between lanes, where cars can see both sides
questions.explanation: If you stop at night, get off the road. A dark or even a lit motorcycle in the lane is a crash target. Do not use a crosswalk as parking.

questions.q: Reflective vests you packed because you felt foolish are the right layer once the sun is down. What do you do with the feeling?
options: Wear it only if it rains
Wear it under the jacket where it cannot reflect
Wear the vest anyway, with the headlight on
Leave the vest packed so the jacket stays stylish
questions.explanation: Be seen. Wear the reflective gear you have. Style is not a lighting system, and a vest under a jacket does nothing. Drivers still may not judge your speed, so ride to the headlight.

questions.q: Black jackets without reflective panels are all you brought, but you do have tape. What is the useful step?
options: Skip the tape
Turn the headlight off so the tape is the only story
Ride faster so you spend less time unseen
Put the tape on the helmet or jacket and keep the headlight on
questions.explanation: Use reflective tape if you have it, and ride with the headlight on. Being more visible still does not mean a driver judged your closing speed. Keep a speed you can stop from.

questions.q: Passenger reflectivity does not cover the rider in dark gear. Who needs the visible layer?
options: You do, on the motorcycle
Only the passenger
Nobody, if the brake light works
Only the bike, if the headlight is on
questions.explanation: Be seen yourself. A reflective passenger does not paint your jacket. Headlight on, reflective gear or tape if you have it, and no assumption that your speed was judged. Only the person behind you.

questions.q: Late dimming, done as you pass an oncoming car, still blinds them through the approach. When should the low beam already be on?
options: Only at the moment your handlebars are beside theirs
Only after they flash you
Only if they dim first
Well before you meet them, as soon as you are approaching
questions.explanation: Dim when you approach, not as you pass. The glare you cause on the way in is the dangerous part. Do not wait to see if they dim first.

questions.q: Debris between you and a braking car is invisible if you only watch the brake lights. What distance makes room for that debris?
options: A longer gap than your daytime habit
A one-second gap
A gap of a few feet
Whatever gap keeps you out of the wind
questions.explanation: Increase following distance at night. Brake lights do not show you the road between you and the car. Leave room to see and to stop.

questions.q: Railroad tracks at night show up late under a single beam. How do you cross?
options: With the headlight off so the rails do not glare
Slow, upright, and straight within your lane
Leaned along the rails to follow their shine
At speed, so the crossing is brief
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "Usually it is safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks." At night, ride slow enough to stop within the distance your headlight shows.

questions.q: Black-ice season nights hide shine until you are on it. What inputs do you allow?
options: A sudden lean to test for ice
A grabbed front brake on the shiny patch
Small, smooth inputs at a much lower speed
Hard throttle to spin across the shine
questions.explanation: If the night may be icy, slow a lot and keep inputs smooth, or do not ride. Do not test with a grab or a sharp lean. The headlight will not give you a long warning. Small, smooth inputs at a much lower speed, or you do not ride if the surface is unknown.

questions.q: Practicing night speed by riding faster each block is a poor way to learn. What is the actual limit?
options: The speed of the car that is pushing you
The speed you used on this street in July at noon
The speed that makes the engine smoother
The distance the headlight shows, which does not grow
questions.explanation: As speed rises, the headlight still only shows a fixed patch of road. Practice does not extend that patch. Ride only as fast as you can stop inside it.

questions.q: Group pressure to keep a brisk night pace is not a headlight upgrade. What do you tell the group?
options: You will ride slow enough to stop inside the beam
You will match them and outrun the light
You will ride between them with your lamp off
You will follow at a few feet with the high beam on
questions.explanation: As speed rises, the headlight still only shows a fixed patch. Do not let the group pick a pace beyond that patch. Dim if you are following, and let them go if they will not slow. You will ride at a speed that can stop inside the beam, even if that means they go ahead.

questions.q: Parking lights mistaken for a night setup are what a new rider leaves selected. What do you require before the street?
options: No lights, if the street is lit
A working headlight on, plus a clear shield
The parking light and a reflective hat
The parking light and a fast pace
questions.explanation: Do not ride at night on a parking light. The headlight has to be on, the shield clear, and the speed inside the beam. A hat is not a lamp.

questions.q: Dim beams that still are not the high beam are correct when a car is ahead. What else is correct about distance?
options: Ride in their blind spot with the low beam
Pass immediately on a hill
Drop back farther than you would in daylight
Close up so the low beam seems brighter
questions.explanation: Dim when you follow, and increase following distance. A low beam behind a car shows even less of the gap. Do not close up to make the lamp feel stronger. Their body hides the road.

questions.q: Residential alleys at night hide bins, dogs, and people in a short beam. What pace belongs there?
options: A slow pace that can stop inside the beam
A brisk pace so you are not in the alley long
The high beam into windows and a fast pace
A feet-down paddle with the light off
questions.explanation: Alleys show hazards late. Slow to the beam and scan the edges. Do not ride dark, and do not use speed to shorten a place you cannot see through. A slow pace that can stop inside the headlight, scanning the edges.

questions.q: First night rides on a new motorcycle are a reason to shorten the plan. What do you shorten?
options: The headlight use, to save the battery
The gear, because a new bike is more visible
The speed and distance, until you know its reach
Nothing, if the bike is newer than your last one
questions.explanation: Learn the actual patch of that headlight before you ask it to cover a fast trip. Slow so you can stop within what this lamp shows. A new bike is not a longer beam. The speed and the distance, until you know how far that headlight really reaches.

questions.q: Rain grooves and metal plates at night are shine with poor traction. How do you cross?
options: Leaned and braking
In the oncoming lane at speed
With the clutch dumped in a low gear while leaned
Upright, already slow, with no braking in the lean
questions.explanation: Night rain hides low-traction shine until late. Slow a lot and cross upright. Do not add a lean and a brake at the same time on a plate you just found.

questions.q: Right-edge discipline during a long glare meeting includes your own beam as well. What is your beam doing?
options: It is off
It is on high and pointed at their mirror
It is already on low
It is on high until they dim
questions.explanation: Dim for the oncoming driver, and look at the right edge of your lane. Do not fight their high beam with yours. Both of you blinded is not a solution. You are not adding glare to theirs.

questions.q: Lane positions past a row of dark parked cars should favor which side of your lane?
options: The side inside the door swing
The oncoming lane
The gutter, as close to the cars as the pegs allow
The side farther from the doors, at low speed
questions.explanation: Opening doors are harder to see at night. Give the parked row a wider lane position, and be able to stop within the headlight. Do not borrow the oncoming lane to do it. The side farther from the doors, with speed low enough to stop if a door opens.

questions.q: Speed that rises on a familiar night road still leaves the headlight showing only a fixed patch. What do you refuse to believe?
options: That familiarity makes the patch longer
That you should dim for oncoming cars
That reflective gear helps
That rain shortens the useful view further
questions.explanation: As speed rises, the headlight still only shows a fixed patch of road. Knowing the street does not extend it. Refuse the faster pace, and slow again if rain or glare shrinks the useful part of that patch.

questions.q: Animals that you cannot swerve around without leaving your lane at night are handled how?
options: By speeding up to pass over them
By slowing and braking straight
By always swerving left
By always laying the bike down
questions.explanation: If a swerve would put you into traffic, brake straight and keep the lane. Night is when that choice matters most, because the animal appears inside a short beam. Do not practice a lay-down.

questions.q: Visor cracks that throw headlight glare into a star pattern are a reason to continue or to stop?
options: To continue with sunglasses over the crack
To continue on the high beam
To stop and replace or repair the shield
To continue if the crack is only on the left
questions.explanation: A cracked shield wrecks the small night view you have. Stop and put a clear, intact shield on. Do not add sunglasses and do not outrun the star pattern. To stop and replace or repair the shield before more night miles.

questions.q: Hotel parking exits at night dump you from a lit garage into a dark street. What do you reset?
options: Your speed, down to the new headlight patch
Nothing, because the garage was bright
The high beam on into the cars waiting outside
The dark shield you used in the garage lights
questions.explanation: When the light around you collapses, the headlight is the new limit. Slow so you can stop inside it. Dim for people waiting outside, and do not wear a dark shield into that change. Your speed, down to the new headlight patch, with a clear shield already on.

questions.q: Last miles of a long night are when fatigue and a short beam stack. If you are blinking, what are those miles?
options: Miles you ride one second behind a truck
Miles you do not ride
Miles you ride faster to finish
Miles you ride with the visor up and no eye protection
questions.explanation: If you are blinking hard, get off the bike at a safe place. The last miles are the ones fatigue wants. Do not trade them for a draft or for missing eye protection.

questions.q: Work-zone flaggers at night are easy to miss until the beam hits the vest. How do you approach the glow?
options: Use the high beam into the flagger's face so they see you
Pass the flagger in the oncoming lane if the cone line looks slow
Slow early so you can stop within the headlight if the flagger's direction changes
Hold highway pace until the vest is beside you
questions.explanation: Night work zones appear late. Slow so the headlight's reach is a distance you can stop in, and obey the flagger. Do not blind them with a sustained high beam.

questions.q: Bridge decks at night often look dry when the road before them was only damp. What do you assume about the surface?
options: Assume it is drier and open the throttle
Assume paint on the bridge is the best place to lean
Assume the railing lights replace your headlight
Assume it may be colder and slicker, and slow before you are on it
questions.explanation: Bridges can be slick when the road is not, and at night you see that change late. Slow before the deck. Do not use extra throttle or a lean on the paint to learn the surface.

questions.q: Shadowed driveways crossing your night lane can hide a car's nose. What arrival speed is honest?
options: Slow enough to stop if a car rolls out of the shadow
Fast enough that the car will wait
The speed of the car behind you
A speed with the headlight off so you can see their lamps
questions.explanation: Driveways hide vehicles in shadow. At night your beam finds them late, so your speed has to fit the patch you can actually see. Keep the headlight on and be ready to brake.

questions.q: Unmarked curves that you know by heart still go dark beyond the beam. What is the entry compared with this afternoon?
options: Identical if a passenger remembers the curve
Slower, since the beam won't show the exit early
Identical, because memory replaces the exit view
Faster, so the beam sweeps the exit sooner
questions.explanation: A curve at night needs more slowing than the same curve in daylight. Memory is not a headlight. Enter slow enough that the unseen exit is not a surprise you must brake for while leaned. Slower, because the headlight will not show the exit until you are in the turn.

questions.q: Crosswalks at night may hold a person who has not stepped into the beam yet. What do you do as you approach?
options: Ride the crosswalk line leaned over if it is painted
Move into the oncoming lane to see around a parked car
Cover the brakes and slow so a person at the edge is inside your stop
Speed up to clear the crosswalk before anyone steps
questions.explanation: Pedestrians show up late. Slow and cover the brakes as you approach a night crosswalk. Do not clear it with speed, and do not borrow the oncoming lane for a better view.

questions.q: Van taillights close ahead block more of the night road than a low car does. What gap do you choose?
options: A smaller gap
A gap inside the van's blind spot
A gap that requires your high beam into the van's mirrors
A larger gap than you would leave behind a low car
questions.explanation: Increase following distance at night, and add more behind a tall vehicle that hides the road. Dim so you are not blasting their mirrors. Their lamps are not your view of the pavement. Your beam can see some surface.

questions.q: Fresh asphalt on a hot day is soft under the side stand and starting to dimple. Where should the motorcycle be?
options: On the soft patch if you leave it in neutral
On the soft patch if the stand is only partly down
On the soft patch if you point the wheel at traffic
On a solid spot, or on a pad if the ground is soft
questions.explanation: A hot pipe area or soft asphalt can sink the stand. If the ground is soft, find a solid spot or use a pad. Do not leave the bike to fall in a hole it makes itself. Sunk into the asphalt.

questions.q: Soft dirt shoulders look convenient beside a rural road. What do you put under the stand?
options: A pad or a move to firm pavement
Nothing, if the dirt looks dry
The passenger's foot, holding the bike while you leave
A rock that can kick out from under the stand
questions.explanation: Soft ground is a bad place for a side stand. Find a solid spot or use a pad. Do not trust a loose rock, and do not leave a person as the stand. Dirt can let the stand sink.

questions.q: You park in a parallel parking space next to a curb. How does the MSF manual say to position the motorcycle?
options: Parallel to the curb, a full car length out
At an angle, with the rear wheel to the curb
With the front wheel against the curb
Across the sidewalk, clear of the road
questions.explanation: MSF manual: "If parking in a parallel parking space next to a curb, position the motorcycle at an angle with the rear wheel to the curb. (Note: Some cities have ordinances that require motorcycles to park parallel to the curb.)"

questions.q: Uphill camber that puts the left side stand on the uphill side will let the bike roll off the stand. What is the decision?
options: Park there on the center stand as well, on the same slope
Do not park there
Park there in neutral so the bike can settle
Park there and turn the wheel toward traffic
questions.explanation: If the only slope would fold the stand or roll the bike off it, do not park there. A left side stand belongs on the downhill side. Choose another spot. Find a spot where the stand is downhill or the ground is level.

questions.q: Folding stands are what a steep gutter will do to a left side stand when the lean is wrong. What should you do with that gutter?
options: Use the gutter if a passenger holds the bike
Use the gutter and point the wheel at the lane
Park where the stand can lock down on firm ground
Use the gutter if you leave the bike in neutral
questions.explanation: If the slope would fold the stand, it is not a parking place. Find firm, level pavement or a slope that puts the side stand on the downhill side, and leave the bike in gear. Leave it and park somewhere the stand can lock down on firm ground.

questions.q: Sunk stands after a hot afternoon mean the bike is lower than you left it. How do you get it out?
options: Lift it carefully onto a pad or firm ground
Ride it out in gear with the stand still down
Pull the bars toward traffic until it pops free
Leave it in neutral and roll it
questions.explanation: If the stand sank, the ground was too soft. Lift with care, use a pad or find solid pavement, and next time do not park on soft asphalt. Do not ride off with the stand down. Lift carefully, get a pad or move to firm ground, and do not yank it sideways out of a hole.

questions.q: Garage ramps are slopes even when the concrete looks clean. Where do you avoid parking the motorcycle?
options: Anywhere that is under a roof
Only on the side stand
Only in first gear
Sideways across the ramp slope
questions.explanation: A parking-garage ramp is a slope. Do not stop sideways on it, and do not stop on the grease strip in the center of a lane. Find level, firm pavement that does not stick the bike into traffic.

questions.q: Gravel aprons at a store look flat and are loose. What happens to a side stand there?
options: It can sink or slide
It digs in and becomes safer than pavement
It works if you face downhill in neutral
It works if the bars are straight
questions.explanation: Loose gravel is soft ground. Find a solid spot or use a pad. Do not leave the bike in neutral on a loose apron.

questions.q: Right-side slopes with a left-only side stand put the stand uphill. What is the likely result if you park there anyway?
options: The bike can roll off the stand or fold it
The bike will be more stable than on level ground
The center of the lane's grease will hold it
Neutral will keep it from rolling
questions.explanation: If the slope would roll the bike off the stand, do not park there. A left side stand wants the left side downhill. Find another orientation or another place.

questions.q: Cambered roads that lean the wrong way for a left side stand are common on the crown. If the left side is uphill, what do you decide?
options: To park with the wheel pointed into traffic
To park on the grease of a garage ramp instead
Not to park there
To park in neutral so the crown is gentler
questions.explanation: If the slope would roll the bike off the stand, do not park there. The side stand should be on the downhill side. A crown that lifts the stand side is the wrong spot.

questions.q: Steep hills that you could park on only by folding the stand under the bike should be handled how?
options: By leaving it in neutral so it rests harder on the stand
By pointing the wheel into traffic
By using the center stand on the same steep hill
By not parking there and finding a flatter, firmer spot
questions.explanation: If the only slope would fold the stand or roll the bike off it, do not park there. A flatter spot, in gear, stand on the downhill side when that is correct, is the park. By not parking there and walking the bike to a flatter, firmer spot if you can do that safely.

questions.q: Level concrete pads beside soft asphalt are the right choice on a hot day for which reason?
options: The concrete is always cooler for the engine
The concrete allows neutral
The concrete allows you to block a ramp
The stand will not sink the way it will in soft asphalt
questions.explanation: Prefer the solid spot. Soft asphalt can swallow a side stand, especially when hot. Use a pad if you must be on a soft surface, and still do not block a ramp or a walk.

questions.q: Multi-level garages with a slope at every stall mean some stalls are still wrong. Which ones?
options: Every stall with the key removed
Ones that fold the stand or block ramps
Every stall that uses a side stand
Every stall in gear
questions.explanation: A garage ramp is a slope. If that slope would fold the stand or roll the bike off it, do not park there. Do not block the curb ramp. Level, firm, in gear, key out is the pattern.

questions.q: Wheel chocks you do not have are not replaced by a soft bag under the stand. What is a real substitute when pavement is soft?
options: Neutral, which reduces weight on the stand
A proper pad or a move to firm ground
A jacket under the stand
The passenger's shoe
questions.explanation: If the ground is soft, use a pad meant to support the stand or find a solid spot. A slippery jacket or a shoe can kick out. Leave the bike in gear only after it is truly supported. A bag that can squirt out.

questions.q: Driveway slopes that point the motorcycle at the street, with the only stand fold risk high, should be rejected. Where do you go?
options: Deeper into the driveway in neutral
Onto the sidewalk above the driveway
Onto the grease of the street center
To a level, firm place instead
questions.explanation: If the slope would fold the stand or send a roll into traffic, do not park there. Do not climb onto the sidewalk to solve it. Find a spot that holds the bike and leaves the walk open. To a level firm place, or a slope that puts the side stand downhill without aiming a roll at traffic.

questions.q: Uphill driveways where the left stand is downhill can be usable. What else must be true?
options: The center stand must also be down
The key must stay in
It must not fold or roll into traffic
Neutral must be selected
questions.explanation: If the left side is downhill and the stand will hold, you may park there, in gear, wheel set so a roll goes to the curb rather than the lane. If any of that fails, choose another spot. The stand must not fold, the wheel must not aim a roll into traffic, and the bike must not block the walk.

questions.q: Alley slopes that would fold the side stand toward the motorcycle are not a clever urban park. What do you do?
options: Find a spot where the stand stays down firmly
Park in the fold and leave it in neutral
Park in the fold with the key in the switch
Park across the alley mouth on the sidewalk
questions.explanation: If the slope would fold the stand, do not park there. An alley is also a travel path. Find firm level ground, in gear, without blocking a walk or a ramp. Find another spot where the stand stays down on firm ground and the bike is out of the alley traffic.

questions.q: Cemetery hills and similar quiet slopes still obey the stand rule. If the left side is uphill, what is the choice?
options: Do not use the left side stand there
Park anyway because traffic is light
Park in neutral
Park on the sidewalk above the hill
questions.explanation: Quiet does not change physics. If the slope would roll the bike off the stand, do not park there. Do not move onto the sidewalk to solve a hill. Find level ground or a slope that puts the stand downhill.

questions.q: Post-rain sand left on a lot can act like marbles under the stand. What do you do when the stand foot is in that sand?
options: Aim the wheel at the driving aisle
Move to clean firm pavement or put a real pad under the stand
Rev the engine so vibration settles the sand
Leave the bike in neutral so it can skate to a stop
questions.explanation: Sand can let the stand slip as surely as oil or ice. Find firm pavement or use a pad. Leave the bike in gear, out of the aisle, with the key in your pocket.

questions.q: Before anyone climbs on behind you, the motorcycle is still on the side stand and you are standing beside it. When may the passenger mount?
options: As the bike starts to roll so the mount feels smoother
Once the engine is running, even if the front brake is free
Only after you are seated, braced, and holding the front brake with the stand up
While you are still beside the bike so they can help you lift it
questions.explanation: The passenger mounts only when you are braced on the seat and holding the front brake. Do not let them climb on a bike that is still on the stand or already moving.

questions.q: Your passenger's boots hang in the air because this motorcycle has no passenger pegs. What is the decision?
options: Ride if they promise to keep their feet on the muffler
Ride if the trip is only around the block
Have them sit sideways and put one foot down at every stop
Do not carry them
questions.explanation: No passenger without pegs and a seat. A promise, a short trip, or a foot on the exhaust is not a substitute for footrests.

questions.q: A luggage pad sits where a passenger seat would be, and the pegs were removed for solo riding. A friend asks to ride along. What do you say?
options: No, not until a real passenger seat and pegs are on the motorcycle
Yes, if they hold your shoulders and keep their knees in
Yes, if you stay at a walking pace the whole way
Yes, if they wear the same jacket you do
questions.explanation: Same gear does not create a seat. Without a passenger seat and pegs, you do not carry a passenger.

questions.q: A child can sit on the passenger seat but cannot reach the pegs with either foot. What rule do you follow?
options: The child rides in front of you on the tank so the pegs do not matter
The child does not ride
The child rides if an adult names an age that sounds old enough
The child rides if you tell them to hook their heels on the exhaust
questions.explanation: Do not invent an age law. If the child cannot reach the pegs, the child does not ride. Do not put a child on the tank or on the exhaust. Both feet must be able to stay on the pegs.

questions.q: A tall teenager's boots rest flat on the passenger pegs, the seat is made for a passenger, and the load rating still has room. What decides the ride?
options: Whether they can hold the handlebars with you
Whether they sit on the tank where you can see them
Whether they can keep both feet on the pegs, wear full gear, and fit the load rating
A minimum age you choose for this ride even though their feet reach
questions.explanation: Do not invent an age cutoff. Feet on the pegs, a real seat, full gear, and the motorcycle's load rating are the tests. A child who cannot reach the pegs does not ride.

questions.q: The only helmet in the garage is the one you are wearing, and your passenger has a knit cap. What happens to the ride?
options: You go, because one helmet on the rider covers the bike
You trade the helmet back and forth at each stop
The passenger wears your helmet and you ride without one
It waits until the passenger has a fastened helmet and gear
questions.explanation: The passenger wears the same protection you do, including a fastened motorcycle helmet. One helmet for two people is not a plan, and a cap is not a helmet. It waits until the passenger also has a fastened motorcycle helmet and the rest of the gear.

questions.q: Your passenger's chin strap is dangling, and they say they will fasten it at the first light. What do you do before the wheels turn?
options: Fasten the helmet before you move, same as your own
Leave and let them fasten it once you are up to speed
Tuck the strap into a pocket so it does not flap
Start the ride if the helmet at least sits on their head
questions.explanation: A helmet that is not fastened is not worn. Do it before you move. Do not wait for a light, and do not leave the strap loose. Fasten the helmet before you move, as part of the same gear standard you use for yourself.

questions.q: Your passenger shows up in sandals, shorts, and a helmet, and says the evening is warm. What gear rule applies?
options: Shorts are acceptable if the route has no intersections
The same coverage as yours: jacket, pants, gloves, and boots
Warm weather drops the boot and jacket requirement for the passenger only
Sandals are acceptable if both feet stay on the pegs
questions.explanation: The passenger dresses for a slide, not for the air temperature. Same gear as the rider, including boots that cover the ankles. Pegs do not replace pants or boots.

questions.q: A bicycle helmet is offered to the passenger because it is lighter than a motorcycle helmet. What do you tell them?
options: Any hard hat is enough if the chin strap is tight
They may skip headgear if they sit behind your back
A bicycle helmet is not a substitute
A bicycle helmet is better
questions.explanation: The passenger uses a motorcycle helmet, fastened. A bicycle helmet or a hard hat is not the gear you ride in. Weight on the rear is not a reason to downgrade protection. They need a fastened motorcycle helmet like yours.

questions.q: You are about to leave with a passenger who has never been on a motorcycle. When do you give the briefing?
options: At the first merge, when the rules will feel more real
By turning your head and explaining once you are in the lane
Only if they ask a question after the ride is over
While you are still stopped, before the motorcycle moves
questions.explanation: Brief the passenger before you move: hold on, feet on the pegs, lean with the bike, and signal with a tap. Do not turn around to teach once you are rolling.

questions.q: The briefing is your last chance to set the passenger's job before the motorcycle moves. Which instruction belongs in it?
options: Hold on, keep both feet on the pegs, and lean with the bike
Sit upright against the lean so the bike stays vertical in curves
Put a foot down whenever you stop so the bike cannot tip
Hold the handlebars outside your hands and help steer
questions.explanation: The passenger holds on, keeps feet on the pegs even when stopped, and leans with the bike. They do not steer, and they do not prop the bike with a foot. Hold the waist, hips, or passenger handholds, keep both feet on the pegs, and lean with the motorcycle.

questions.q: Your passenger grabs the left handlebar to feel more secure as you leave the curb. What should they hold instead?
options: The front brake lever together with you
Your waist, your hips, or the passenger handholds, never the bars
The clutch lever
The mirror stalk, which feels stronger than a handhold
questions.explanation: Hands on the bars fight the steering and can hit the clutch or the brake. The passenger holds your waist, your hips, or the handholds.

questions.q: A turn is coming and your passenger tries to stay vertical while the motorcycle leans. What should their body do?
options: Stand on the pegs so their weight stays high and still
Slide to the outside edge of the seat and hold one bar
Lean with the motorcycle, looking over your shoulder
Lean the opposite way to cancel the lean
questions.explanation: The passenger leans with the bike, not against it. Staying upright relative to the horizon is leaning the wrong way. They look through the turn with you. Lean with the motorcycle, looking over your shoulder in the direction of the turn.

questions.q: Conversation starts to matter halfway down a freeway on-ramp. How do you handle the question they shouted?
options: Slow on the ramp and talk while you ride the fog line
Have them lean the bike upright so talking is easier
Wait until you are stopped in a safe place
Turn your head for a second and answer before the merge
questions.explanation: Do not look back while moving, including on a ramp. Talk at a stop. In the merge they hold on, keep feet on the pegs, and lean with you.

questions.q: Solo, your following gap feels comfortable, and today a passenger is on the back with the bags empty. What changes about the stop?
options: Use the same gap and squeeze the brakes harder at the very end
Ride closer so the passenger can draft behind your helmet
Coast in neutral from farther back so the stop feels gentler
Start braking earlier and leave more following space
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight. Stops take longer, so you add following distance and begin braking sooner. Do not erase the gap and do not coast in neutral. The extra weight lengthens the stop.

questions.q: A curve you usually enter briskly is ahead, and a passenger is aboard for the first time. How should the entry change?
options: Slower than your solo entry, with the braking finished while you are still upright
Faster, so the extra weight stabilizes the motorcycle
The same speed, with a deeper lean to make up the difference
The same speed if the passenger has been told to lean opposite the turn
questions.explanation: Enter curves slower with a passenger, and finish serious braking before you lean. Extra weight does not let you go faster, and a wrong lean is not a technique.

questions.q: The passenger's helmet is on, but they have no eye protection and the bike has no windshield. What belongs on their face?
options: A very dark lens even though the ride will finish after sunset
Eye protection, as part of the same gear you wear, before you leave
Nothing, if they are willing to squint
Sunglasses held in one hand so they can pocket them in traffic
questions.explanation: The passenger gets the same eye protection you do. An open face at speed hurts. If the ride will end in the dark, choose clear protection rather than a dark lens.

questions.q: At a red light the passenger starts to put both feet down to help you balance. What should their feet do?
options: Hook the curb when you are first in line
Stay on the pegs even while stopped
Come down at every light so the bike has extra points of contact
Rest on the exhaust so their knees do not cramp
questions.explanation: The passenger's feet stay on the pegs at stops. Your feet hold the bike. Their feet on the ground can get caught or pull the bike when you leave.

questions.q: The light turns green and the passenger shifts hard to one side as you launch. What should have been set before you moved?
options: A harder launch so their weight sticks to the seat
A stop in the intersection so they can resettle
A briefing to stay centered, then a smooth launch
A look back to center them while you cross the intersection
questions.explanation: Brief them before you move: stay centered, hold on, feet on the pegs. Leave smoothly. Do not look back in the intersection, and do not use a hard launch to pin them down.

questions.q: A sportbike still wears the solo seat cowl, and the passenger pegs fold but will not lock down. What has to happen before anyone rides behind you?
options: The passenger may sit on the cowl if they hold your waist
The pegs can stay folded if the passenger's legs are long
You may ride only to the end of the block as a test
A real seat goes on and the pegs lock, or no passenger
questions.explanation: No passenger without a seat and pegs that actually work. A cowl is not a seat, and pegs that will not lock are not pegs.

questions.q: Combined, you, the passenger, and their pack exceed the load rating printed for the motorcycle. What do you carry?
options: Only a combination that stays inside the load rating
All of it, because no single item felt heavy by itself
All of it if you add air until the tires look round from behind
All of it if the passenger stands on the pegs over the bumps
questions.explanation: A passenger plus cargo can be too much even when each part seemed small. Follow the load rating. Do not invent a pound limit or judge the load by how the tires look. Leaving the pack or the passenger.

questions.q: The swingarm sticker shows a higher rear pressure for a loaded ride, and you are about to ride two-up on cold tires. What do you set?
options: Whatever a car tire of a similar width would use
The loaded number printed on the motorcycle, checked cold
The solo number
A number above the sticker so the bike cannot squat
questions.explanation: Set the pressure the manufacturer printed for a load, cold, before the two-up ride. Do not invent a higher number and do not borrow a car habit.

questions.q: The passenger has ridden many times, but never with you and never on this motorcycle. Do you still brief them?
options: Only if they look nervous at the first curve
You can brief them by looking back once you are on the road
Yes, before you move
No, because experience replaces the briefing
questions.explanation: Even an experienced passenger gets a briefing before you move: where to hold, feet on the pegs, lean with the bike, and how to signal. Do not look back to do it. This bike and this rider are new to them.

questions.q: You feel the passenger bounce on the pegs to change position while you are leaned over. What do you do now?
options: Slow gently, keep your eyes on the exit, and talk only after you stop
Let the bounce continue as long as they hold your shoulders
Look down at the pegs and correct them in the lean
Match the bounce with a throttle blip so the bike stays loose
questions.explanation: The passenger does not bounce or stand up in a curve. Slow gently, finish the curve, and reset at a stop. Do not look down at the pegs while leaned.

questions.q: A friend on the back wants a photo as you ride past a sign they like. What is the photo plan?
options: They stand on the pegs so the shot is clearer
The photo waits until you are stopped
They may twist at the waist for a second if one hand stays on you
You look back to smile at the same moment they take it
questions.explanation: Do not look back while moving, and the passenger does not twist, stand, or handle a camera on the move. Stop if you want a picture. They hold on and leave the camera alone while you move.

questions.q: The passenger says they get nervous unless the motorcycle stays perfectly upright in every curve. What do you tell them before you move?
options: The bike must lean to turn, and they must lean with it
You will keep it upright and steer only with the bars at speed
They should lean the opposite way so the bike can lean less
You will skip every curve by riding in a straight line only
questions.explanation: A motorcycle leans to turn. The passenger leans with it. If they cannot accept that after a briefing, they should not be on the bike.

questions.q: During the briefing the passenger jokes that they will balance you by leaning out of every turn. What do you correct?
options: Leaning out is correct if they keep at least one foot on a peg
They lean with the bike
Leaning out is the right help at every speed, including the highway
Leaning out is correct if they warn you first by shouting
questions.explanation: Leaning the wrong way fights the turn. Correct it in the briefing before you move. A shout mid-corner is not a technique, and a foot off the peg is another mistake. Against it; leaning out is the mistake, not the help.

questions.q: A group ride is leaving, and your passenger has not heard what you need from them. What do you cover before you roll?
options: Only the route
That they should watch the rider behind you and lean toward that bike
The usual briefing, including that you won't turn to talk
Nothing more, because the group leader's talk replaces yours
questions.explanation: Group or not, brief the passenger before you move. The leader's route talk does not replace hold on, feet on the pegs, and lean with the bike. The same passenger briefing, including that you will not turn around to talk once you are moving.

questions.q: The passenger is heavier than you expected, and the motorcycle squats onto the suspension stops. What does that mean?
options: Go anyway if you avoid bumps and keep the turns gentle
Go if the passenger leans forward over your shoulders
Add air past the sticker until the stops separate by eye
The load is too much; reduce passenger or cargo weight
questions.explanation: If the bike sits on the stops, the load is too big. Follow the load rating. Do not invent a pressure past the sticker, and do not hang the passenger over your shoulders.

questions.q: A parent asks you to carry a small child in front of you, between your arms, because the bike has no passenger pegs. What do you refuse?
options: The whole idea: nobody rides in front of you, and no child rides who cannot reach passenger pegs
Only the part where the child holds the bars, which you replace with your own hands over theirs
Only rides that leave the neighborhood, which you replace with a loop of the block
Only the helmet
questions.explanation: Do not carry anyone in front of you on the tank, and do not carry a child who cannot reach the pegs. No pegs means no passenger. Do not invent an age that makes an exception.

questions.q: The passenger seat and pegs are real, and a young rider's feet plant firmly on those pegs. A relative blocks the ride with an age they just made up. What matters?
options: Whether you can ride one-handed and hold them with the other
Feet on the pegs, complete gear, and the load rating
The made-up age, which you treat as if it were the law
Whether the young rider can see over the top of your helmet
questions.explanation: Do not invent an age law. Feet on the pegs, a real seat, full gear, and the motorcycle's load rating decide it. One-handed riding is not a way to carry anyone.

questions.q: Before you move you see the passenger's right foot on the peg and the left foot still on the ground. What do you do?
options: Have them drag the left foot for balance until the first turn
Look back as you launch so you can watch the left foot come up
Stay stopped until both feet are on the pegs, and only then leave
Leave, and let the left foot find the peg once you are moving
questions.explanation: Confirm both feet are on the pegs before you move. Do not launch and hope, do not drag a foot, and do not look back to supervise the start.

questions.q: The passenger's hands are on your shoulders, and they are steering you like a cart. Where should those hands move?
options: To the grips, outside your hands, so steering is shared
To the mirror stalks
To the front brake reservoir
To your waist, your hips, or the passenger handholds
questions.explanation: The passenger holds waist, hips, or handholds. Hands that steer your shoulders, or hands on the bars, change the steering. Set this before you move. They cannot steer the motorcycle.

questions.q: A backrest is fitted, and the passenger uses it to stay upright while you lean into a curve. What do you want instead?
options: They may touch the backrest, but their body still leans with the motorcycle
They should press the backrest so the bike stays vertical through the curve
They should lean the opposite way and let the backrest catch them
They should turn around and sit facing the backrest for the curves
questions.explanation: A backrest is not a reason to resist the lean. The passenger still leans with the bike, feet on the pegs, holding on.

questions.q: The passenger says they have ridden before and refuses a helmet because the trip is three blocks. What is your answer?
options: A bicycle helmet is enough for three blocks and no farther
You will carry the spare helmet and hand it over if you see enforcement
No fastened motorcycle helmet means no ride, even for three blocks
Three blocks is short enough to skip the helmet and the boots
questions.explanation: Distance does not change the gear. The passenger wears a fastened motorcycle helmet and the rest of the gear, or they do not get on.

questions.q: Your jacket, pants, gloves, and boots are on, and the passenger has a fastened helmet with shorts. Is the gear matched?
options: Yes, because the helmet is the only piece that matters for the person on the back
Yes, if they sit close enough that your jacket covers their legs
Yes, if you promise to keep the pace low in the neighborhood
No; match the coverage, including pants, jacket, gloves, and boots, not the helmet alone
questions.explanation: Same gear means helmet, eyes, jacket, pants, gloves, and over-the-ankle boots. A helmet alone does not cover their legs.

questions.q: You finish the briefing, and the passenger still cannot say where to hold, what their feet do, or which way to lean. What do you do?
options: Stay parked and repeat it until they can follow it, or do not take them
Leave, because the briefing only has to be spoken, not understood
Leave, and quiz them by looking back at the first stop sign
Have them hold the bars so the details matter less
questions.explanation: A briefing they cannot repeat is not done. Hold point, feet on the pegs, lean with the bike. Do not roll, and do not test them by turning your head.

questions.q: Heat is coming off the right-side exhaust as you brief the passenger. What do you tell them about their legs?
options: Stand on the pegs whenever you are stopped so the pipes can cool
Keep both feet on the pegs and both legs in, off the pipes, even when you are stopped
Rest the right calf on the muffler so the foot can relax at lights
Put the right foot down at every stop and leave the left foot on the peg
questions.explanation: Feet stay on the pegs and legs stay off the exhaust, including at stops. The passenger does not use the pipe as a rest and does not stand up on the pegs.

questions.q: The passenger's backpack is high and heavy, and the bike feels top-heavy in a slow turn. An empty side case is available. What do you change?
options: Hang the backpack from the handlebar so the height comes off their shoulders
Have them hold the backpack in front of your arms
Leave the pack, and lean more on every turn to cancel the height
Move the heavy items into the lowest bag, and leave only a light layer on their back
questions.explanation: Heavy items belong in the lowest bags. A high pack raises the center of gravity. Do not hang it from the bars or carry it in their arms.

questions.q: You and the passenger stay inside the load rating only if the side cases stay home. The passenger needs the ride. What do you leave?
options: The cases, to stay inside the load rating
Nothing, as long as the first mile stays slow
The passenger's helmet
The pegs, because that metal is optional weight
questions.explanation: Passenger plus cargo can exceed the rating. Leave the optional cargo. Do not remove a helmet or the pegs. The cases, so you and the passenger remain inside the motorcycle's load rating.

questions.q: The passenger's helmet slides forward over their eyes when you test a gentle stop in the lot. What do you fix before any road ride?
options: The fit and the strap, while stopped, until the helmet stays put, or they do not ride
Nothing, if they can push the helmet back with one hand as you ride
The strap routed behind the head, which feels more comfortable
A faster stop
questions.explanation: A helmet that slides over the eyes is not fitted and not fastened correctly. Fix it while stopped. Do not ride while they hold it.

questions.q: Night is close, and the passenger's only eye protection is a very dark sunglass lens. What should they wear instead for this ride?
options: Your spare dark shield stacked on top of the sunglasses
Clear eye protection, put on before it gets dark
The dark lens
No lens at all, so more light reaches their eyes
questions.explanation: In the dark, a dark lens hides the road. The passenger uses clear eye protection, just as you should use a clear shield. Do not stack dark lenses.

questions.q: A second friend wants to sit behind the passenger on a motorcycle with one passenger seat and one pair of pegs. What is the limit?
options: Two people, if you agree to stay in first gear the whole way
Two people, if their combined weight is under a number you guess
One passenger on that seat, with feet on the pegs
Two people, if the rear one holds the first person's shoulders
questions.explanation: One seat and one set of pegs means one passenger. Do not stack people, and do not invent a weight number to justify it. The second person does not ride.

questions.q: Someone offers a child who cannot reach any pegs a spot squeezed between you and the passenger. What do you do?
options: Accept, if the child holds onto your jacket with both hands
Accept, for a single slow loop of an empty parking lot
Accept, if all three of you agree to lean together
Refuse; that child cannot reach pegs, and there is no extra riding position
questions.explanation: A child who cannot reach the pegs does not ride. Do not invent a middle seat. The passenger belongs on the passenger seat with feet on the pegs.

questions.q: Rain starts, and the passenger's boot soles are wet on the pegs. How do you change the rest of the ride?
options: Both boots dragging on the pavement for extra stability
A higher pace so you spend less time on the wet road
More space, slower corners, and a reminder about the pegs
More looks back to see whether a foot has slipped
questions.explanation: Wet pavement and a passenger mean longer stops and slower entries. Feet stay on the pegs. Do not look back, and do not use boots as skids. More following space, slower corner entries, and a stop to remind them both feet stay on the pegs.

questions.q: You want the passenger to watch for a landmark at the next turn. When do you tell them which landmark?
options: As you lean into the previous curve, with a quick look back
By pointing with your clutch hand while you are shifting
By twisting your shoulders at speed so they can see your face
Before you move, or at a later stop
questions.explanation: Route talk happens in the briefing or at a stop. Do not look back while moving, and do not take a hand off the controls to point out a landmark. Not by turning your head on the way there.

questions.q: Brand-new boots are so bulky the passenger cannot feel the pegs and keeps missing them. What test do you use?
options: If they miss the pegs, they may stand on your heels instead
If they miss the pegs, one short neighborhood ride is still allowed
If they can't keep both feet on the pegs, they don't ride
If the boots are tall enough, the pegs become optional
questions.explanation: The rule is feet on the pegs. If the boots will not stay planted, fix that before the ride. Your heels are not their footrests. If they cannot reliably keep both feet on the pegs, they do not ride until the setup works.

questions.q: The passenger holds one grab rail and waves at traffic with the free hand, shifting the bike each time. What do you want?
options: Both hands on you or the holds, with waving saved for a stop
The waving, because being noticed matters more than holding on
The waving, if they drop one foot for balance while they do it
A look back so you can wave with them at the same car
questions.explanation: The passenger holds on and stays centered. Waving that moves the bike can wait until you stop. Do not look back to join in.

questions.q: A downhill stop with the passenger takes longer than the same stop did yesterday solo. What do you change next time?
options: Move closer to the vehicle ahead so the hill feels shorter
Begin braking earlier, still upright, with more space ahead
Rely on engine braking alone and stay off both brakes
Look back so the passenger can brace by grabbing the bars
questions.explanation: Downhill and two-up both lengthen the stop. Brake earlier while you are straight, and add following space. The passenger does not grab the bars. The extra weight is real.

questions.q: You are braced with the front brake held, and the passenger's swing onto the seat starts to tilt the motorcycle. What does that tilt mean?
options: They should hurry and jump the rest of the way on before it falls
They should remount from a short run so momentum holds the bike up
You should put the side stand down and twist the throttle while they climb
The brace was not ready
questions.explanation: If the bike tilts during the mount, reset: seated, braced, front brake held, stand up, then a calm mount. Do not rush it, and do not twist the throttle on the stand. Reset both feet and the brake, and mount again only when the bike is steady.

questions.q: The bike rolls because you released the front brake before the passenger's feet were on the pegs. What order do you use next time?
options: Keep the brake held through the mount until both feet are on the pegs and you are ready to ride
Release the brake so they can find the pegs while the bike creeps
Release the brake and look back to supervise their feet
Hold only the rear brake, with your right foot off the ground the whole time
questions.explanation: Keep the front brake held while they mount and settle their feet. Do not roll during the mount, and do not look back to watch their boots.

questions.q: A loose chin strap on the passenger ticks the seat as you idle away, even though you already briefed them. What is the priority?
options: Turn your head and tell them to grab the strap while you roll
Stop, fasten it, confirm both feet on the pegs, and only then leave
Finish this block and fasten it at the next sign
Let it tick, because the briefing already mentioned helmets
questions.explanation: A fastened helmet is part of the gear, and you fix it while stopped. Do not ride with the strap loose, and do not look back to coach it.

questions.q: The passenger will ride with you every day this week, and today is the first of those days. How do you treat today?
options: As a chance to feel how fast the motorcycle is with two people
As a night loop
As a first ride: familiar streets, slower entries, more space, and a briefing before you move
As the commute you already know, at your solo pace, with the briefing optional
questions.explanation: The first day with a passenger is a familiar slow ride and a real briefing. Do not open the week with speed or darkness.

questions.q: A mirror check shows the passenger looking at a phone, with one hand off you. What do you do?
options: Leave them to it
Coach them by looking back and tapping your own helmet
Let them finish the message so they will sit still afterward
Stop safely and put the phone away before you continue
questions.explanation: The passenger holds on and does not use a phone. You do not look back to nag. Stop, then the phone goes away, then you ride. Both hands hold on while the bike moves.

questions.q: The passenger's right peg folds up as soon as a boot rests on it. What does that mean for the ride?
options: You ride if you agree to avoid right turns
You do not carry them until that peg locks and can hold a foot
You ride if the left peg works and the right foot hangs free
You ride if they hold the folded peg down with one hand
questions.explanation: Both pegs have to work. A peg that folds under a foot is not a peg. Do not hang a foot or skip turns as a workaround.

questions.q: A new passenger wants one hand on your shoulder and the other hand free for balance once you are riding. What do you set instead?
options: Both hands on your waist, hips, or the handholds once they are seated
One hand on your shoulder for the entire ride
One hand on the bars and one hand on your shoulder
One hand on a grab rail and one hand holding a shopping bag
questions.explanation: Once they are seated, both hands hold your waist, your hips, or the handholds. A mount touch on the shoulder is not the riding grip, and a bag does not get a hand.

questions.q: The load rating allows this passenger only if the high top case stays home. What do you take off the motorcycle?
options: Nothing at all, and you lean more so the high weight is less obvious
The top case
The passenger's boots, which you judge heavier than the case
The passenger pegs, to save a little metal
questions.explanation: A high top case raises the center of gravity. If it cannot come with the passenger, the case stays home. Do not remove boots or pegs to cheat the load. The passenger rides with the weight lower and inside the rating.

questions.q: Day two with the same passenger on the same bike, and they remembered the pegs yesterday. Do you skip the briefing?
options: Yes, because one successful day replaces it
Yes, if you look back once and nod
Yes, if the route is the same familiar loop as yesterday
No; a short briefing still belongs at the start
questions.explanation: Brief before you move even when they rode with you before. People forget feet, hands, and which way to lean. A look back is not the briefing. No; a short briefing before you move still belongs at the start of the ride.

questions.q: The passenger's gloves are too bulky to close on the handhold, so they grab your elbows instead. What do you change before you leave?
options: Gloves they can grip with, and hands on your waist or holds
Nothing, because elbows give them a useful say in the steering
The plan, so they hold the clutch side only
The gloves, by pocketing them and riding with bare hands
questions.explanation: They need gloves and a grip that does not steer you. Fix that while stopped. Bare hands and a grip on your elbows are the wrong compromise. Gloves they can actually hold with, and hands on your waist, hips, or the handholds.

questions.q: A cone on the inside of the U-turn has your eyes stuck to it. Where do you put your eyes instead?
options: On the exit, with the cone in your peripheral view
On the cone, so you keep a constant gap from it
On the front tire
On the friend who is standing right beside that cone
questions.explanation: You ride toward what you look at. Staring at the cone pulls you into it. Look through to the exit, and keep the clutch and rear brake steady. On the exit of the turn, with the cone only in your peripheral vision.

questions.q: The motorcycle has just begun to roll in a slow slalom and you are balanced. Where do both feet go?
options: Out onto the passenger pegs so your knees can shove the bike
Onto the pegs, and they stay there until you are actually stopped
Dragging along the pavement for the entire slalom
One on a peg and one walking beside the motorcycle
questions.explanation: Once you are moving and balanced, both feet belong on the pegs. Dragging a foot can catch an ankle and makes the turn worse. A foot comes down when you stop, not as a skid.

questions.q: Loose gravel covers the driveway apron, and you are still leaned over from the turn that brought you there. How do you cross?
options: Look down at the gravel and paddle across with both feet
Straighten first and cross upright at a steady creep, without a front-brake grab
Stay leaned so the tire cuts a path through the stones
Squeeze the front brake hard while the bike is still on its side
questions.explanation: Cross gravel upright, not leaned, with a steady clutch and no front-brake grab. Keep your eyes up. Feet go to the pegs once you are moving.

questions.q: You are about to turn left at a walking pace inside the practice box. What leads the motorcycle into the turn?
options: Your head and eyes, turned toward the exit before the bike follows
A hard look down at the left cone
A shove on the inside grip while you stare at the tank
A foot stuck out on the inside as a pivot
questions.explanation: Look through the turn first. Head and eyes go to the exit, then the bike follows, with the friction zone and rear brake controlling speed. Do not pivot on a foot or stare at the cone.

questions.q: Each cone in the weave is getting your full attention, and the gaps are surprising you. Where should your eyes be?
options: On a helper's hands beside the last cone
Farther ahead, on the next opening
On the cone closest to the axle so you do not clip it
On the pavement directly under the front tire
questions.explanation: Look to the next gap in the weave, not at the cone by the wheel. Peripheral vision covers the cone. Feet stay on the pegs, and speed stays in the friction zone with the rear brake. Stuck on the cone beside your front wheel.

questions.q: Dabbing a foot down on every slow turn has become your habit, even though you are not stopping. What replaces the dab?
options: One foot down for the whole circle
A higher rpm so the foot only dabs on the right
Both feet on the pegs once the bike is balanced
A longer dab
questions.explanation: Once you are moving, feet belong on the pegs. A dabbing foot can catch and it pulls your eyes down. Stop cleanly if you must put a foot down, then set up again. Both feet on the pegs as soon as the motorcycle is balanced and moving.

questions.q: A friend stands at the exit of the practice turn and waves you toward the cone instead of the gap. What do you look at?
options: The gap you intend to ride through
The friend's hands
The cone, because the wave made it the target
Your clutch hand
questions.explanation: Look where you want the motorcycle to go. A waving friend and a bright cone are both distractions. Keep the rear brake and the friction zone steady while your eyes stay on the exit gap.

questions.q: The wall at the edge of the lot is close, and your eyes stick to the bricks during the U-turn. What happens if you keep looking there?
options: Looking at the wall lets you ignore the friction zone
You ride toward the wall
The wall becomes a safe aiming point that tightens the circle correctly
Looking at the wall is right if the front brake is covered
questions.explanation: Target fixation works on walls too. Look at the exit, not the obstacle. Stay slow with the rear brake and the friction zone, and if the space is too small, stop and multi-point. Move your eyes to the exit and keep the turn slow.

questions.q: A large painted arrow fills the spot where you wanted to finish a leaned U-turn. How do you treat that paint?
options: Lean farther on the paint
Grab the front brake on the paint with the bars turned
Stare at the arrowhead so you follow it exactly
Cross it upright, or move the turn off it
questions.explanation: Paint, especially when dusty or damp, is a poor place to lean. Cross it upright with light, smooth inputs. Do not turn a U-turn into a lean across the arrow.

questions.q: The lot is wet and the stall lines are glossy. Your practice U-turn is aimed along one of those lines. What do you change?
options: Move the turn off the paint and slow before turning
Stay on the line and lean more so the tire bites the paint
Accelerate on the paint to get the lean over with
Look down at the line and drag both feet
questions.explanation: Wet paint is slick. Do not lean the slow turn on it. Slow while you are upright, then turn where the surface is better, eyes on the exit. Move the turn off the paint, stay more upright, and slow down before the bars turn.

questions.q: A round metal cover lies where your slow turn would lean hardest. How should the motorcycle meet that cover?
options: With the bars turned and the front brake applied
With your eyes on the cover until the wheel has passed it
Upright, with light hands
Leaned over, so the edge cannot catch the tire
questions.explanation: Metal covers are slick and uneven. Cross them upright with a steady friction zone, eyes beyond the cover, not locked on it. Do not lean the U-turn across the cover. In a hard lean and not with a grabbed front brake.

questions.q: A speed bump crosses the lot lane you are using to return to your start cone. How do you take the bump?
options: Leaned, so only one side of the tire climbs it
With a front-brake grab just as the wheel climbs
With a foot dragging on the bump for balance
Slow, upright, and as square to the bump as you can
questions.explanation: Take a bump slowly and upright, not in a lean and not while braking hard. Feet stay on the pegs once you are moving. Eyes look beyond the bump, not down at it. Slow, upright, and as square to the bump as you can, then resume the drill.

questions.q: The driveway lip is sharper than it looked, and you are still finishing a turn as you reach it. What should the bike's posture be on that lip?
options: Upright, after you have finished the lean, at a steady creep
Still leaned, so the peg clears the lip
Front brake on, bars turned, creeping sideways over the lip
Eyes down on the lip, clutch pulled in, coasting
questions.explanation: Finish the turn first, then cross the lip upright and slowly. Do not combine a lean, a turned front brake, or a coast with the obstacle. Look ahead, not at the lip.

questions.q: This motorcycle is new to you, and you have not felt its clutch yet. How do you find the friction zone before you join any traffic?
options: Stopped, brake held, ease the clutch out until it pulls
By dumping the clutch in traffic and remembering the stall
By copying the lever position you used on your last motorcycle
By revving hard in neutral and guessing
questions.explanation: Find the friction zone while you are stopped and holding a brake. It will not match the last bike's hand position. Do not discover it by stalling in traffic. Stopped, with a brake held, ease the clutch out until you feel the bike start to pull, then pull it back in.

questions.q: You keep missing the bite point because your fingers are set for a different motorcycle's lever. What should you trust?
options: The front brake, used as the speed control in the turn instead
The feel of this bike starting to pull, found at a stop with the brake held
The old lever angle, even if this bike stalls or lunges
A written guess about halfway out on every clutch
questions.explanation: The friction zone is a feeling on this motorcycle, not a memorized finger spot from another one. Find it stopped, brake on, then use it with the rear brake and your eyes up.

questions.q: You need to stop from a straight, slow creep, and the handlebars are pointed ahead. Which brake plan fits?
options: Both brakes, smoothly, while the motorcycle is straight
Only the front brake after you turn the bars to full lock
Only a foot on the ground, with the brakes unused
A panic grab the moment the bars leave straight ahead
questions.explanation: When you are straight and slow, use both brakes smoothly and pull the clutch in so you do not stall. The special warning is about grabbing the front brake while the wheel is turned at walking speed.

questions.q: A figure-eight is laid out with two circles, and you keep staring at the cone where the circles meet. What do you look through?
options: Your front fender
The friend timing you with a phone
The exit of the circle you are in
The meeting cone
questions.explanation: Look through each circle to its exit. The cone is peripheral. Keep low rpm, the friction zone, and the rear brake. Do not ride toward the phone or the cone.

questions.q: A cone topples into your path mid-weave. Your eyes jump to it and stay there. What should take your eyes back?
options: The fallen cone, until the tire has passed it
The clutch lever
The person who knocked it over
The clear path where you want the bike to go
questions.explanation: If you stare at the fallen cone, you ride toward it. Look to the path you want. If the path is blocked, stop cleanly rather than swerving on a grab of the front brake.

questions.q: The lot is empty and the pace will be a walk, so a friend says shorts and sneakers are enough for practice. What do you wear?
options: The same protective gear you ride in
Shorts, because a low speed cannot cause a slide
Sneakers, if you keep both feet on the pegs
A helmet only, with the jacket left on the car
questions.explanation: Practice does not soften the ground. Wear your helmet, eye protection, jacket, pants, gloves, and over-the-ankle boots. Feet still go on the pegs once you move. The pavement is the same.

questions.q: Rain has made the lot's painted arrows shiny, and your loop crosses two of them. How do you ride the paint?
options: With the front brake held as you cross each arrow at full lock
Looking down at the shine so you can dodge within the lean
Upright and slower, with smooth controls
Leaned at your usual dry angle
questions.explanation: Rain on paint is slick. Slow down, stay upright across the paint, and save the lean for better surface. Do not grab the brake with the bars turned. Leaned over and not with a sudden brake.

questions.q: A tank bag you just strapped on hits the bars before they reach the lock you need for the U-turn. What do you do before the next attempt?
options: Ride with the steering stopped where the bag starts
Force the bars until the bag moves
Hang the bag from the mirror so the tank is clear
Move or repack the bag until the bars turn fully, then practice
