questions.explanation: A slow U-turn needs steering room. If the tank bag blocks the bars, fix the bag before you practice. Do not hang it from the bars or the mirror.

questions.q: The phone map is mounted low on the tank, and the U-turn has you reading the next street. Where do your eyes belong during the turn?
options: On the exit of the turn
On the screen
On the screen if the rear brake is dragging
On the screen if a passenger is reading it too
questions.explanation: Eyes up to the exit. A low screen steals the look that steers the motorcycle. The route can wait until you are stopped and straight.

questions.q: Someone behind you calls your name in the middle of the practice circle. What do you do with your head?
options: Point it at them while you hold full lock
Keep it toward the exit until you finish or stop
Snap it around to answer, then look back at the cone
Drop it to the tank so you can hear better
questions.explanation: Do not look back while the motorcycle is turning, even for a friend. Eyes stay on the exit. If you must answer, finish or stop first. Keep it turned toward the exit until the circle is finished or you have stopped.

questions.q: At a true walking pace with the bars straight, a pedestrian steps out close ahead. How do you stop?
options: A stare at the pedestrian until the bike stops itself
A foot dragged beside a turned front wheel
Clutch in, both brakes smoothly, motorcycle straight
A full-lock turn combined with a front-brake grab
questions.explanation: Straight and slow, both brakes and the clutch will stop you. Do not turn and grab. Look where you need to go, not only at the person, or you may ride toward them.

questions.q: You have been seated and paddling with the clutch out for half a parking row because the turn felt too tight. What is wrong with that?
options: It is correct if the engine is screaming
Your feet can catch, and it is not a controlled creep
It is the preferred slow ride whenever cones are present
It is correct if the front brake is locked
questions.explanation: Do not paddle along seated with the clutch engaged. Either creep with feet on the pegs, friction zone, and rear brake, or get off and walk the bike properly.

questions.q: The U-turn ends exactly where a gravel patch starts. You are still leaned as the front tire reaches the stones. What failed in the plan?
options: The front brake should come on as the stones start, bars still turned
You should look down at the stones until you are across
The lean should have finished before the gravel
The gravel is a good place to deepen the lean
questions.explanation: Separate the lean from the gravel. Finish the turn on decent surface, then cross upright. Do not brake-turn onto the stones, and do not stare down at them.

questions.q: Wet leaves are piled in the gutter at the edge of your practice circle. How do you treat the pile?
options: Aim the lean through the leaves so you learn low traction
Stop on the leaves with the front wheel turned
Use the leaves as a soft place to dab a foot at speed
Keep the lean off it; cross upright and slowly if needed
questions.explanation: Leaves are low traction. Do not lean or brake-turn on them. Cross upright if you must, with a steady creep and your eyes ahead of the pile. Keep the leaned turn off it, and cross it upright and slowly if there is no other path.

questions.q: You are stopped, the turn is to the left, and you are about to release the brake. What happens before the motorcycle moves?
options: You look back over your shoulder to set the lean
Your head turns toward the exit and the friction zone starts to pull
You stare at the left cone, then drag the inside foot
You release the front brake after the bars are at full lock and you grab it again
questions.explanation: Head and eyes lead. Find the friction zone, then feet up as soon as you are balanced. Do not start by staring at the cone or by looking back.

questions.q: Instructors keep saying to turn your head in the slow box, and you have been turning the bars first while looking at the tank. What is the sequence?
options: Foot out first, then eyes, then clutch
Front brake first, then head, then a high rpm
Head and eyes to the exit, then the bike follows
Bars first, eyes on the tank, throttle later
questions.explanation: The head turn leads the slow turn. Eyes on the exit, a little drive in the friction zone, rear brake for speed. Looking at the tank steers you short.

questions.q: Counterbalancing the slow turn, you stick a knee out toward a car parked on the inside of the circle. What is the better body position?
options: A modest upright posture, knees in, eyes on the exit
A knee against the car door so you can push off
A look at the door so you know how close the knee is
A deeper lean that puts the peg into the door
questions.explanation: Keep knees in and eyes on the exit. Do not push off a car or stare at a door. If the circle only works by hitting the car, the circle does not fit; stop and multi-point. A modest upright posture over the bike, knees in, eyes on the exit, without reaching into the car.

questions.q: The U-turn you marked starts on decent pavement and finishes on a slick of wet leaves you did not see yesterday. What do you do today?
options: Move the drill off the leaves, or cross them upright
Lean the turn across them to keep the old layout
Brake with the front lever as you reach them, bars turned
Stare at the leaves so the tire misses the shiniest spot
questions.explanation: If the exit is now leaves, do not lean there. Relocate the practice, or straighten and cross upright. Do not brake-turn on the leaves or stare at them.

questions.q: The friction zone on this bike bites farther out than you expected, and the first launch lunged. How do you rehearse the next launch?
options: Hold a high rpm and slip for a full minute
Use the front brake during a full-lock creep to dull the lunge
Stopped, brake held, ease out slowly until you feel pull
Lunge again in the aisle so the memory sticks
questions.explanation: Rehearse the friction zone at a stop with the brake on until the pull is smooth and small. Do not practice lunges in the aisle, and do not cover the mistake with a turned front brake. Stopped, brake held, ease out slowly until you just feel pull, then repeat without joining traffic.

questions.q: A helper stands in the exit gap and tells you to look at them so they can judge your head turn. Where do you actually look?
options: At their face
At the cone, which is the real test
At your own shoulder to feel the head turn
Through the exit beyond them
questions.explanation: Look through the exit, not at a person standing in it. If they are in the path, abort the turn. Head turn means eyes to where the motorcycle should go. At their face and not at the cone.

questions.q: In the picture, there is an oil slick in the center of your lane. Which path should you use to maintain the best traction?
options: Path 1 or Path 3
Path 2 only
The left shoulder
The right shoulder
questions.explanation: The center of the lane (Path 2) is where oil and fluids from other vehicles collect; using the tire tracks (Path 1 or 3) provides better traction.

questions.q: You are the motorcycle labeled You. Car A is waiting to turn left across your path. What should you do?
options: Speed up to pass quickly
Slow down and be prepared to stop
Maintain speed and honk your horn
Move into the left-turn lane
questions.explanation: Drivers turning left often fail to see motorcycles; slowing down and preparing to react is the safest approach at intersections.

questions.q: In the picture, there is gravel scattered across the road ahead. How should you handle this hazard?
options: Lean the bike more to turn quickly
Brake hard while on the gravel
Slow down before reaching the gravel
Shift to a higher gear and accelerate
questions.explanation: Gravel reduces traction significantly; you should reduce your speed before reaching the hazard and avoid sudden changes in direction or speed while on it.

questions.q: You are the motorcycle labeled You. Why is your current position relative to Car A dangerous?
options: You are following too closely
You are in a head-on collision path
You are blocking the intersection
You are in the driver's blind spot
questions.explanation: Riding beside another vehicle puts you in their blind spot; you should either move ahead or drop back to remain visible to the driver.

questions.q: In a staggered formation, if you are the lead rider in Path 1, where should the second rider be positioned?
options: In Path 3, at least one second behind you
Directly behind you in Path 1, close up
In Path 2, right next to you
In the lane to your left
questions.explanation: A staggered formation uses Path 1 for the leader and Path 3 for the second rider to maintain safety cushions while keeping the group compact.

questions.q: You and Car A arrive at this 4-way stop at the same time. Who has the right-of-way?
options: You, because motorcycles are smaller
Car A, because it is to your right
You, because you are going straight
Whoever accelerates the fastest
questions.explanation: At a 4-way stop, when two vehicles arrive at the same time, the vehicle on the left must yield to the vehicle on the right.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are passing a row of parked cars on your right. Which path is usually the safest?
options: Path 3, to stay close to the cars
Path 2, to stay in the center
Path 1, to stay away from opening doors
The center line of the road
questions.explanation: Riding in the left part of the lane (Path 1) provides a cushion of space from parked cars and drivers who might open their doors without looking.

questions.q: It has just started to rain. Which part of the lane is likely to be the most slippery?
options: Path 2 (the center)
Path 1 (the left)
Path 3 (the right)
The white lines on the edge
questions.explanation: When rain first starts, it mixes with oil and grease dropped by cars in the center of the lane (Path 2), making it extremely slick.

questions.q: You are riding next to a large truck (A). What is the main danger of this position?
options: The truck will speed up suddenly
You are in the truck's large blind spot
The truck's exhaust will block your vision
The truck will stop faster than you
questions.explanation: Large trucks have significant blind spots (No-Zones) on both sides; you should avoid riding alongside them for extended periods.

questions.q: You are at a T-junction and want to turn left. There are no signs or signals. Who must yield?
options: Traffic on the through road
The vehicle turning right
You, as you are on the terminating road
No one, everyone stops and goes
questions.explanation: At a T-junction, the driver on the road that ends must yield the right-of-way to vehicles on the through road.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You encounter a patch of ice on the road. What is the best way to cross it?
options: Keep the bike upright and coast straight
Brake firmly to slow down on the ice
Downshift quickly to use engine braking
Lean the bike to turn away from it
questions.explanation: On ice, any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid; keep the bike vertical and avoid braking or accelerating.

questions.q: Your group needs to pass Car A on a two-lane road. How should the pass be performed?
options: All riders pass at the same time
One rider at a time, returning to formation
The last rider passes first to clear the way
Riders should pass on the right shoulder
questions.explanation: Group members should pass one at a time when it is safe for each individual, never as a single block.

questions.q: The traffic signal turns yellow as you approach the intersection. What should you do?
options: Accelerate to beat the red light
Stop immediately, even if in the intersection
Honk to warn others you are coming through
Stop if you can do so safely
questions.explanation: A yellow light means the signal is about to turn red; you must stop unless you are so close that stopping would be unsafe.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You see a large puddle of water (A) ahead. What is the primary risk of riding through it?
options: The water will clean your tires
Hydroplaning and loss of control
The bike will speed up automatically
The water will stall the engine instantly
questions.explanation: Riding through standing water can cause tires to lose contact with the road (hydroplaning), leading to a total loss of steering and braking.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the motorcycle labeled You. Car A is waiting at a side road. How can you best ensure the driver sees you?
options: Ride in the driver's blind spot
Turn off your headlight
Use a lane position that makes you visible
Stop and wait for the car to move first
questions.explanation: Choosing a lane position that provides a clear line of sight to the driver helps ensure they see you before pulling out.

questions.q: You are the motorcycle labeled You. Is it safe or legal to share the lane side-by-side with Car A?
options: No, motorcycles need a full lane width
Yes, if the car is moving slowly
Yes, it helps reduce traffic congestion
Only if you are in a residential area
questions.explanation: Motorcycles are entitled to the full width of a lane; lane sharing with a car is unsafe and illegal in most jurisdictions.

questions.q: When a group of riders enters a sharp curve, what should they do?
options: Maintain a tight staggered formation
Move into a single-file formation
Ride side-by-side to stay close
Increase speed to finish the turn faster
questions.explanation: Riders should switch to single-file formation through curves or when visibility is poor to allow each rider their own line.

questions.q: You are the motorcycle labeled You. Where should your eyes be focused during this turn?
options: At the front tire
At the road directly in front of you
Through the turn to where you want to go
At the speedometer
questions.explanation: In a turn, you should look through the curve to the exit; the motorcycle will generally go where you are looking.

questions.q: You are approaching an intersection with a flashing red light. How should you proceed?
options: Slow down and look both ways
Stop completely and yield to cross traffic
Maintain speed if no cars are coming
Treat it as a flashing yellow light
questions.explanation: A flashing red light must be treated exactly like a stop sign; you must come to a complete stop and yield the right-of-way.

provenance.manual: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)

questions.q: You are approaching a bridge deck in cold weather. What should you expect?
options: The bridge will be warmer than the road
The bridge will have more traction
The bridge will be closed to motorcycles
The bridge may be icy even if the road is not
questions.explanation: Bridge surfaces freeze before the rest of the roadway because they are exposed to cold air from both above and below.

questions.q: In a group of riders, what is the primary responsibility of the leader?
options: To watch for hazards and signal the group
To ride as fast as possible
To stay in the back and watch everyone
To ignore traffic signs to keep the group together
questions.explanation: The lead rider is responsible for navigating, spotting hazards early, and communicating changes to the rest of the group.

questions.q: You are approaching a yield sign at an intersection. What must you do?
options: Stop only if a police officer is present
Slow down and yield to any cross traffic
Speed up to merge before other cars
Always come to a complete stop
questions.explanation: A yield sign means you must slow down and be prepared to stop if there is traffic on the intersecting road.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: The railroad tracks cross the road at a sharp angle. How should you cross them?
options: Weave to stay off the rails
Ride straight across within your lane
Turn to cross at 90 degrees, even into another lane
Brake hard while you are on the rails
questions.explanation: It is usually safer to ride straight within your lane, crossing at an angle of at least 45 degrees, than to turn across lanes to take the tracks head-on.

questions.q: You are riding past parked cars, and Car A's driver opens a door into your path. What is the best lane position here?
options: The left portion of your lane
The right portion, close to the cars
The center of the lane, near the cars
On the shoulder beside the cars
questions.explanation: When passing parked cars, ride in the left portion of the lane. You are farther from opening doors and people stepping out, and drivers pulling out can see you sooner.

questions.q: You want to change into the right lane. Car A is just behind you in that lane. What must you do?
options: Rely on your mirrors and move over
Signal and move over right away
Speed up and cut in front of Car A
Check over your shoulder and wait for a gap
questions.explanation: Mirrors do not show everything. Turn your head to check the blind spot and only change lanes when there is a safe gap.

questions.q: Truck A is passing you in the left lane. Where should you ride in your lane?
options: The right edge, on the line
On the shoulder
The center portion
The left portion
questions.explanation: When you are being passed, stay in the center portion of your lane. The left portion brings you close to the passing vehicle and its wind blast.

questions.q: At night, a deer is standing on the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Sound the horn and keep your speed
Brake and be ready to stop
Speed up to get past it
Swerve sharply onto the shoulder
questions.explanation: Large animals such as deer are unpredictable. Brake and be prepared to stop. Do not try to outrun them.

questions.q: A dog runs into the road toward you. What should you do?
options: Downshift, approach slowly, then speed away
Kick at the dog to scare it off
Stop and wait for the dog to leave
Swerve sharply across the lanes
questions.explanation: Downshift and approach the animal slowly. As you reach it, accelerate away and leave it behind. Never kick at an animal while riding.

questions.q: You can't avoid the object (A) in your path. How should you ride over it?
options: Brake hard just as you reach it
Lean the bike over and swerve at the last second
Sit down hard and close the throttle fully
Keep the bike straight and rise slightly off the seat
questions.explanation: Hold the bike upright and straight, rise slightly off the seat to absorb the shock with your knees and elbows, and keep a firm grip. Check the tires and rims afterward.

questions.q: Car A is merging from the on-ramp into your lane. What should you do?
options: Ride on the shoulder beside the ramp
Speed up to block the merge
Change lanes or adjust speed to give it room
Hold your lane and speed so A sees you
questions.explanation: Drivers on an on-ramp may not see you. Give them plenty of room by changing to another lane if one is open, or by adjusting your speed.

questions.q: You are riding at night behind Car A. How can Car A help you?
options: Its high beams light your lane best
Its taillights show bumps and curves ahead
Its headlights blind oncoming drivers for you
You can follow it closely to stay warm
questions.explanation: The car ahead's headlights show more of the road, and its taillights bouncing up and down can warn you about bumps or rough pavement.

questions.q: Car A is following you too closely. What should you do?
options: Change lanes or let it pass
Brake suddenly to warn the driver
Speed up well over the limit
Wave the driver back angrily
questions.explanation: If you can, change lanes and let a tailgater pass. If you can't, slow down and open up extra space in front so neither of you has to stop suddenly.

questions.q: You are stopped at a red light, and Car A is coming up fast behind you. What should you do?
options: Shift to neutral and relax
Look only at the traffic light ahead
Put both feet up on the pegs
Stay in first gear and watch your mirror
questions.explanation: While stopped, keep the bike in first gear and watch your mirrors, ready to move out of the way if a vehicle behind you does not stop.

questions.q: School bus A has stopped ahead in the other lane with its red lights flashing and its stop arm out. What should you do?
options: Pass quickly before children come out
Stop and wait until the lights stop flashing
Ride past slowly on your side
Stop only if children are in the road
questions.explanation: On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions stops for a school bus with red lights flashing. Wait until the lights stop and the arm is pulled in.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: It has just started to rain at this intersection. Which parts will be the most slippery?
options: The painted crosswalk and stop lines
The tire tracks in the lane
The middle of the dry lanes
The rough pavement past the lines
questions.explanation: Painted lines, crosswalks and metal covers get very slippery when wet. Avoid braking or leaning on them.

questions.q: At night, Car A is coming toward you with its high beams on. Where should you look?
options: Straight into Car A's headlights
At your speedometer
At the center line
Toward the right edge of your lane
questions.explanation: Don't look into oncoming headlights. Look toward the right edge of your lane until the vehicle has passed.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: An ambulance (A) with its lights and siren on is coming up behind you. What should you do?
options: Stop right where you are in the lane
Move to the left lane
Pull to the right edge and stop
Speed up to stay ahead of it
questions.explanation: Yield to emergency vehicles. Pull over to the right edge of the road and stop until they have passed.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)
